docs.title: Java Design Patterns Playbook
docs.text: From your first class diagram to the judgement of a 15-year principal engineer. Every GoF pattern and the modern, enterprise, concurrency and distributed patterns around them, written for Java 21 with runnable examples, trade-offs and war stories.

docs.title: Choose your path
docs.text:
• New to design patterns

    Start with what patterns are, set up Java, then learn the nine patterns you'll meet first.

    Start at L0

  • Working with patterns

    Fill in the full GoF catalogue, then learn modern Java idioms, Spring and concurrency patterns.

    Go to L2

  • Leading with patterns

    Architecture, DDD, microservices, resilience and the internals behind it all.

    Go to L4

  • Interview sprint

    Graded questions, scenarios and hands-on tasks, plus the Interview Corner on every page.

    Interview guide

docs.title: How every page is structured
docs.text:
Every topic page uses the same template, so you always know where to look:

  1. TL;DR, then What it is, Why it exists and a Mental model.
  2. How it works, with a diagram.
  3. Subtopics, each with a description, how to use it, pros, cons, a best practice and a gotcha.
  4. Three examples (minimal, realistic in the FreshCart grocery-delivery domain, production-grade), each with the exact command to run and its exact output.
  5. Pros, cons and trade-offs, when to use / when not to, best practices and pitfalls.
  6. Expert deep dive with a production war story, an interview corner, practice exercises and a quick revision card.

See How to use this playbook for learning paths.

docs.title: Further Reading
docs.text:
TL;DR

The books, specifications and references behind this playbook, grouped by level. Start with Head First Design Patterns or Effective Java if you're new, Refactoring and Java Concurrency in Practice as you grow, and the architecture and DDD books at L4 and L5. Every item here is a real, published work.

docs.title: Foundations (L0 to L2)
docs.text: Resource Why read it Erich Gamma, Richard Helm, Ralph Johnson, John Vlissides, Design Patterns: Elements of Reusable Object-Oriented Software (1994) The original catalogue of 23 patterns; read the intent and applicability sections Eric Freeman and Elisabeth Robson, Head First Design Patterns, 2<sup>nd</sup> ed. (2020) The friendliest introduction, with Java examples Joshua Bloch, Effective Java, 3<sup>rd</sup> ed. (2018) Idiomatic Java: static factories, builders, immutability, enums, lambdas Robert C. Martin, Clean Architecture (2017) SOLID principles and dependency rules explained by their author Andrew Hunt and David Thomas, The Pragmatic Programmer, 20<sup>th</sup> anniversary ed. (2019) DRY, orthogonality and everyday design judgement Steve Freeman and Nat Pryce, Growing Object-Oriented Software, Guided by Tests (2009) Designing with tests and test doubles Refactoring.Guru: Design Patterns Illustrated pattern catalogue with Java code

docs.title: Professional Java (L3)
docs.text: Resource Why read it Martin Fowler, Refactoring, 2<sup>nd</sup> ed. (2018) Safe, small steps from smells to better design Joshua Kerievsky, Refactoring to Patterns (2004) Moving towards, and away from, patterns through refactoring Brian Goetz et al., Java Concurrency in Practice (2006) Thread safety, publication and the java.util.concurrent patterns Martin Fowler, Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture (2002) Repository, unit of work, data mapper, service layer Michael Feathers, Working Effectively with Legacy Code (2004) Seams and characterisation tests Spring Framework reference documentation How Spring uses proxies, DI, templates and events JEP index The design notes behind records, sealed types, pattern matching and virtual threads

docs.title: Distributed systems and architecture (L4)
docs.text: Resource Why read it Eric Evans, Domain-Driven Design (2003) Bounded contexts, aggregates, ubiquitous language Vaughn Vernon, Implementing Domain-Driven Design (2013) Practical DDD with code Gregor Hohpe and Bobby Woolf, Enterprise Integration Patterns (2003) The messaging pattern language: channels, routers, translators, dead letters Chris Richardson, Microservices Patterns (2018) Sagas, outbox, API gateway, CQRS with Java examples Sam Newman, Building Microservices, 2<sup>nd</sup> ed. (2021) Service boundaries and the cost of distribution Michael T. Nygard, Release It!, 2<sup>nd</sup> ed. (2018) Stability patterns: timeouts, circuit breakers, bulkheads Martin Kleppmann, Designing Data-Intensive Applications (2017) Replication, consistency, streams and the theory behind the patterns Resilience4j documentation Configuration of the resilience patterns used here Caffeine wiki Eviction, refresh and caching behaviour in Java

docs.title: Staff and principal (L5)
docs.text: Resource Why read it Neal Ford, Rebecca Parsons, Patrick Kua, Pramod Sadalage, Building Evolutionary Architectures, 2<sup>nd</sup> ed. (2022) Fitness functions and guided change Mark Richards and Neal Ford, Fundamentals of Software Architecture (2020) Architecture characteristics and trade-off analysis Neal Ford et al., Software Architecture: The Hard Parts (2021) Decomposition and distributed data trade-offs Jaroslav Tulach, Practical API Design (2008) Designing Java APIs that can evolve Matthew Skelton and Manuel Pais, Team Topologies (2019) Aligning teams and architecture Tanya Reilly, The Staff Engineer's Path (2022) Technical leadership beyond one team The Java Language Specification and The Java Virtual Machine Specification (docs.oracle.com/javase/specs) Binary compatibility (JLS 13), the memory model (JLS 17), class initialisation (JLS 12.4) Aleksey Shipilëv, JMM Pragmatics A practical tour of the Java Memory Model Michael Nygard, Documenting Architecture Decisions (2011) The original ADR format

docs.title: Interview preparation
docs.text: Resource Why read it Alex Xu, System Design Interview, volumes 1 and 2 (2020, 2022) Structured approach to high-level design rounds This playbook's Interview Guide Round types, level expectations and practice tasks

docs.title: How to keep learning
docs.text:
• Re-read one GoF pattern a week and find it in code you use (the JDK, Spring, your own services).
  • Write an ADR for your next design decision and review it three months later.
  • Run the playbook's examples, then break them: remove a timeout, drop volatile, publish before commit, and watch what happens.

docs.title: Glossary
docs.text:
TL;DR

Every term used in the playbook, alphabetically, with a one-line definition and a link to the page that explains it. Acronyms also show as tooltips when you hover over them on any page.

docs.title: A
docs.text: Abstract Factory A creational pattern that creates families of related objects through one interface. Page ACL (anti-corruption layer) A translation layer that keeps another system's model from leaking into yours. DDD Strategic Adapter Converts one interface into another that clients expect. Page ADR (architecture decision record) A short document recording a decision, its context, the options and the consequences. Choosing Patterns Aggregate A cluster of domain objects treated as one unit for consistency, changed only through its root. DDD Tactical Anemic domain model Domain classes with data but no behaviour, with all logic in services. Usually an anti-pattern. Anti-Pattern Catalogue AOP (aspect-oriented programming) Applying cross-cutting behaviour (transactions, logging) around methods, in Java usually through proxies. Patterns in Spring API gateway A single entry point that routes, authenticates and aggregates requests to backend services. Microservice Patterns ArchUnit A Java library for writing architecture rules as unit tests. Evolutionary Architecture At-least-once delivery A messaging guarantee where a message may arrive more than once but is never lost; consumers must be idempotent.

docs.title: B
docs.text: BFF (backend for frontend) An API layer tailored to one client, such as the mobile app. UI and Mobile Patterns Binary compatibility Whether code compiled against an older library version still links and runs with a newer one. Designing Frameworks and Libraries Bounded context A boundary within which one domain model and its language apply consistently. DDD Strategic Branch by abstraction Replacing an implementation behind an interface inside one codebase, switching gradually. Legacy Modernisation Bridge Separates an abstraction from its implementation so both can vary independently. Page Builder Constructs complex objects step by step. Page Bulkhead Isolates resources (threads, connections) per dependency so one failure can't exhaust everything. Resilience Patterns

docs.title: C
docs.text: Cache stampede Many requests loading the same expired key at once, overloading the source. Caching Patterns Cache-aside The application reads from the cache, loads from the database on a miss and stores the result. Caching Patterns CDC (change data capture) Streaming database changes from the transaction log as events. Distributed Data Patterns Chain of Responsibility Passes a request along a chain of handlers until one handles it. Page Characterisation test A test that records what existing code does today, used as a safety net before refactoring. Legacy Modernisation Circuit breaker Stops calling a failing dependency for a while after too many failures, then probes it. Resilience Patterns Class loader The JVM component that loads classes; a class's identity is its name plus its loader. JVM Internals Command Encapsulates a request as an object, enabling queues, logging and undo. Page Competing consumers Several consumers reading from one queue to share the work. Messaging Patterns Composite Treats individual objects and groups of objects uniformly. Page Context map A diagram of bounded contexts and the relationships between them. DDD Strategic CQRS Separating the model that handles writes from the model that serves reads. Distributed Data Patterns

docs.title: D
docs.text: Dead letter channel A queue or topic for messages that can't be processed after retries. Messaging Patterns Decorator Adds behaviour to an object by wrapping it with the same interface. Page Dependency injection Supplying an object's collaborators from outside instead of creating them inside. Page Domain event A record of something that happened in the domain, such as OrderPaid. DDD Tactical Double-checked locking Lazy initialisation that checks a field before and after locking; correct in Java only with volatile. Concurrency Patterns DRY Don't Repeat Yourself: every piece of knowledge has one authoritative representation. DRY, KISS, YAGNI

docs.title: E
docs.text: Entity A domain object defined by its identity rather than its attributes. DDD Tactical Event sourcing Storing state as the sequence of events that produced it. Distributed Data Patterns

docs.title: F
docs.text: Facade A simplified interface to a complex subsystem. Page Factory Method Lets a method or subclass decide which class to instantiate. Page Fallback A degraded response used when a dependency fails. Resilience Patterns Feature toggle A switch that enables or disables a code path at run time. Legacy Modernisation Fitness function An automated check that an architectural characteristic still holds. Evolutionary Architecture Flyweight Shares immutable state between many objects to save memory. Page

docs.title: G
docs.text: Gang of Four Gamma, Helm, Johnson and Vlissides, authors of Design Patterns (1994), which catalogued 23 patterns. What Are Design Patterns God class A class that knows or does too much. Anti-Patterns and Code Smells

docs.title: H
docs.text: Happens-before The Java Memory Model relation that guarantees one action's effects are visible to another. JVM Internals Hexagonal architecture Ports and adapters: the domain at the centre, with infrastructure plugged in through interfaces. Architectural Patterns

docs.title: I
docs.text: Idempotency key A client-supplied key that lets a server recognise and safely ignore repeated requests. API Design Patterns Idempotent consumer A message consumer that produces the same result if a message is delivered more than once. Messaging Patterns Interpreter Represents a grammar as classes and evaluates sentences in it. Page Inversion of control The framework calls your code, instead of your code calling the framework. Designing Frameworks and Libraries invokedynamic A JVM instruction whose call target is linked at run time by a bootstrap method; used for lambdas. JVM Internals Iterator Accesses elements of a collection sequentially without exposing its structure. Page

docs.title: J
docs.text: JPMS The Java Platform Module System (Java 9+): modules declare what they export and require. Evolutionary Architecture

docs.title: K
docs.text: KISS Keep It Simple: prefer the simplest design that works. DRY, KISS, YAGNI

docs.title: M
docs.text: Mediator Centralises communication between objects so they don't refer to each other directly. Page Memento Captures an object's state so it can be restored later without exposing internals. Page Modular monolith One deployable application divided into modules with enforced boundaries. Architectural Patterns MVVM Model-View-ViewModel: the ViewModel exposes screen state and logic that the view observes. UI and Mobile Patterns

docs.title: N
docs.text: Null Object A do-nothing implementation used instead of null. Page

docs.title: O
docs.text: Object Pool Reuses expensive objects instead of creating new ones. Page Observer Notifies dependents automatically when a subject changes. Page

docs.title: P
docs.text: Parallel run Running old and new implementations side by side and comparing results before switching. Legacy Modernisation Prototype Creates objects by copying an existing instance. Page Proxy A placeholder that controls access to another object. Page

docs.title: R
docs.text: Ratchet A check that allows existing violations but fails on new ones, so the count only goes down. Evolutionary Architecture Rate limiter Limits how many calls are made in a period. Resilience Patterns Record A Java class (16+) for immutable data with generated constructor, accessors, equals, hashCode and toString. Patterns in Modern Java Reference implementation A real, running example of the approved way to build something. Governing Patterns Repository A collection-like interface for loading and saving aggregates. DDD Tactical Retry with backoff and jitter Retrying failed calls with growing, randomised delays so clients don't retry in sync. Resilience Patterns Rule of three Extract an abstraction only when the third real variation appears. Choosing Patterns

docs.title: S
docs.text: Safe publication Making an object visible to other threads only after it's fully constructed, via final fields, volatile, locks or static initialisation. JVM Internals Saga A sequence of local transactions with compensating actions instead of one distributed transaction. Distributed Data Patterns Sealed type A class or interface (Java 17+) that lists its permitted subtypes, enabling exhaustive switches. Patterns in Modern Java Semantic versioning MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH, where MAJOR means breaking changes. Designing Frameworks and Libraries Service discovery Finding the network location of service instances at run time. Microservice Patterns Service locator Looking up dependencies from a global registry; usually replaced by dependency injection. Dependency Injection ServiceLoader The JDK mechanism that discovers SPI implementations at run time. Designing Frameworks and Libraries Sidecar A helper process deployed next to a service to add capabilities such as proxies or log shipping. Microservice Patterns Singleton Ensures a class has exactly one instance with a global access point. Page SOLID Five object-oriented design principles: SRP, OCP, LSP, ISP, DIP. Page Specification A business rule as a composable predicate object. Page SPI (service provider interface) An interface a library defines for others to implement. Designing Frameworks and Libraries State Lets an object change behaviour when its internal state changes. Page Strangler fig Replacing a system piece by piece by routing features to the new implementation. Legacy Modernisation Strategy Defines interchangeable algorithms behind one interface. Page

docs.title: T
docs.text: Technical debt Design or code shortcuts whose ongoing cost (interest) grows until fixed (principal). Governing Patterns Template Method Defines an algorithm's skeleton and lets subclasses fill in steps. Page Test double Any stand-in for a real dependency in tests: dummy, stub, spy, mock or fake. Testing Patterns Timeout An upper limit on how long to wait for a response. Resilience Patterns Tolerant reader A consumer that ignores unknown fields so producers can add data without breaking it. API Design Patterns Transactional outbox Writing events to an outbox table in the same transaction as the state change, then publishing them. Distributed Data Patterns

docs.title: U
docs.text: Ubiquitous language Shared vocabulary between developers and domain experts within a bounded context. DDD Strategic

docs.title: V
docs.text: Value object An immutable object defined by its attributes, such as Money. DDD Tactical VarHandle A typed reference to a variable with atomic and memory-ordering operations (Java 9+). JVM Internals Virtual thread A lightweight JVM-managed thread (Java 21) that makes blocking code cheap. Concurrency Patterns Visitor Adds operations to a class hierarchy without changing its classes. Page

docs.title: W
docs.text: Write-behind Writing to the cache immediately and to the database later in batches. Caching Patterns

docs.title: Y
docs.text: YAGNI You Aren't Gonna Need It: don't build for imagined future needs. DRY, KISS, YAGNI

docs.title: Learning paths
docs.text: You are… Read Skip or skim New to Java design L0 → L1 → L2 in order, doing the Practice section on every page Expert Deep Dive until your second pass A working Java developer (1–3 yrs) L1 quickly, then L2 and L3 L0 A senior engineer or tech lead L3 → L4 → L5, and the Reference section L0–L1, except the Expert Deep Dive on each page Preparing for interviews The Interview Corner on each page, then the Interview guide Long examples

docs.title: Anatomy of a page
docs.text: Each topic page has the same numbered sections: TL;DR, What It Is, Why It Exists, Mental Model, How It Works, Subtopics, Examples, Pros/Cons & Trade-offs, When to Use / Not Use, Best Practices, Pitfalls, Configuration & Tuning, Security, Performance, Testing, Observability, Version Notes, Expert Deep Dive, Interview Corner, Practice, Quick Revision Card and Further Reading. Sections that don't apply to a topic are left out rather than left empty.

docs.title: Running the examples
docs.text:
All examples target Java 21 and are single-file programs, so you don't need a build tool:

java ShippingCostDemo.java

The same programs live in examples/ in the repository. CI runs every example and fails if its output no longer matches what the page shows.

docs.title: The running domain
docs.text: Realistic examples use FreshCart, an imaginary grocery delivery company with customers, orders, baskets, products, stores, riders and delivery slots. The same names appear on every page and in the capstone project.

docs.text:
• !!! warning "Verify against the official docs" marks anything you should double-check for your exact JDK or library version.
  • Opinions are labelled as opinions; industry consensus is labelled as consensus.

docs.title: L0 · Orientation
docs.text:
Experience: Day 0 · Pages: 4 · Open level

You're ready for the next level when you can:

  • Explain what a design pattern is and name the three GoF categories
  • Run a single-file Java 21 program from the terminal
  • Read a class diagram and a sequence diagram

docs.title: L1 · Foundations
docs.text:
Experience: 0–1 yr · Pages: 12 · Open level

You're ready for the next level when you can:

  • Apply SOLID to a small class and explain which principle you used
  • Implement Singleton, Factory Method, Builder, Strategy, Observer, Template Method, Adapter, Decorator and Facade from memory
  • Say why you would NOT use a pattern in a given piece of code

docs.title: L2 · Practitioner
docs.text:
Experience: 1–3 yrs · Pages: 19 · Open level

You're ready for the next level when you can:

  • Implement all 23 GoF patterns and pick between similar ones (Strategy vs. State, Adapter vs. Bridge)
  • Wire an application with constructor injection and no container
  • Unit test code that uses patterns with the right test doubles

docs.title: L3 · Professional
docs.text:
Experience: 3–6 yrs · Pages: 11 · Open level

You're ready for the next level when you can:

  • Rewrite classic patterns with records, sealed types, pattern matching and lambdas
  • Recognise the patterns inside the JDK and Spring and use them correctly
  • Write thread-safe code with concurrency patterns and measure a pattern's cost with JMH

docs.title: L4 · Senior / Lead
docs.text:
Experience: 6–10 yrs · Pages: 9 · Open level

You're ready for the next level when you can:

  • Choose and defend an application architecture (layered, hexagonal, modular monolith)
  • Model a domain with aggregates, value objects and bounded contexts
  • Design resilient, consistent distributed flows with sagas, outbox and circuit breakers

docs.title: L5 · Staff / Principal
docs.text:
Experience: 10–15+ yrs · Pages: 6 · Open level

You're ready for the next level when you can:

  • Set pattern standards, review checklists and fitness functions for many teams
  • Explain the JVM mechanisms behind proxies, lambdas and safe publication
  • Lead a legacy modernisation without a big-bang rewrite

docs.title: Interview Guide
docs.text:
TL;DR

Design-pattern interviews rarely ask "define Decorator". They give you a problem and watch how you find the variation, pick the simplest structure, explain the trade-offs and change your mind when constraints change. This guide explains the common round types, what each level is judged on, and how to practise with the rest of this section.

docs.title: Round types
docs.text: Round Typical prompt What it tests Practise with Concept questions "When would you choose Strategy over State?" Vocabulary and intent Questions by Level Low-level design (LLD) "Design a parking lot / a coupon engine / a cart" Class design, patterns, SOLID, testability Hands-on Tasks Live coding / refactoring "Here is a 200-line class, make it extensible" Refactoring steps, tests, naming Hands-on Tasks, Refactoring to Patterns System design (HLD) "Design grocery delivery checkout for 1M orders per day" Architecture, data consistency, resilience Scenario Questions, Capstone Incident / debugging scenario "Payments are double-charged after a deploy" Production reasoning Scenario Questions Staff behavioural / architecture "Tell me about a design decision you reversed" Judgement, influence, governance L5 pages

docs.title: What each level is judged on
docs.text: Level Interviewers look for Red flags L1 Junior Knows the common patterns by intent; writes clean classes; explains SOLID with an example Memorised UML without being able to apply it L2 Mid Picks a pattern for a stated problem; writes tests; knows when not to use one Patterns everywhere; no tests L3 Senior (individual) Combines patterns; knows Java and Spring idioms (lambdas, records, DI, proxies); discusses performance and concurrency Ignores thread safety or failure handling L4 Senior / Lead Distributed patterns (sagas, outbox, idempotency, resilience); clear trade-offs; designs for operations Hand-waves consistency; no timeouts or retries discussed L5 Staff / Principal Chooses between options with evidence; plans evolution and migration; considers teams, governance, reversibility Only one option considered; no cost or risk discussion

docs.title: A repeatable approach for design questions
docs.text:
1. Clarify the use cases, scale and what changes most often. Write them down.
  2. Model the domain with nouns and verbs; find the invariants.
  3. Find the variation points: what will differ by city, partner, customer type, or over time?
  4. Choose the simplest structure for each variation (a lambda before a class hierarchy) and name the pattern.
  5. Walk through a scenario end to end, including a failure.
  6. State trade-offs and what would make you change the design.
  7. Show how you would test it.

Say the trade-off out loud

"I'd use a Strategy here because fee rules change per city every month. If they only ever had two variants, an if would be simpler." This one sentence shows more seniority than a perfect UML diagram.

docs.title: Preparing in two weeks
docs.text: Days Focus 1–3 L1 and L2 patterns: read the TL;DR, run the examples, answer the L1–L3 questions 4–6 Hands-on tasks with a timer (45 minutes each), then compare with the solutions 7–9 Modern Java, Spring, concurrency and error-handling pages 10–12 L4 distributed patterns and scenario questions 13–14 Capstone milestones 3 to 4; mock interview with a friend

docs.title: Hands-on Tasks
docs.text:
TL;DR

Five take-home and live-coding tasks in the FreshCart domain, from L2 to L4, each with requirements, hints and a complete, runnable solution with its real output. Set a timer, write your own version and tests first, then compare.

How interviewers grade these. Working code matters, but so do: the names you choose, whether the variation point is easy to extend, tests for edge cases, and what you say about trade-offs. A short "what I'd do with more time" note at the end is always welcome.

All solutions live in examples/interview/hands-on-tasks/ and run with java <File>.java; examples/run-all.sh checks their output.

docs.title: Task 1: Coupon engine (L2, 45 minutes)
docs.text:
FreshCart has three coupons. Given a cart, return the single best coupon and how much it saves.

Code Eligible when Discount WELCOME100 First order and basket at least Rs 300 Rs 100 off (never more than the basket) DAIRY15 Cart has dairy items and basket at least Rs 200 15% off dairy items BIG5 Basket at least Rs 1000 5% off everything

Requirements: adding a coupon must not change the selection code; eligibility rules must be combinable and testable on their own; ties go to the coupon listed first.

Hints

Eligibility is a Predicate<Cart> (Specification); the discount is a small Strategy. A coupon is a record of code, predicate and discount.

Solution CouponEngineDemo.java
import java.util.List;
import java.util.function.Predicate;

/** Task 1 solution: coupon rules as composable specifications, each coupon a discount strategy. */
public class CouponEngineDemo {

    record Item(String sku, String category, long paise, int qty) { long total() { return paise * qty; } }
    record Cart(String customer, boolean firstOrder, List<Item> items) {
        long subtotal() { return items.stream().mapToLong(Item::total).sum(); }
    }

    interface Discount { long apply(Cart cart); }
    record Coupon(String code, Predicate<Cart> eligibility, Discount discount) {}

    static Predicate<Cart> minBasket(long paise) { return c -> c.subtotal() >= paise; }
    static Predicate<Cart> hasCategory(String cat) { return c -> c.items().stream().anyMatch(i -> i.category().equals(cat)); }
    static final Predicate<Cart> FIRST_ORDER = Cart::firstOrder;

    static Discount percentOff(int pct) { return c -> c.subtotal() * pct / 100; }
    static Discount percentOffCategory(String cat, int pct) {
        return c -> c.items().stream().filter(i -> i.category().equals(cat)).mapToLong(Item::total).sum() * pct / 100;
    }
    static Discount flat(long paise, long cap) { return c -> Math.min(paise, Math.min(cap, c.subtotal())); }

    static final List<Coupon> COUPONS = List.of(
            new Coupon("WELCOME100", FIRST_ORDER.and(minBasket(30000)), flat(10000, 10000)),
            new Coupon("DAIRY15", hasCategory("dairy").and(minBasket(20000)), percentOffCategory("dairy", 15)),
            new Coupon("BIG5", minBasket(100000), percentOff(5)));

    /** Picks the best eligible coupon; ties go to the coupon listed first. */
    static String best(Cart cart) {
        Coupon best = null;
        long bestValue = 0;
        for (Coupon c : COUPONS) {
            if (!c.eligibility().test(cart)) continue;
            long value = c.discount().apply(cart);
            if (value > bestValue) { best = c; bestValue = value; }
        }
        return best == null ? "no coupon applies" : best.code() + " saves Rs " + bestValue / 100.0;
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Cart small = new Cart("asha", false, List.of(new Item("MILK-1L", "dairy", 6800, 2)));
        Cart firstOrder = new Cart("dev", true, List.of(new Item("MILK-1L", "dairy", 6800, 3), new Item("RICE-5KG", "staples", 64000, 1)));
        Cart dairyHeavy = new Cart("chen", false, List.of(new Item("PANEER-200G", "dairy", 9000, 4), new Item("CURD-500G", "dairy", 4500, 2)));
        Cart big = new Cart("bilal", false, List.of(new Item("OIL-5L", "staples", 90000, 1), new Item("MILK-1L", "dairy", 6800, 5)));
        for (Cart c : List.of(small, firstOrder, dairyHeavy, big)) System.out.println(c.customer() + " (Rs " + c.subtotal() / 100.0 + "): " + best(c));
    }
}

Output:

asha (Rs 136.0): no coupon applies
dev (Rs 844.0): WELCOME100 saves Rs 100.0
chen (Rs 450.0): DAIRY15 saves Rs 67.5
bilal (Rs 1240.0): BIG5 saves Rs 62.0

Discussion points: money in paise as long, coupons as data so they could come from configuration, and why "best coupon" logic belongs in one place. Patterns: Specification, Strategy.

docs.title: Task 2: Undoable cart (L2, 45 minutes)
docs.text:
The mobile app needs undo and redo for cart edits: set a quantity (0 removes the line) and clear the cart.

Requirements: undo restores exactly the previous state, including after "clear cart"; redo works until a new edit is made; the cart class must not know about undo.

Hints

Each edit is a Command that records what it needs to reverse itself when executed. Two stacks: undo and redo. A new command clears the redo stack.

Solution CartUndoDemo.java
import java.util.ArrayDeque;
import java.util.Deque;
import java.util.Map;
import java.util.TreeMap;

/** Task 2 solution: cart edits as commands with undo and redo; each command remembers what it needs to reverse itself. */
public class CartUndoDemo {

    static final class Cart {
        final Map<String, Integer> lines = new TreeMap<>();
        int qty(String sku) { return lines.getOrDefault(sku, 0); }
        void set(String sku, int qty) { if (qty == 0) lines.remove(sku); else lines.put(sku, qty); }
        @Override public String toString() { return lines.toString(); }
    }

    interface Command { void execute(Cart cart); void undo(Cart cart); String label(); }

    record SetQuantity(String sku, int qty, int[] previous) implements Command {
        SetQuantity(String sku, int qty) { this(sku, qty, new int[1]); }
        public void execute(Cart cart) { previous[0] = cart.qty(sku); cart.set(sku, qty); }
        public void undo(Cart cart) { cart.set(sku, previous[0]); }
        public String label() { return "set " + sku + " to " + qty; }
    }

    record ClearCart(Map<String, Integer> snapshot) implements Command {
        ClearCart() { this(new TreeMap<>()); }
        public void execute(Cart cart) { snapshot.clear(); snapshot.putAll(cart.lines); cart.lines.clear(); }
        public void undo(Cart cart) { cart.lines.putAll(snapshot); }
        public String label() { return "clear cart"; }
    }

    static final class Editor {
        final Cart cart = new Cart();
        final Deque<Command> undo = new ArrayDeque<>(), redo = new ArrayDeque<>();
        void run(Command c) { c.execute(cart); undo.push(c); redo.clear(); System.out.println(c.label() + " -> " + cart); }
        void undo() { if (undo.isEmpty()) return; Command c = undo.pop(); c.undo(cart); redo.push(c); System.out.println("undo " + c.label() + " -> " + cart); }
        void redo() { if (redo.isEmpty()) { System.out.println("nothing to redo (a new edit cleared the redo stack)"); return; } Command c = redo.pop(); c.execute(cart); undo.push(c); System.out.println("redo " + c.label() + " -> " + cart); }
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Editor e = new Editor();
        e.run(new SetQuantity("MILK-1L", 2));
        e.run(new SetQuantity("CURD-500G", 1));
        e.run(new SetQuantity("MILK-1L", 5));
        e.run(new ClearCart());
        e.undo();
        e.undo();
        e.redo();
        e.run(new SetQuantity("BREAD", 1));
        e.redo();
    }
}

Output:

set MILK-1L to 2 -> {MILK-1L=2}
set CURD-500G to 1 -> {CURD-500G=1, MILK-1L=2}
set MILK-1L to 5 -> {CURD-500G=1, MILK-1L=5}
clear cart -> {}
undo clear cart -> {CURD-500G=1, MILK-1L=5}
undo set MILK-1L to 5 -> {CURD-500G=1, MILK-1L=2}
redo set MILK-1L to 5 -> {CURD-500G=1, MILK-1L=5}
set BREAD to 1 -> {BREAD=1, CURD-500G=1, MILK-1L=5}
nothing to redo (a new edit cleared the redo stack)

Discussion points: commands store only the previous value (cheap) except "clear", which stores a snapshot (Memento); limits on history size; how this maps to a ViewModel on mobile. Patterns: Command, Memento.

docs.title: Task 3: Refactor the fee calculator (L3, live, 40 minutes)
docs.text:
You are given this method and asked to make it easy to add new customer types and cities, without changing behaviour:

static long legacyFee(String customerType, String city, long basketPaise) {
    switch (customerType) {
        case "MEMBER":
            return 0;
        case "REGULAR":
            if (city.equals("Pune")) return basketPaise >= 60000 ? 0 : 3900;
            return basketPaise >= 50000 ? 0 : 2900;
        case "CORPORATE":
            if (city.equals("Pune")) return 1500;
            return 1500;
        default:
            throw new IllegalArgumentException(customerType);
    }
}

Requirements: prove the new code matches the old for boundary values before deleting it; remove the duplicated corporate branch; make invalid customer types impossible to pass.

Hints

Start with a characterisation test over customer types × cities × boundary baskets. Then introduce an enum for customer types and a small set of fee rules (free, free above a threshold, flat).

Solution FeeRefactorDemo.java
import java.util.List;

/**
 * Task 3 solution: the legacy fee calculator (a switch on strings with duplicated rules) refactored to a sealed set
 * of fee rules chosen by a factory. A characterisation check proves both versions agree on every sample before the
 * legacy code is deleted.
 */
public class FeeRefactorDemo {

    // ---- before: the code given in the task ----
    static long legacyFee(String customerType, String city, long basketPaise) {
        switch (customerType) {
            case "MEMBER":
                return 0;
            case "REGULAR":
                if (city.equals("Pune")) return basketPaise >= 60000 ? 0 : 3900;
                return basketPaise >= 50000 ? 0 : 2900;
            case "CORPORATE":
                if (city.equals("Pune")) return 1500;
                return 1500;
            default:
                throw new IllegalArgumentException(customerType);
        }
    }

    // ---- after ----
    sealed interface FeeRule permits Free, FreeAbove, Flat {
        long feePaise(long basketPaise);
    }
    record Free() implements FeeRule { public long feePaise(long b) { return 0; } }
    record FreeAbove(long thresholdPaise, long feePaise) implements FeeRule {
        public long feePaise(long b) { return b >= thresholdPaise ? 0 : feePaise; }
    }
    record Flat(long feePaise) implements FeeRule { public long feePaise(long b) { return feePaise; } }

    enum CustomerType { MEMBER, REGULAR, CORPORATE }

    static FeeRule ruleFor(CustomerType type, String city) {
        return switch (type) {
            case MEMBER -> new Free();
            case REGULAR -> city.equals("Pune") ? new FreeAbove(60000, 3900) : new FreeAbove(50000, 2900);
            case CORPORATE -> new Flat(1500);
        };
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        int checked = 0, mismatches = 0;
        for (CustomerType type : CustomerType.values()) {
            for (String city : List.of("Bengaluru", "Pune")) {
                for (long basket : new long[] {0, 49999, 50000, 59999, 60000, 150000}) {
                    long before = legacyFee(type.name(), city, basket);
                    long after = ruleFor(type, city).feePaise(basket);
                    checked++;
                    if (before != after) { mismatches++; System.out.println("MISMATCH " + type + " " + city + " " + basket); }
                }
            }
        }
        System.out.println("characterisation: " + checked + " cases, " + mismatches + " mismatches");
        System.out.println("REGULAR in Pune, Rs 550 basket: rule " + ruleFor(CustomerType.REGULAR, "Pune") + ", fee " + ruleFor(CustomerType.REGULAR, "Pune").feePaise(55000) + " paise");
        System.out.println("CORPORATE anywhere: " + ruleFor(CustomerType.CORPORATE, "Bengaluru"));
    }
}

Output:

characterisation: 36 cases, 0 mismatches
REGULAR in Pune, Rs 550 basket: rule FreeAbove[thresholdPaise=60000, feePaise=3900], fee 3900 paise
CORPORATE anywhere: Flat[feePaise=1500]

Discussion points: characterisation before refactoring, sealed types so a new rule kind is a compile-time decision, and why a rule table in configuration could be the next step. Pages: Refactoring to Patterns, Patterns in Modern Java.

docs.title: Task 4: Retrying partner client (L4, take-home, 90 minutes)
docs.text:
Write a client for QuickDrop's booking API. The API sometimes returns 503 under load; 400 means the request is wrong.

Requirements: retry only transient failures, at most 4 attempts, with exponential backoff and full jitter capped at 2 seconds; send the same idempotency key on every attempt so the partner never books twice; tests must not sleep.

Hints

Use a virtual clock and an injectable random source. Full jitter means sleeping a random time between 0 and the current backoff ceiling.

Solution RetryingPartnerClientDemo.java
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.HashMap;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Map;

/**
 * Task 4 solution: a delivery-booking client that retries transient failures with exponential backoff and full
 * jitter, never retries client errors, and sends the same idempotency key on every attempt so the partner books once.
 * A virtual clock and a seeded jitter source keep the output deterministic.
 */
public class RetryingPartnerClientDemo {

    static final class TransientException extends RuntimeException { TransientException(String m) { super(m); } }
    static final class ClientErrorException extends RuntimeException { ClientErrorException(String m) { super(m); } }

    /** Fake partner: fails the first N calls per key with 503, books at most once per idempotency key. */
    static final class FakeQuickDrop {
        final Map<String, String> bookings = new HashMap<>();
        final Map<String, Integer> calls = new HashMap<>();
        final int failuresBeforeSuccess;
        FakeQuickDrop(int failuresBeforeSuccess) { this.failuresBeforeSuccess = failuresBeforeSuccess; }

        String book(String idempotencyKey, String orderId) {
            int n = calls.merge(idempotencyKey, 1, Integer::sum);
            if (orderId.isBlank()) throw new ClientErrorException("400 missing order id");
            if (n <= failuresBeforeSuccess) throw new TransientException("503 busy");
            return bookings.computeIfAbsent(idempotencyKey, k -> "QD-" + orderId);
        }
    }

    static final class RetryingClient {
        final FakeQuickDrop partner;
        final int maxAttempts = 4;
        final long baseMillis = 100, capMillis = 2000;
        long virtualNow = 0;
        long seed = 42;
        final List<String> log = new ArrayList<>();

        RetryingClient(FakeQuickDrop partner) { this.partner = partner; }

        long jitter(long bound) {                       // small deterministic LCG instead of a real random source
            seed = (seed * 6364136223846793005L + 1442695040888963407L);
            return Math.floorMod(seed >>> 33, bound + 1);
        }

        String book(String orderId) {
            String key = "book-" + orderId;              // stable across attempts
            for (int attempt = 1; ; attempt++) {
                try {
                    String id = partner.book(key, orderId);
                    log.add("t=" + virtualNow + "ms attempt " + attempt + " ok " + id);
                    return id;
                } catch (TransientException e) {
                    if (attempt == maxAttempts) { log.add("t=" + virtualNow + "ms attempt " + attempt + " " + e.getMessage() + ", giving up"); throw e; }
                    long ceiling = Math.min(capMillis, baseMillis << (attempt - 1));
                    long sleep = jitter(ceiling);
                    log.add("t=" + virtualNow + "ms attempt " + attempt + " " + e.getMessage() + ", retry in " + sleep + "ms (max " + ceiling + ")");
                    virtualNow += sleep;
                } catch (ClientErrorException e) {
                    log.add("t=" + virtualNow + "ms attempt " + attempt + " " + e.getMessage() + ", not retried");
                    throw e;
                }
            }
        }
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        for (int failures : new int[] {2, 5}) {
            RetryingClient client = new RetryingClient(new FakeQuickDrop(failures));
            System.out.println("partner fails " + failures + " times:");
            try { client.book("FC-1001"); } catch (RuntimeException ignored) { }
            client.log.forEach(l -> System.out.println("  " + l));
            System.out.println("  bookings at partner: " + client.partner.bookings.size());
        }
        RetryingClient client = new RetryingClient(new FakeQuickDrop(0));
        try { client.book(" "); } catch (RuntimeException ignored) { }
        System.out.println("bad request:");
        client.log.forEach(l -> System.out.println("  " + l));
    }
}

Output:

partner fails 2 times:
  t=0ms attempt 1 503 busy, retry in 100ms (max 100)
  t=100ms attempt 2 503 busy, retry in 176ms (max 200)
  t=276ms attempt 3 ok QD-FC-1001
  bookings at partner: 1
partner fails 5 times:
  t=0ms attempt 1 503 busy, retry in 100ms (max 100)
  t=100ms attempt 2 503 busy, retry in 176ms (max 200)
  t=276ms attempt 3 503 busy, retry in 257ms (max 400)
  t=533ms attempt 4 503 busy, giving up
  bookings at partner: 0
bad request:
  t=0ms attempt 1 400 missing order id, not retried

Discussion points: why jitter prevents synchronised retry waves, why the key is derived from the order and not generated per attempt, retry budgets across a fleet, and where Resilience4j would replace this. Pages: Resilience Patterns, API Design Patterns.

docs.title: Task 5: Single-flight price cache (L3 to L4, live, 45 minutes)
docs.text:
Hot product prices are requested by hundreds of threads at once. When a price is missing from the cache, only one load may hit the pricing database; the others wait for its result. A failed load must not be cached.

Requirements: thread-safe without a global lock; no load inside a map lock (loads can be slow); demonstrate with 50 concurrent requests.

Hints

Store a CompletableFuture per key with putIfAbsent. Whoever inserted it loads; everyone else joins. On failure, remove that exact future.

Solution SingleFlightCacheDemo.java
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Set;
import java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture;
import java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap;
import java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch;
import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService;
import java.util.concurrent.Executors;
import java.util.concurrent.Future;
import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger;
import java.util.function.Function;

/**
 * Task 5 solution: a thread-safe price cache with single-flight loading. Concurrent misses for the same key share one
 * in-flight load (a CompletableFuture stored with computeIfAbsent); failed loads are removed so the next caller retries.
 */
public class SingleFlightCacheDemo {

    static final class SingleFlightCache<K, V> {
        private final ConcurrentHashMap<K, CompletableFuture<V>> entries = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();
        private final Function<K, V> loader;
        SingleFlightCache(Function<K, V> loader) { this.loader = loader; }

        V get(K key) {
            CompletableFuture<V> created = new CompletableFuture<>();
            CompletableFuture<V> existing = entries.putIfAbsent(key, created);
            if (existing != null) return existing.join();          // someone else is loading or has loaded
            try {
                V value = loader.apply(key);                         // load outside any map lock
                created.complete(value);
                return value;
            } catch (RuntimeException e) {
                entries.remove(key, created);                        // let the next caller retry
                created.completeExceptionally(e);
                throw e;
            }
        }
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        AtomicInteger loads = new AtomicInteger();
        CountDownLatch start = new CountDownLatch(1);
        SingleFlightCache<String, Long> cache = new SingleFlightCache<>(sku -> {
            loads.incrementAndGet();
            try { Thread.sleep(50); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); }
            return 6800L;
        });

        try (ExecutorService pool = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
            List<Future<Long>> results = new ArrayList<>();
            for (int i = 0; i < 50; i++) results.add(pool.submit(() -> { start.await(); return cache.get("MILK-1L"); }));
            start.countDown();
            Set<Long> values = new java.util.TreeSet<>();
            for (Future<Long> f : results) values.add(f.get());
            System.out.println("50 concurrent requests for MILK-1L: loader called " + loads.get() + " time(s), values " + values);
        }

        AtomicInteger attempts = new AtomicInteger();
        SingleFlightCache<String, Long> flaky = new SingleFlightCache<>(sku -> {
            if (attempts.incrementAndGet() == 1) throw new IllegalStateException("pricing DB timeout");
            return 4500L;
        });
        try { flaky.get("CURD-500G"); } catch (IllegalStateException e) { System.out.println("first load failed: " + e.getMessage()); }
        System.out.println("second call retries and gets " + flaky.get("CURD-500G") + " paise (loader attempts " + attempts.get() + ")");
    }
}

Output:

50 concurrent requests for MILK-1L: loader called 1 time(s), values [6800]
first load failed: pricing DB timeout
second call retries and gets 4500 paise (loader attempts 2)

Discussion points: why computeIfAbsent with a slow loader blocks other keys in the same bin, adding expiry and size bounds (or using Caffeine's AsyncLoadingCache, which does this for you), and virtual threads for the demo. Pages: Caching Patterns, Concurrency Patterns.

docs.text:
• The Hands-on tab in every topic page's Interview Corner has a smaller task with a solution.
  • The FreshCart capstone milestones make good 2 to 4 hour take-homes.

docs.title: Questions by Level
docs.text:
TL;DR

Graded questions from L1 to L5 with model answers. Try to answer out loud before opening each answer, then follow the link to the page that covers it in depth.

How to use this page. Each answer is the core of a good response, about 30 to 60 seconds spoken. In a real interview, add an example from your own work. Topic pages have five more questions per level in their Interview Corner.

docs.title: L1 Junior
docs.text:
1. What is a design pattern, and what is it not?

    Model answer

    A named, reusable solution to a recurring design problem in a context, described by intent, structure and trade-offs. It is not a library or copy-paste code; you adapt it. Patterns give teams a shared vocabulary: saying "wrap it in a Decorator" communicates a whole design. (Read more)

  2. Explain the Single Responsibility Principle with an example.

    Model answer

    A class should have one reason to change. If OrderService calculates prices, saves orders and sends SMS, a change to SMS templates risks breaking pricing. Split it into PricingService, OrderRepository and Notifier, each owned by the people who change it. (Read more)

  3. How do you make a thread-safe Singleton in Java?

    Model answer

    Use an enum with one constant, or the holder idiom (a nested static class holding the instance). Both rely on class initialisation being thread-safe and lazy. In applications, prefer a DI container's singleton scope so the object stays replaceable in tests. (Read more)

  4. Strategy vs Template Method?

    Model answer

    Both vary part of an algorithm. Strategy uses composition: the caller passes an object (often a lambda) that implements the varying algorithm. Template Method uses inheritance: a base class fixes the steps and subclasses override some. Prefer Strategy in modern Java; it is easier to test and combine. (Read more)

  5. When would you use a Builder?

    Model answer

    When an object has many optional parameters, needs validation across fields, or must be immutable once built. For a few required fields, a record or constructor is simpler. (Read more)

  6. What problem does Observer solve, and what is a common bug?

    Model answer

    It lets one object notify many dependents without knowing them. A common bug is forgetting to unregister listeners, which leaks memory and causes duplicate notifications; another is a slow listener blocking the publisher. (Read more)

  7. Adapter vs Facade?

    Model answer

    Adapter converts one interface into another that callers expect (a ParcelGo SDK behind your DeliveryPartner). Facade gives a simpler interface to a whole subsystem (one checkout method over stock, payment and delivery). (Read more)

docs.title: L2 Mid
docs.text:
1. Decorator vs Proxy: they have the same structure, so what differs?

    Model answer

    Intent. Decorator adds behaviour and is usually composed by the caller in stacks (logging, caching). Proxy controls access to the real object (lazy loading, security, remote calls, transactions) and often creates or locates it itself. (Read more)

  2. Why is constructor injection preferred over field injection?

    Model answer

    Dependencies are explicit and final, objects are always fully initialised, tests can construct them without a container, and circular dependencies fail fast instead of being hidden. (Read more)

  3. How would you model an order lifecycle?

    Model answer

    With the State pattern or, in Java 21, a sealed interface of state records whose methods return the next state and throw for illegal transitions. Transitions are tested as a table: from state, action, expected result. (Read more)

  4. When is Visitor a good idea, and what replaces it in Java 21?

    Model answer

    When the type hierarchy is stable and you keep adding operations over it. In Java 21, a sealed hierarchy with exhaustive pattern-matching switch gives the same benefit without accept methods, and the compiler reports missing cases. (Read more)

  5. What's the difference between a fake, a stub and a mock?

    Model answer

    A stub returns canned answers; a mock also verifies interactions; a fake is a working lightweight implementation (an in-memory repository). Prefer fakes for domain logic and mocks only at boundaries where the interaction is the behaviour. (Read more)

  6. Composite: what makes it tricky?

    Model answer

    Deciding where child-management methods live (on the component or only the composite), avoiding cycles, and controlling traversal cost for deep trees. Sealed interfaces help by making leaf and composite explicit. (Read more)

  7. Why might an Object Pool make performance worse?

    Model answer

    Allocation of short-lived objects is very cheap on modern JVMs, while pools add synchronisation, contention and bugs from returning dirty objects. Pool only expensive resources such as connections. (Read more)

docs.title: L3 Senior
docs.text:
1. Why doesn't @Transactional work when a method calls another method in the same class?

    Model answer

    Spring applies it through a proxy. A call on this goes directly to the target object, bypassing the proxy, so no transaction starts. Move the method to another bean or use TransactionTemplate. (Read more)

  2. Where does the JDK itself use patterns?

    Model answer

    Iterator (Iterator), Strategy (Comparator), Decorator (java.io streams, Collections.unmodifiableList), Factory (List.of, Executors), Builder (StringBuilder, HttpRequest.newBuilder), Observer (Flow), Template Method (AbstractList), Proxy (java.lang.reflect.Proxy). (Read more)

  3. How do you handle errors consistently in a layered service?

    Model answer

    Domain exceptions express business failures; adapters translate infrastructure exceptions into domain or application exceptions; one boundary handler maps them to HTTP Problem Details; logs happen once at the boundary; retries only for transient failures. (Read more)

  4. What does the producer-consumer pattern look like with virtual threads?

    Model answer

    A bounded BlockingQueue between producers and consumers still provides back-pressure. Virtual threads make blocking cheap, so consumers can be simple blocking loops; limit concurrency to protect downstream resources with semaphores, not thread pool size. (Read more)

  5. How do you measure the performance cost of a pattern?

    Model answer

    With JMH microbenchmarks for hot paths and profiling under realistic load for the whole service. Most pattern indirection is inlined by the JIT; allocation in hot loops, megamorphic call sites and reflection are the usual real costs. (Read more)

  6. How would you refactor a 500-line switch on order type?

    Model answer

    Add characterisation tests, extract each branch into a method, introduce an interface (Strategy) or sealed type per branch, move the methods, then replace the switch with polymorphism or one exhaustive switch in a factory. (Read more)

  7. MVVM on mobile: what goes in the ViewModel?

    Model answer

    Screen state and presentation logic, exposed as observable state; no Android/Flutter UI types. Repositories behind it handle data sources and caching, which makes ViewModels unit-testable. (Read more)

docs.title: L4 Senior / Lead
docs.text:
1. How do you publish an event reliably after saving to the database?

    Model answer

    Use a transactional outbox: write the event to an outbox table in the same transaction as the state change, then a relay (polling or CDC) publishes it. Consumers must be idempotent because delivery is at least once. (Read more)

  2. Orchestration vs choreography for sagas?

    Model answer

    Orchestration has a coordinator that tells each step what to do; it's easier to understand, monitor and change. Choreography lets services react to events; it has fewer central parts but the flow is implicit. Use orchestration for business-critical flows with many steps. (Read more)

  3. In what order do you apply timeout, retry and circuit breaker?

    Model answer

    Fallback outside, then circuit breaker, then retry, then timeout around each attempt, with a bulkhead limiting concurrency. Then the breaker counts final outcomes, each attempt has its own timeout, and an open breaker stops retries immediately. (Read more)

  4. How do you prevent a cache stampede?

    Model answer

    Single-flight loading (one load per key), refresh-ahead so hot keys are reloaded before expiry, jittered TTLs, and serving stale values while refreshing. (Read more)

  5. What makes a good microservice boundary?

    Model answer

    A business capability or bounded context with its own data, few synchronous dependencies, and a team that owns it. Entity-based services (ProductService, OrderService) usually produce chatty, coupled systems. (Read more)

  6. How do you make a payment API safe to retry?

    Model answer

    Require an idempotency key; store the key with the request hash and the response; return the stored response for repeats and reject a different payload with the same key. (Read more)

  7. What is an aggregate, and how big should it be?

    Model answer

    A consistency boundary: invariants inside it are enforced in one transaction, and outside objects reference it by ID. Keep it as small as the invariants allow; large aggregates cause contention. (Read more)

docs.title: L5 Staff / Principal
docs.text:
1. How do you decide whether a pattern is worth introducing?

    Model answer

    Compare the cost of indirection (more types, harder navigation) with the cost of change it removes, using evidence: how often this area changed, how many variants exist now. Prefer reversible choices, record the decision in an ADR, and revisit it. (Read more)

  2. How do you keep an architecture from eroding?

    Model answer

    Fitness functions in CI: ArchUnit or JPMS for dependencies, performance and API compatibility checks, with a ratchet baseline for existing violations. Review them like product code. (Read more)

  3. How would you replace a legacy billing system without a big-bang rewrite?

    Model answer

    Characterisation tests and seams first, then a strangler fig or branch by abstraction, an anti-corruption layer to keep the legacy model out, a parallel run comparing results, and a toggle-based cutover per segment with rollback. (Read more)

  4. What breaks binary compatibility in a library?

    Model answer

    Removing or renaming anything, changing parameter or return types (including widening int to long), adding abstract methods to interfaces others implement, making classes or methods final. Additions and default methods are safe. Enforce with japicmp and semantic versioning. (Read more)

  5. Why can there be two instances of a Singleton in one JVM?

    Model answer

    Class identity is name plus class loader. Two web applications or plugins loading the same class with different loaders each get their own static state. (Read more)

  6. How do you govern patterns across 10 teams without slowing them down?

    Model answer

    A catalogue with owners and ADOPT/TRIAL/HOLD statuses enforced by lint, risk-based design review, reference implementations, a funded debt strategy, and scorecards used to offer help, with guards against gaming. (Read more)

docs.title: Scenario Questions
docs.text:
TL;DR

"Production is down, what do you do?" style questions on pattern-heavy systems. Each scenario gives the symptoms; the strong answer shows how to stabilise first, then diagnose, then fix the design so it can't happen again. Most root causes are a missing or misused pattern.

How to answer. Interviewers want a calm sequence: (1) limit customer impact, (2) form hypotheses from the symptoms and check them with data, (3) fix the immediate cause, (4) prevent recurrence with a design or process change. Name the patterns you'd use and why.

docs.title: 1. Customers charged twice
docs.text:
Scenario: After a mobile app release, about 0.5% of FreshCart orders show two PayLink charges. The new app retries POST /checkout when a request takes more than 5 seconds.

Strong answer

Stabilise: stop automatic retries in the app via a remote config flag; refund duplicates using PayLink's ledger joined with orders. Diagnose: the checkout is not idempotent. A slow first request still completes on the server while the retry creates a second order and charge. Fix: require an Idempotency-Key header generated once per checkout attempt; store key, request hash and response; return the stored response for repeats; pass the key to PayLink if it supports one. Prevent: contract tests that send the same request twice; make retry policies part of the API contract. Patterns: idempotency key (API Design Patterns), idempotent consumer.

docs.title: 2. Checkout down because a partner is slow
docs.text:
Scenario: ParcelGo's API latency jumps from 200 ms to 30 seconds. Within minutes, all of FreshCart's checkout endpoints time out, even for Bengaluru orders that use QuickDrop.

Strong answer

Stabilise: disable ParcelGo routing with a feature toggle so Pune falls back to QuickDrop. Diagnose: no timeout on the ParcelGo client, and it shares the request thread pool. Threads pile up waiting on ParcelGo, starving all requests. Fix: connect and response timeouts; a bulkhead (separate limited concurrency) per partner; a circuit breaker with a fallback partner. Prevent: "every remote call has a timeout" in the production checklist; chaos tests that inject partner latency. Patterns: timeout, bulkhead, circuit breaker, fallback (Resilience Patterns).

docs.title: 3. Order events lost
docs.text:
Scenario: Some orders are paid but the warehouse never receives OrderPaid. It happens a few times a day, more during deploys.

Strong answer

Stabilise: a reconciliation job compares paid orders with warehouse records and republishes missing events. Diagnose: dual write: the service commits the database transaction and then publishes to Kafka. A crash or deploy between the two loses the event. Fix: transactional outbox (event row written in the same transaction, relay publishes) or CDC from the database log; consumers deduplicate by event ID. Prevent: ban direct publishing after commits with a lint rule or ArchUnit check. Patterns: transactional outbox, CDC, idempotent consumer (Distributed Data Patterns).

docs.title: 4. Database overloaded every hour
docs.text:
Scenario: At the top of every hour, the catalogue database CPU hits 100% for about a minute and home-screen latency spikes.

Strong answer

Diagnose: all cached category menus were loaded at startup with the same one-hour TTL, so they expire together and thousands of requests miss at once (cache stampede). Fix: single-flight loading per key, refresh-ahead (refreshAfterWrite) so hot keys reload in the background, and jittered TTLs. Prevent: cache metrics (miss rate, load time) with alerts; load tests that include expiry. Patterns: cache-aside with refresh-ahead (Caching Patterns).

docs.title: 5. Kafka consumer stuck
docs.text:
Scenario: The loyalty service stopped awarding points two hours ago. Consumer lag on order-events keeps growing; logs show the same exception repeating.

Strong answer

Stabilise: move the failing message aside so the partition can progress. Diagnose: a poison message (a new event version with a field the consumer can't parse) is retried forever, blocking the partition. Fix: bounded retries, then a dead letter topic with alerting and a replay tool; a tolerant reader that ignores unknown fields; schema compatibility checks in the producer's CI. Patterns: dead letter channel, message translator, tolerant reader (Messaging Patterns).

docs.title: 6. Memory grows after every redeploy
docs.text:
Scenario: A legacy app server hosts three FreshCart web apps. After each hot redeploy, metaspace grows by about 150 MB until the server crashes.

Strong answer

Diagnose: a class loader leak: something in a parent class loader (a JDBC driver registration, a ThreadLocal, a static listener registry) holds a reference to the old web app's classes. Fix: deregister drivers and listeners on shutdown, clear ThreadLocals, avoid static registries shared across apps; confirm with a heap dump (GC roots of the old class loader). Prevent: move to one app per JVM or container. Patterns: Singleton and registry pitfalls across class loaders (JVM Internals).

docs.title: 7. A library upgrade breaks a partner
docs.text:
Scenario: ParcelGo reports NoSuchMethodError in their integration after they upgraded an unrelated library that pulls in FreshCart's SDK 1.4. FreshCart's own services work fine.

Strong answer

Stabilise: release 1.4.1 restoring the old method signature, delegating to the new one. Diagnose: 1.4 changed a parameter from int to long. Source-compatible for FreshCart (recompiled), binary-incompatible for ParcelGo's compiled code. Prevent: japicmp or revapi in CI with semantic versioning enforcement; deprecate before removing; changes like this only in a major release. Patterns: API evolution and binary compatibility (Designing Frameworks and Libraries).

docs.title: 8. Add a new delivery partner in two days
docs.text:
Scenario: Business signs a third partner for Hyderabad and wants it live by Friday. Today, partner logic is spread across checkout, tracking and billing code with if (partner == ...) checks.

Strong answer

Introduce a DeliveryPartner interface for the operations checkout needs (quote, book, track, cancel). Wrap each partner SDK in an Adapter, select the adapter in one factory or router by city, and move the if branches into the adapters. Add contract tests that every adapter must pass. The new partner is then one adapter plus one routing entry. Mention that you'd do this as a strangler-style refactor behind tests, not a rewrite. (Adapter, Factory Method, Designing Frameworks and Libraries)

docs.title: 9. Split the monolith?
docs.text:
Scenario: A new CTO wants FreshCart's monolith split into 20 microservices this year. The team is 15 engineers.

Strong answer

Ask what problem the split solves: deploy contention, scaling hotspots, team autonomy. With 15 engineers, 20 services would mean more operational load than benefit. Propose a modular monolith first: enforce module boundaries along bounded contexts with ArchUnit or JPMS, separate data ownership per module, then extract the one or two modules with a proven need (for example search for scale) using a strangler fig. Record the decision in an ADR with criteria for further extraction. (Architectural Patterns, Microservice Patterns, Choosing Patterns)

docs.title: 10. Read-heavy order history
docs.text:
Scenario: The "My orders" screen needs filters by status, partner and month, and it slows down checkout because both use the same tables.

Strong answer

Separate the read model: publish order events through the outbox, build a denormalised order-history projection (CQRS) in a store suited to the queries, and serve the screen from it. Accept a few seconds of staleness and show it in the UI. Keep checkout on the write model. Rebuild projections from events when the schema changes. (Distributed Data Patterns)

docs.title: 11. Price rules are changing weekly
docs.text:
Scenario: Marketing changes discount and fee rules every week, and each change needs a deploy and touches PricingService in several places.

Strong answer

Model rules as Strategies and Specifications composed from configuration, with a small rule language (Interpreter) only if marketing must author rules themselves. Version rule sets, validate them before activation, and roll out with feature toggles. Keep a test suite of example baskets with expected prices that every rule change must pass. (Strategy, Specification, Interpreter)
