docs.title: Setting Up Java to Run the Examples
docs.text:
L0 ⚪ Orientation · ⏱ 10 min read · Prerequisites: What Are Design Patterns

TL;DR

Install a JDK 21, check it with java -version, and you can run every example in this playbook with java File.java. Use Maven when an example has several files or tests, and JShell when you want to try one line. Any major IDE works.

docs.title: 1. What It Is
docs.text:
Plain English. Before you can run Java code you need the JDK (Java Development Kit): the compiler, the runtime and tools such as jshell. This page gets you from nothing to running the playbook's examples.

Precise definition. The examples target Java SE 21, a long-term-support (LTS) release. They use:

  • the source-file launcher (java File.java, JEP 330, Java 11+), which compiles and runs a single file in memory;
  • Maven for multi-file projects with tests;
  • JShell (JEP 222, Java 9+), the read-eval-print loop.

New terms:

  • JDK vs. JRE: the JDK includes the compiler and tools; a runtime alone can only run compiled code. You need the JDK.
  • LTS: a release supported with updates for several years. Java 17, 21 and 25 are LTS releases.
  • Distribution: builds of OpenJDK from different vendors (Eclipse Temurin, Amazon Corretto, Microsoft, Oracle, Azul Zulu and others). They behave the same for this playbook.

docs.title: 2. Why It Exists
docs.text: Every page shows the exact command and the exact output, so you can check your understanding by running the code. That only works if your setup matches: an older JDK fails on records, sealed types and switch patterns with confusing compiler errors. Five minutes of setup saves hours of "why doesn't this compile?".

docs.title: 3. Mental Model / Analogy
docs.text:
Analogy. The JDK is a kitchen. java File.java is cooking one dish straight from the recipe card. Maven is a restaurant kitchen with prep lists, stations and a health inspection (tests) before anything goes out. JShell is tasting a spoonful.

Technical model. javac turns .java source into .class bytecode; java starts a JVM that loads and runs the bytecode. The source launcher does both steps in memory for one file. Maven runs the same steps, plus downloading dependencies and running tests, in a fixed order called the lifecycle.

docs.title: 4. How It Works
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    A["Source: HelloDemo.java"] --> B{"How do you run it?"}
    B -- "single file" --> C["java HelloDemo.java (compiles in memory)"]
    B -- "project" --> D["mvn package"]
    D --> E["compile"] --> F["test (JUnit)"] --> G["package (jar)"]
    C --> H["JVM runs bytecode"]
    G --> H
    B -- "one expression" --> I["jshell"]

Maven's default lifecycle runs phases in order: validate, compile, test, package, verify, install, deploy. Asking for one phase runs all the earlier ones, which is why mvn package also runs the tests.

docs.title: Installing JDK 21 (SDKMAN!, package managers)
docs.text:
• Description: Install any OpenJDK 21 distribution. A version manager makes switching between JDKs easy.

  • How to use it:

    macOS / Linux (SDKMAN!)macOS (Homebrew)Ubuntu / DebianWindows (winget) 
    curl -s "https://get.sdkman.io" | bash
sdk list java                 # pick a 21.x identifier from the list
sdk install java 21.0.5-tem   # example identifier; use one from the list

    brew install openjdk@21

    sudo apt install openjdk-21-jdk

    winget install EclipseAdoptium.Temurin.21.JDK

    Then check: java -version should print a version starting with 21.

  • Pros (version manager): several JDKs side by side; per-project switching.

  • Cons (version manager): one more tool; IDEs need to be pointed at the right JDK.
  • Best practice: use the same major version locally and in CI.
  • Gotcha: java -version and javac -version can disagree if PATH and JAVA_HOME point at different JDKs. Check both.

Verify against the official docs

Package names and identifiers change with each update. Check the SDKMAN!, Homebrew or Adoptium pages for the current ones.

docs.title: Running single-file programs with java File.java
docs.text:
• Description: Since Java 11 the launcher compiles and runs a single source file without creating .class files. Every class must be in that one file (nested classes are fine), and the first top-level class must have main.
  • How to use it: java HelloDemo.java arg1 arg2, with JVM options before the file name: java -Dkey=value HelloDemo.java.
  • Pros: zero setup; perfect for examples and scripts.
  • Cons: single file only in Java 21 (Java 22 added multi-file source programs, JEP 458); no dependencies unless you pass --class-path.
  • Best practice: keep examples self-contained so they run with this one command.
  • Gotcha: options placed after the file name are program arguments, not JVM options.

docs.title: Maven project layout for the examples/ folder
docs.text:
• Description: Maven expects code in src/main/java, tests in src/test/java, and configuration in pom.xml. Examples with tests or several files use this layout.
  • How to use it: mvn package to compile, test and build a jar; mvn test to run tests only.
  • Pros: standard everywhere; dependency management; IDEs import it directly.
  • Cons: XML configuration; first build downloads plugins and takes a while.
  • Best practice: set maven.compiler.release (not just source/target), so the compiler also checks you only use Java 21 APIs.
  • Gotcha: forgetting to pin plugin versions gives you different builds on different machines.

docs.title: IDE setup: IntelliJ IDEA, VS Code, Eclipse
docs.text:
• Description: IntelliJ IDEA (Community is free), VS Code with the "Extension Pack for Java", and Eclipse all support Java 21 and Maven.
  • How to use it: open the folder containing pom.xml (or a single .java file), then set the project SDK / JDK to 21.
  • Pros: navigation ("go to implementation" is essential for pattern-heavy code), refactoring, debugging.
  • Cons: IDE settings can hide build problems that only appear on the command line.
  • Best practice: treat the command-line build (mvn verify) as the source of truth; the IDE is a helper.
  • Gotcha: the IDE's project language level can be lower than the JDK, causing "records are not supported" errors. Set both to 21.

docs.title: JShell for quick experiments
docs.text:
• Description: An interactive shell that evaluates Java declarations, statements and expressions.
  • How to use it: 
    $ jshell
jshell> record Money(long cents) { }
|  created record Money

jshell> new Money(129)
$2 ==> Money[cents=129]

jshell> /exit
|  Goodbye
  • Pros: instant feedback; great for checking an API.
  • Cons: not for multi-class designs; state is lost when you exit.
  • Best practice: use it to try a single idea, then move it into a file.
  • Gotcha: snippets can be redefined silently, so a later definition replaces an earlier one.

docs.title: Example 1: Minimal (L0)
docs.text:
Scenario: Check that your JDK is new enough for the playbook. The program uses a record (Java 16+) and fails clearly on older versions.

Code / Config:

HelloDemo.java
public class HelloDemo {

    record Greeting(String to) { }                                          // (1)!

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        int feature = Runtime.version().feature();                          // (2)!
        if (feature < 21) {
            System.out.println("Java " + feature + " found; the playbook needs Java 21 or newer.");
            System.exit(1);
        }
        var greeting = new Greeting("design patterns");
        System.out.println("Hello, " + greeting.to() + "!");
        System.out.println("Running on Java " + feature);
    }
}
  1. A record: if your JDK is older than 16, compilation fails here.
  2. Runtime.version().feature() returns the major version, such as 21.

Run it:

java -version
java HelloDemo.java

Output (with JDK 21):

Hello, design patterns!
Running on Java 21

What to notice:

  • No javac step and no .class files: the launcher compiled in memory.
  • On a newer JDK the last line shows that version; the examples still work.
  • On JDK 16–20 you get the clear message and exit code 1 instead of a confusing failure later.

docs.title: Example 2: Realistic (in FreshCart grocery delivery)
docs.text:
Scenario: A FreshCart support script checks which delivery slots a customer can still book. It takes the current time as a program argument and the ordering cutoff as a system property, so support staff can try different cases without editing code.

Code / Config:

SlotCheckDemo.java
import java.time.LocalTime;
import java.util.List;

/** Checks which FreshCart delivery slots are still open at a given time. */
public class SlotCheckDemo {

    record Slot(LocalTime start, LocalTime end) {
        Slot {
            if (!end.isAfter(start)) throw new IllegalArgumentException("Slot must end after it starts: " + start + "-" + end);
        }
        @Override public String toString() { return start + "-" + end; }
    }

    static final List<Slot> SLOTS = List.of(
            new Slot(LocalTime.of(8, 0), LocalTime.of(10, 0)),
            new Slot(LocalTime.of(12, 0), LocalTime.of(14, 0)),
            new Slot(LocalTime.of(18, 0), LocalTime.of(20, 0)));

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        // Program arguments: java SlotCheckDemo.java 11:30
        LocalTime now = args.length > 0 ? LocalTime.parse(args[0]) : LocalTime.of(9, 15);       // (1)!
        // System property: java -Dfreshcart.cutoffMinutes=60 SlotCheckDemo.java
        int cutoffMinutes = Integer.getInteger("freshcart.cutoffMinutes", 30);                 // (2)!

        System.out.println("Time " + now + ", ordering closes " + cutoffMinutes + " min before a slot starts");
        for (Slot slot : SLOTS) {
            boolean open = now.plusMinutes(cutoffMinutes).isBefore(slot.start());
            System.out.println("  " + slot + (open ? "  open" : "  closed"));
        }
    }
}
  1. Program arguments arrive in args; a fixed default keeps the output reproducible.
  2. Integer.getInteger reads a -D system property, with a default.

Run it:

java SlotCheckDemo.java
java SlotCheckDemo.java 11:15
java -Dfreshcart.cutoffMinutes=60 SlotCheckDemo.java 11:15

Output:

Time 09:15, ordering closes 30 min before a slot starts
  08:00-10:00  closed
  12:00-14:00  open
  18:00-20:00  open

Time 11:15, ordering closes 30 min before a slot starts
  08:00-10:00  closed
  12:00-14:00  open
  18:00-20:00  open

Time 11:15, ordering closes 60 min before a slot starts
  08:00-10:00  closed
  12:00-14:00  closed
  18:00-20:00  open

A bad argument fails fast with a clear exception:

$ java SlotCheckDemo.java 25:00
Exception in thread "main" java.time.format.DateTimeParseException: Text '25:00' could not be parsed: Invalid value for HourOfDay (valid values 0 - 23): 25

What to notice:

  • -D goes before the file name; 11:15 goes after it.
  • The noon slot flips from open to closed when the cutoff moves from 30 to 60 minutes.
  • The Slot record validates itself, a habit you'll see on every page.

docs.title: Example 3: Production-grade
docs.text:
Scenario: The same slot logic as a proper Maven project: a reusable class, a separate App, unit tests that run on every build, pinned plugin versions, and a compiler that treats warnings as errors. This is the shape of the larger examples and the capstone.

Code / Config:

pom.xmlDeliverySlot.javaApp.javaDeliverySlotTest.java 
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<project xmlns="http://maven.apache.org/POM/4.0.0"
         xmlns:xsi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance"
         xsi:schemaLocation="http://maven.apache.org/POM/4.0.0 https://maven.apache.org/xsd/maven-4.0.0.xsd">
    <modelVersion>4.0.0</modelVersion>

    <groupId>com.freshcart</groupId>
    <artifactId>freshcart-starter</artifactId>
    <version>1.0.0-SNAPSHOT</version>

    <properties>
        <maven.compiler.release>21</maven.compiler.release>  <!-- (1)! -->
        <project.build.sourceEncoding>UTF-8</project.build.sourceEncoding>
        <junit.version>5.11.4</junit.version>
    </properties>

    <dependencies>
        <dependency>
            <groupId>org.junit.jupiter</groupId>
            <artifactId>junit-jupiter</artifactId>
            <version>${junit.version}</version>
            <scope>test</scope>
        </dependency>
    </dependencies>

    <build>
        <plugins>
            <plugin>  <!-- (2)! -->
                <groupId>org.apache.maven.plugins</groupId>
                <artifactId>maven-compiler-plugin</artifactId>
                <version>3.13.0</version>
                <configuration>
                    <compilerArgs>
                        <arg>-Xlint:all</arg>
                        <arg>-Werror</arg>
                    </compilerArgs>
                </configuration>
            </plugin>
            <plugin>
                <groupId>org.apache.maven.plugins</groupId>
                <artifactId>maven-surefire-plugin</artifactId>
                <version>3.5.2</version>
            </plugin>
        </plugins>
    </build>
</project>
  1. release makes the compiler check both language features and JDK APIs against Java 21.
  2. Pinned plugin versions give the same build on every machine; -Xlint:all -Werror fails the build on any compiler warning.
package com.freshcart.starter;

import java.time.LocalTime;
import java.util.Objects;

/** A delivery window. Invalid slots can't be created. */
public record DeliverySlot(LocalTime start, LocalTime end) {

    public DeliverySlot {
        Objects.requireNonNull(start, "start");
        Objects.requireNonNull(end, "end");
        if (!end.isAfter(start)) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("Slot must end after it starts: " + start + "-" + end);
        }
    }

    /** True if an order placed at {@code now} can still make this slot. */
    public boolean isOpenAt(LocalTime now, int cutoffMinutes) {
        if (cutoffMinutes < 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("cutoffMinutes must not be negative");
        return now.plusMinutes(cutoffMinutes).isBefore(start);
    }

    @Override
    public String toString() {
        return start + "-" + end;
    }
}

package com.freshcart.starter;

import java.time.LocalTime;
import java.util.List;

public final class App {

    private App() { }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        LocalTime now = args.length > 0 ? LocalTime.parse(args[0]) : LocalTime.of(9, 15);
        List<DeliverySlot> slots = List.of(
                new DeliverySlot(LocalTime.of(8, 0), LocalTime.of(10, 0)),
                new DeliverySlot(LocalTime.of(12, 0), LocalTime.of(14, 0)));
        for (DeliverySlot slot : slots) {
            System.out.println(slot + (slot.isOpenAt(now, 30) ? " open" : " closed"));
        }
    }
}

package com.freshcart.starter;

import static org.junit.jupiter.api.Assertions.assertFalse;
import static org.junit.jupiter.api.Assertions.assertThrows;
import static org.junit.jupiter.api.Assertions.assertTrue;

import java.time.LocalTime;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;

class DeliverySlotTest {

    private final DeliverySlot noon = new DeliverySlot(LocalTime.of(12, 0), LocalTime.of(14, 0));

    @Test
    void openWhenOrderedBeforeTheCutoff() {
        assertTrue(noon.isOpenAt(LocalTime.of(11, 29), 30));
    }

    @Test
    void closedExactlyAtTheCutoff() {
        assertFalse(noon.isOpenAt(LocalTime.of(11, 30), 30));
    }

    @Test
    void rejectsSlotsThatEndBeforeTheyStart() {
        assertThrows(IllegalArgumentException.class,
                () -> new DeliverySlot(LocalTime.of(14, 0), LocalTime.of(12, 0)));
    }
}

Project layout:

freshcart-starter/
├── pom.xml
└── src/
    ├── main/java/com/freshcart/starter/
    │   ├── App.java
    │   └── DeliverySlot.java
    └── test/java/com/freshcart/starter/
        └── DeliverySlotTest.java

Run it:

cd examples/l0-orientation/java-setup/freshcart-starter
mvn package
java -cp target/classes com.freshcart.starter.App

Output (the relevant lines of mvn package, then the program):

[INFO] Tests run: 3, Failures: 0, Errors: 0, Skipped: 0
[INFO] BUILD SUCCESS
08:00-10:00 closed
12:00-14:00 open

What to notice:

  • mvn package ran the tests first; a failing test stops the jar from being built.
  • The test closedExactlyAtTheCutoff pins down the boundary that Example 2 only showed by trying times.
  • isOpenAt rejects a negative cutoff, and the constructor rejects an inverted slot, so bad data can't get in.
  • CI runs mvn verify on this project on every pull request.

docs.title: 7. Pros, Cons & Trade-offs
docs.text: Aspect Pros Cons Simplicity java File.java needs nothing else Maven adds XML and a directory convention Performance In-memory compile is fast for small files Source launcher recompiles on every run; Maven's first build downloads plugins Scalability Maven scales to many modules and dependencies Single-file programs don't scale past a few hundred lines Operability Maven builds are reproducible in CI Version drift between local JDK and CI JDK causes surprises Security Pinned dependencies and plugins are auditable Downloading dependencies is a supply-chain risk to manage Testability Maven runs tests on every build Single-file programs need a separate test runner Cost All tools here are free Time to learn Maven's lifecycle Learning curve JShell and the launcher are beginner friendly IDE, build tool and JDK settings must agree

docs.title: 8. When to Use / When NOT to Use
docs.text:
Use the source launcher for examples, scripts and experiments that fit in one file without dependencies. Use Maven (or Gradle) for anything with tests, dependencies or more than one file you want to keep. Use JShell to check one API call or expression.

Don't use the source launcher for production services, and don't add a build tool to a five-line experiment. Gradle is an equally good choice to Maven for real projects; this playbook uses Maven because its XML is easier to show on a page.

docs.title: 9. Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Pin the Java version in the build (maven.compiler.release) and in CI. (Consensus.)
  2. Pin plugin and dependency versions. (Consensus.)
  3. Run the command-line build before pushing, not only the IDE build. (Consensus.)
  4. Treat compiler warnings as errors in new projects (-Xlint:all -Werror). (Opinion; relax it for legacy code.)
  5. Use a JDK version manager if you work on projects with different Java versions. (Opinion.)

docs.title: 10. Pitfalls & Anti-Patterns
docs.text:
Mismatched JDKs

Symptom: error: records are not supported in -source 11 or class file has wrong version 65.0, should be 55.0. Root cause: compiling or running with an older JDK than the code needs (class file version 65 is Java 21, 55 is Java 11). Fix: check java -version, javac -version, echo $JAVA_HOME and the IDE's project SDK; make them all 21.

Unpinned build (production failure mode)

Symptom: a release built on the CI server failed at startup with NoSuchMethodError, though it worked on every laptop. Root cause: the CI image's default JDK was updated to a newer major version, and the build compiled with -source/-target but not --release, so code linked against an API that doesn't exist on the production JDK. Fix: use maven.compiler.release, pin the CI JDK, and run the same JDK in CI and production.

Options in the wrong place

Symptom: a -D setting has no effect. Root cause: it was written after the file name, so it became a program argument. Fix: java -Dkey=value File.java args....

docs.title: 11. Configuration & Tuning
docs.text: Setting Default What it does When to change it Risk of changing maven.compiler.release depends on plugin version Target language level and JDK API Always set it explicitly Too high: code won't run on older production JDKs JAVA_HOME unset or system JDK Which JDK Maven and many tools use When you install several JDKs Pointing at a JRE or old JDK breaks builds -Xlint:all -Werror off Fails the build on compiler warnings New code bases Legacy code may need many fixes first -ea (JVM option) off Enables assert statements Local runs and tests Assertions with side effects change behaviour

docs.title: 12. Security Considerations
docs.text:
• Download JDKs only from the vendor's official site or a trusted package manager.
  • Keep the JDK patched: each quarterly update includes security fixes.
  • Review curl ... | bash installers before running them, as with any script from the internet.

docs.title: 14. Testing It
docs.text: The Maven project in Example 3 is the template: tests in src/test/java, run by mvn test or as part of mvn package. For single-file examples, this repository's examples/run-all.sh runs each program and compares its output with the expected text shown on the page.

docs.title: 16. Version Notes
docs.text:
• Java 11: single-file source launcher (JEP 330).
  • Java 17: LTS; sealed classes final.
  • Java 21: LTS; pattern matching for switch, record patterns, virtual threads final. This playbook's baseline.
  • Java 22: multi-file source-code programs (JEP 458), so java Main.java can use other source files next to it.
  • Java 25: the next LTS after 21. The examples should run unchanged on it.

Verify against the official docs

Check the OpenJDK project pages for the support timelines of the distribution you choose.

docs.title: 17. Expert Deep Dive
docs.text:
• Reproducible builds are a team property. Seniors pin the JDK (toolchains, .sdkmanrc or a container image), plugins and dependencies, and use the Maven Wrapper (mvnw) so every machine runs the same Maven.
  • --release vs. -source/-target. Only --release checks API usage against the target JDK's API signatures. It's the single most common cause of "works on my machine" Java bugs between major versions.
  • The JDK you build with isn't always the one you run on. Containers, application servers and mobile toolchains (Android uses its own runtime and supports a subset of Java language features) may differ. Know your runtime before using new APIs.
  • Upgrades are routine work. Moving across LTS versions (11 → 17 → 21) is easier in small steps with the build already pinned, tests green and deprecation warnings fixed.

War story: the Friday JDK update

A team's build agents pulled latest for their JDK image. On a Friday, a new major JDK became latest. Builds stayed green, but the service failed in production with UnsupportedClassVersionError: the jars now contained class files for a JVM newer than the one in production. It took two hours to find because nobody had changed the code. The fix was pinning the image tag and adding maven.compiler.release; the lesson they wrote in the postmortem was "the toolchain is part of the code".

docs.title: 18. Interview Corner
19. Practice
docs.text:
• Install JDK 21 and run Example 1. ??? tip "Hint" If java -version shows an older version, check PATH and JAVA_HOME.
  • Run Example 2 with a cutoff of 0 at 11:59. ??? tip "Hint" java -Dfreshcart.cutoffMinutes=0 SlotCheckDemo.java 11:59: the noon slot is open.
  • Break a test in Example 3 on purpose and watch mvn package refuse to build the jar. ??? tip "Hint" Change assertTrue to assertFalse in openWhenOrderedBeforeTheCutoff.
  • Open the Maven project in your IDE and run the test from there. ??? tip "Hint" Open the folder containing pom.xml, not the repository root.

docs.title: 20. Quick Revision Card
docs.text:
Remember in 30 seconds

  • Install a JDK 21 and check java -version.
  • One file: java File.java args; JVM options go before the file.
  • Projects: Maven, src/main/java, src/test/java, mvn package.
  • Pin maven.compiler.release, plugin and dependency versions.
  • JShell to try one line.
java -version
java -Dfreshcart.cutoffMinutes=60 SlotCheckDemo.java 11:15
mvn package && java -cp target/classes com.freshcart.starter.App

docs.title: Reading UML for Patterns
docs.text:
L0 ⚪ Orientation · ⏱ 15 min read · Prerequisites: What Are Design Patterns, Setting Up Java

TL;DR

Every pattern page shows its structure as a UML class diagram and its behaviour as a sequence diagram. You need about a dozen symbols to read them: boxes for classes and interfaces, six kinds of lines for relationships, and arrows for calls over time. This page maps each symbol to the Java code that produces it.

docs.title: 1. What It Is
docs.text:
Plain English. UML (Unified Modeling Language) is a standard set of drawings for software. Patterns are described with a few of them: class diagrams show what types exist and how they're connected, sequence diagrams show who calls whom in what order, and state diagrams show how an object moves between states.

Precise definition. UML is a modelling language standardised by the Object Management Group (OMG). This playbook uses a small subset and draws it with Mermaid, a text-based diagram tool that Material for MkDocs renders in the browser.

New terms:

  • Visibility: + public, - private, # protected, ~ package-private.
  • Multiplicity: how many objects take part, such as 1, 0..1 or * (many).
  • Lifeline: in a sequence diagram, the vertical line under a participant, representing time.

docs.title: 2. Why It Exists
docs.text: Code shows one class at a time; a pattern is about how several classes fit together. A diagram shows the whole shape at once, which is why the GoF book gives every pattern a Structure diagram. Without the ability to read them, you're stuck reading 5–10 files to understand an idea that fits in one picture. You'll also be expected to sketch them in design reviews and interviews.

docs.title: 3. Mental Model / Analogy
docs.text:
Analogy. A class diagram is the floor plan of a house: rooms (classes) and doors between them (relationships), with no people in it. A sequence diagram is a video of people moving through the house for one particular event, from top (start) to bottom (end). A state diagram is the light switch on the wall: which positions exist, and what flips it from one to the other.

Technical model. A class diagram is a static graph of types; edges mean "inherits from", "implements", "holds a reference to" or "uses". A sequence diagram is one execution trace of method calls between objects. Both are views of the same code; neither shows everything.

docs.title: 4. How It Works
docs.text:
The six relationship lines, from strongest coupling to weakest:

classDiagram
    class Customer
    class PremiumCustomer
    class Notifier {
        <<interface>>
    }
    class SmsNotifier
    class Order
    class OrderLine
    class Product
    class LocalDate
    Customer <|-- PremiumCustomer : inheritance
    Notifier <|.. SmsNotifier : realisation
    Order *-- OrderLine : composition
    Order o-- Product : aggregation
    Order --> Customer : association
    Order ..> LocalDate : dependency
Line Name Java code that produces it Meaning solid line, hollow triangle Inheritance (generalisation) class B extends A B is an A dashed line, hollow triangle Realisation class B implements I B fulfils the contract I solid line, filled diamond Composition a field holding parts the owner creates and that die with it strong "has-a": owns the lifecycle solid line, hollow diamond Aggregation a field holding things that exist independently weak "has-a": shares, doesn't own solid line, open arrow Association a field referring to another object knows about it long-term dashed line, open arrow Dependency a parameter, local variable or static call uses it briefly

The diamond (or triangle) is always on the side of the whole (or the parent).

docs.title: Class diagrams: classes, interfaces, abstract classes
docs.text:
• Description: A box has up to three compartments: name, fields, methods. Interfaces are marked <<interface>>; abstract classes and methods are shown in italics or marked <<abstract>>. Visibility symbols prefix each member.
  • How to use it: read top to bottom: what type is it, what does it hold, what can you call?
  • Best practice: pattern diagrams usually show only the members that matter to the pattern; don't expect every field.
  • Gotcha: Mermaid writes generics as List~Product~ because < and > have other meanings in its syntax.

docs.title: Relationships: association, aggregation, composition, inheritance, realisation, dependency
docs.text:
• Description: see the table in section 4. The difference between composition and aggregation is ownership of the lifecycle.
  • How to use it: for each line ask: "is this a field (association/aggregation/composition), a parameter (dependency), or a supertype (inheritance/realisation)?"
  • Pros (of drawing all six precisely): exact communication of coupling.
  • Cons: many teams don't distinguish aggregation from association, so the precision can be lost on readers.
  • Best practice: when in doubt, use a plain association and say what you mean in a label.
  • Gotcha: in Java, composition vs. aggregation isn't visible in the type: both are just fields. It's a design intent (who creates and who can share the objects).

docs.title: Sequence diagrams
docs.text:
• Description: participants across the top, time flowing down. A solid arrow is a call, a dashed arrow is a return, and a cross (x) marks a call that failed.
  • How to use it: follow the arrows top to bottom; each arrow is one method call or return.
  • Pros: shows the dynamic behaviour that class diagrams hide, such as the order of calls in Observer or Chain of Responsibility.
  • Cons: shows only one scenario; branches and loops make them messy.
  • Best practice: draw the happy path and one failure path, not every branch.
  • Gotcha: a sequence diagram can drift from the code. Example 3 below generates one from the real calls.

docs.title: State diagrams
docs.text:
• Description: rounded boxes are states; arrows are transitions labelled with the event that causes them; [*] marks start and end.
  • How to use it: essential for the State pattern. Every arrow should become a method or a case in your code.
  • Best practice: make sure every state has a way out, unless it's a final state.
  • Gotcha: forgetting an "impossible" transition is how orders end up stuck in production.
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Placed
    Placed --> Packed : store packs
    Placed --> Cancelled : customer cancels
    Packed --> OutForDelivery : rider picks up
    OutForDelivery --> Delivered : handed over
    OutForDelivery --> Failed : customer not reachable
    Failed --> OutForDelivery : retry
    Delivered --> [*]
    Cancelled --> [*]

docs.title: How Mermaid draws them in this playbook
docs.text:
• Description: diagrams are written as text in a fenced code block with the language mermaid, and rendered in the browser. Text diagrams live in Git and are reviewed like code.
  • How to use it: 
    ```mermaid
classDiagram
    Notifier <|.. SmsNotifier
```
  • Pros: diffs in pull requests; no image files to keep up to date.
  • Cons: less layout control than a drawing tool; a syntax error stops the diagram rendering.
  • Best practice: quote labels with spaces or punctuation (A["Order (pending)"]) and avoid reserved words like end as node names.
  • Gotcha: Mermaid's class diagram uses ..|> / <|.. for realisation and ..> for dependency; similar-looking arrows mean different things.

docs.title: Example 1: Minimal (L0)
docs.text:
Scenario: Read a small class diagram, then see the exact Java that matches it, symbol by symbol.

classDiagram
    class Payable {
        <<interface>>
        +amountDueInCents() long
    }
    class Product {
        <<abstract>>
        -sku String
        +sku() String
        +priceInCents() long*
    }
    class Fruit {
        -grams int
        +priceInCents() long
    }
    class Invoice {
        -product Product
        +amountDueInCents() long
    }
    Product <|-- Fruit
    Payable <|.. Invoice
    Invoice --> Product

Code / Config:

UmlBasicsDemo.java
public class UmlBasicsDemo {

    interface Payable {                                   // (1)!
        long amountDueInCents();
    }

    abstract static class Product {                       // (2)!
        private final String sku;                         // (3)!
        protected Product(String sku) { this.sku = sku; }
        public String sku() { return sku; }               // (4)!
        public abstract long priceInCents();
    }

    static final class Fruit extends Product {            // (5)!
        private final int grams;
        Fruit(String sku, int grams) { super(sku); this.grams = grams; }
        public long priceInCents() { return grams / 10; } // 1 cent per 10 g
    }

    static final class Invoice implements Payable {       // (6)!
        private final Product product;
        Invoice(Product product) { this.product = product; }
        public long amountDueInCents() { return product.priceInCents(); }
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Payable invoice = new Invoice(new Fruit("APPLE-GALA", 650));
        System.out.println("Amount due: " + invoice.amountDueInCents() + " cents");
    }
}
  1. <<interface>> in the diagram.
  2. <<abstract>>; the abstract method is marked with * in Mermaid.
  3. -sku String: the - means private.
  4. +sku() String: public method returning String.
  5. Product <|-- Fruit: solid line with a hollow triangle, because Fruit extends Product.
  6. Payable <|.. Invoice (dashed, implements), and Invoice --> Product (association, because of the field).

Run it:

java UmlBasicsDemo.java

Output:

Amount due: 65 cents

What to notice:

  • Every box and line in the diagram maps to one Java construct.
  • The diagram leaves out main and the constructor: diagrams show what matters to the design.
  • 650 g at 1 cent per 10 g gives 65 cents.

docs.title: Example 2: Realistic (in FreshCart grocery delivery)
docs.text:
Scenario: A FreshCart order uses all six relationships. Match each annotated line to the diagram in section 4.

Code / Config:

RelationshipsDemo.java
import java.time.LocalDate;
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;

/** Every UML relationship, in FreshCart terms. */
public class RelationshipsDemo {

    // Inheritance (generalisation):  Customer <|-- PremiumCustomer
    static class Customer {
        final String name;
        Customer(String name) { this.name = name; }
        int freeDeliveriesPerMonth() { return 0; }
    }
    static final class PremiumCustomer extends Customer {
        PremiumCustomer(String name) { super(name); }
        @Override int freeDeliveriesPerMonth() { return 8; }
    }

    // Realisation:  Notifier <|.. SmsNotifier
    interface Notifier { String notify(Customer c, String text); }
    static final class SmsNotifier implements Notifier {
        public String notify(Customer c, String text) { return "SMS to " + c.name + ": " + text; }
    }

    record Product(String sku) { }
    record OrderLine(Product product, int quantity) { }

    static final class Order {
        private final Customer customer;                                  // (1)!
        private final List<OrderLine> lines = new ArrayList<>();          // (2)!
        private final List<Product> wishlistSuggestions;                  // (3)!

        Order(Customer customer, List<Product> sharedCatalogueSuggestions) {
            this.customer = customer;
            this.wishlistSuggestions = sharedCatalogueSuggestions;
        }

        void add(Product product, int quantity) { lines.add(new OrderLine(product, quantity)); }

        String confirm(Notifier notifier, LocalDate date) {               // (4)!
            return notifier.notify(customer, lines.size() + " lines confirmed for " + date
                    + ", " + customer.freeDeliveriesPerMonth() + " free deliveries this month, "
                    + wishlistSuggestions.size() + " suggestions");
        }
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        List<Product> suggestions = List.of(new Product("HONEY-500G"));
        Order order = new Order(new PremiumCustomer("Asha"), suggestions);
        order.add(new Product("MILK-1L"), 2);
        order.add(new Product("BREAD-WHT"), 1);
        System.out.println(order.confirm(new SmsNotifier(), LocalDate.of(2026, 11, 2)));
    }
}
  1. Association Order --> Customer: a long-lived reference to an object the order doesn't own.
  2. Composition Order *-- OrderLine: the order creates its lines in add, and nobody else holds them.
  3. Aggregation Order o-- Product: the suggestions list is passed in and shared with other orders.
  4. Dependency Order ..> Notifier and Order ..> LocalDate: used only as parameters during one call.

Run it:

java RelationshipsDemo.java

Output:

SMS to Asha: 2 lines confirmed for 2026-11-02, 8 free deliveries this month, 1 suggestions

What to notice:

  • PremiumCustomer overrides freeDeliveriesPerMonth, and the order gets 8 through the Customer reference: inheritance plus polymorphism.
  • Composition vs. aggregation is decided by who creates and who shares: OrderLines are created inside, suggestions come from outside.
  • Dependencies are the weakest link: change SmsNotifier and Order doesn't need to change.

docs.title: Example 3: Production-grade
docs.text:
Scenario: Hand-drawn sequence diagrams go stale. FreshCart's checkout team generates them from real calls instead: a dynamic proxy wraps each component, records every call, return and exception, and prints a Mermaid sequence diagram. One order succeeds; the next fails because stock runs out, and the failure must appear in the diagram.

Code / Config:

SequenceTraceDemo.java
import java.lang.reflect.InvocationHandler;
import java.lang.reflect.InvocationTargetException;
import java.lang.reflect.Proxy;
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Map;

/**
 * Records real calls between components and prints them as a Mermaid sequence diagram,
 * so the diagram in the docs can be checked against what the code actually does.
 */
public class SequenceTraceDemo {

    interface Inventory { int reserve(String sku, int quantity); }
    interface Payments { String charge(String orderId, long cents); }
    interface Checkout { String placeOrder(String orderId, String sku, int quantity); }

    /** Collects diagram lines. One recorder per traced request. */
    static final class SequenceRecorder {
        private final List<String> lines = new ArrayList<>(List.of("sequenceDiagram"));
        private final ArrayList<String> callers = new ArrayList<>(List.of("App"));

        @SuppressWarnings("unchecked")
        <T> T trace(Class<T> type, String participant, T target) {                     // (1)!
            InvocationHandler handler = (proxy, method, args) -> {
                String caller = callers.get(callers.size() - 1);
                lines.add("    " + caller + "->>" + participant + ": " + method.getName() + "(" + join(args) + ")");
                callers.add(participant);
                try {
                    Object result = method.invoke(target, args);
                    lines.add("    " + participant + "-->>" + caller + ": " + result);
                    return result;
                } catch (InvocationTargetException e) {                                 // (2)!
                    lines.add("    " + participant + "--x" + caller + ": " + e.getCause().getMessage());
                    throw e.getCause();
                } finally {
                    callers.remove(callers.size() - 1);
                }
            };
            return (T) Proxy.newProxyInstance(type.getClassLoader(), new Class<?>[] {type}, handler);
        }

        String diagram() { return String.join("\n", lines); }

        private static String join(Object[] args) {
            if (args == null) return "";
            List<String> parts = new ArrayList<>();
            for (Object a : args) parts.add(String.valueOf(a));
            return String.join(", ", parts);
        }
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Map<String, Integer> stock = new java.util.HashMap<>(Map.of("MILK-1L", 5));
        SequenceRecorder recorder = new SequenceRecorder();

        Inventory inventory = recorder.trace(Inventory.class, "Inventory", (sku, qty) -> {
            int available = stock.getOrDefault(sku, 0);
            if (available < qty) throw new IllegalStateException("only " + available + " left");
            stock.put(sku, available - qty);
            return available - qty;
        });
        Payments payments = recorder.trace(Payments.class, "Payments", (orderId, cents) -> "PAID-" + orderId);
        Checkout checkout = recorder.trace(Checkout.class, "Checkout", (orderId, sku, qty) -> {
            inventory.reserve(sku, qty);
            return payments.charge(orderId, qty * 129L);                                // (3)!
        });

        checkout.placeOrder("FC-4001", "MILK-1L", 2);
        try {
            checkout.placeOrder("FC-4002", "MILK-1L", 9);
        } catch (IllegalStateException e) {
            // already recorded in the diagram as a failed call
        }
        System.out.println(recorder.diagram());
    }
}
  1. java.lang.reflect.Proxy creates an object that implements the interface and sends every call to the handler, which records it. This is the Proxy pattern.
  2. Exceptions from the real object arrive wrapped in InvocationTargetException; the handler records a failed call (--x) and rethrows the original exception.
  3. Calls made inside a traced component go through the other proxies, so nested calls appear with the right caller.

Run it:

java SequenceTraceDemo.java

Output:

sequenceDiagram
    App->>Checkout: placeOrder(FC-4001, MILK-1L, 2)
    Checkout->>Inventory: reserve(MILK-1L, 2)
    Inventory-->>Checkout: 3
    Checkout->>Payments: charge(FC-4001, 258)
    Payments-->>Checkout: PAID-FC-4001
    Checkout-->>App: PAID-FC-4001
    App->>Checkout: placeOrder(FC-4002, MILK-1L, 9)
    Checkout->>Inventory: reserve(MILK-1L, 9)
    Inventory--xCheckout: only 3 left
    Checkout--xApp: only 3 left

The output is valid Mermaid, so it renders like this:

sequenceDiagram
    App->>Checkout: placeOrder(FC-4001, MILK-1L, 2)
    Checkout->>Inventory: reserve(MILK-1L, 2)
    Inventory-->>Checkout: 3
    Checkout->>Payments: charge(FC-4001, 258)
    Payments-->>Checkout: PAID-FC-4001
    Checkout-->>App: PAID-FC-4001
    App->>Checkout: placeOrder(FC-4002, MILK-1L, 9)
    Checkout->>Inventory: reserve(MILK-1L, 9)
    Inventory--xCheckout: only 3 left
    Checkout--xApp: only 3 left

What to notice:

  • Solid arrows (->>) are calls, dashed arrows (-->>) are returns, crosses (--x) are calls that threw.
  • The second order never reaches Payments: the diagram shows exactly where the flow stopped.
  • Because the diagram comes from real calls, it can be regenerated in a test and compared, so it can't drift from the code.
  • The recorder keeps a caller stack in a plain list, so it assumes one thread per recorder. For concurrent requests, create one recorder per request.

docs.title: 7. Pros, Cons & Trade-offs
docs.text: Aspect Pros Cons Simplicity One picture explains several files Full UML is large; most teams use a small subset Performance No runtime cost (except generated diagrams like Example 3) Tracing proxies add overhead if left on in production Scalability Diagrams scale communication across teams Big diagrams of whole systems become unreadable Operability Sequence diagrams make incident timelines clearer Static diagrams don't show runtime configuration Security Diagrams help threat modelling (who calls whom) Diagrams in public docs can reveal internal structure Testability Generated diagrams can be checked in tests Hand-drawn ones can't Cost Mermaid diagrams are free and live in Git Keeping hand-drawn diagrams current takes effort Learning curve A dozen symbols cover pattern diagrams The fine distinctions (aggregation vs. composition) confuse people

docs.title: 8. When to Use / When NOT to Use
docs.text:
Draw a diagram when:

  • explaining a pattern or a design to someone else;
  • a design spans more than three classes;
  • the order of calls matters (sequence) or an object has a lifecycle (state).

Skip it when:

  • the code is a single class: the code is clearer;
  • the diagram would have to show everything; draw the part that matters instead.

The Cheat Sheet has the diagram for every pattern.

docs.title: 9. Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Show only what matters to the point you're making. (Consensus.)
  2. Keep diagrams as text (Mermaid, PlantUML) in the repository. (Opinion, widely practised.)
  3. Draw the happy path and one failure path in sequence diagrams. (Opinion.)
  4. Label relationships with the role (Order --> Customer : placed by). (Consensus.)
  5. Generate diagrams from code or traces where drift is costly. (Opinion.)

docs.title: 10. Pitfalls & Anti-Patterns
docs.text:
Arrow pointing the wrong way

Symptom: a reviewer reads your diagram as "Customer extends PremiumCustomer". Root cause: the triangle was drawn on the child's side. Fix: the triangle and the diamond always sit on the parent or the whole: Customer <|-- PremiumCustomer.

The diagram that lied (production failure mode)

Symptom: an on-call engineer followed the architecture diagram during an outage and spent an hour on a service that was no longer in the call path. Root cause: the diagram was drawn once and never updated after a refactoring. Fix: keep diagrams next to the code, review them in pull requests, and generate sequence diagrams from traces (distributed tracing tools can do this for whole systems).

Everything diagram

Symptom: a 60-box class diagram that nobody reads. Root cause: trying to document the whole system in one view. Fix: one diagram per question ("how does checkout call payments?").

docs.title: 14. Testing It
docs.text: Because Example 3 produces text, a test can assert on it: run the scenario and compare recorder.diagram() with a checked-in .mmd file. A change in call order then fails the build and forces the diagram to be updated in the same pull request.

docs.title: 16. Version Notes
docs.text:
• UML 2.5.1 (OMG, 2017) is the current version of the standard; the subset used in pattern diagrams hasn't changed in decades.
  • Mermaid adds diagram types and syntax regularly. The diagrams in this playbook use only long-standing classDiagram, sequenceDiagram, stateDiagram-v2 and flowchart syntax.

docs.title: 17. Expert Deep Dive
docs.text:
• Diagrams are for decisions, not documentation. Seniors draw a diagram to make a design review faster, then often throw it away. Long-lived diagrams are kept only at the levels that change slowly (system context, container).
  • The C4 model (context, containers, components, code) gives each audience a fitting zoom level. Pattern-level class diagrams are the "code" level, the most detailed and the most likely to go stale.
  • Composition vs. aggregation matters for lifecycle bugs. "Who deletes this?" and "who else holds a reference?" are the questions behind memory leaks, cascade deletes in JPA (CascadeType.REMOVE) and DDD aggregate boundaries. The diamond is a cheap way to make that decision explicit.
  • Generated sequence diagrams scale up. Distributed tracing (OpenTelemetry) turns production traffic into the same picture across services, which beats any hand-drawn diagram during an incident.

War story: the cascade that deleted products

A grocery platform modelled Order to Product with JPA CascadeType.ALL, because the whiteboard diagram showed a filled diamond (composition) between them. When the team added a "delete abandoned orders" job, it also deleted the products those orders referenced, and the catalogue lost hundreds of items overnight. The diagram should have shown aggregation (products exist independently and are shared by many orders), and the cascade should have been on Order to OrderLine only. Lesson: the hollow vs. filled diamond isn't pedantry; it's the lifecycle rule your code will enforce.

docs.title: 18. Interview Corner
docs.text:
🟢 L1–L2🟡 L3🔴 L4–L5💻 Hands-on
  1. What do +, - and # mean in a class diagram? Public, private, protected.
  2. How is an interface shown? A box marked <<interface>>, implemented with a dashed line and hollow triangle.
  3. Composition vs. aggregation? Composition owns the lifecycle of its parts (filled diamond); aggregation shares objects that exist independently (hollow diamond).
  4. What does a sequence diagram show? Calls between objects over time, top to bottom.
  5. Association vs. dependency? Association is a field (long-lived); dependency is a parameter or local use (short-lived).
  1. Draw the Strategy pattern. Context associated with a Strategy interface, realised by concrete strategies.
  2. How do you show a failed call in a sequence diagram? A cross at the end of the arrow (Mermaid --x), or an exception return.
  3. How would you keep diagrams in sync with code? Text diagrams in the repo, reviewed in PRs, and generated from traces where possible.
  4. Why does composition vs. aggregation matter in JPA? It decides cascade behaviour and orphan removal.
  5. When is a state diagram worth drawing? When an object has a lifecycle with rules, such as orders and payments.
  1. How do you document architecture for 30 teams? C4 levels, owned per team, diagrams as code, reviewed with changes.
  2. An incident reveals the diagrams were wrong. What do you change? Make diagrams part of the definition of done, and use tracing for runtime truth.
  3. What can't UML class diagrams show that matters in production? Runtime configuration, concurrency, deployment and failure behaviour.
  4. How would you diagram a saga across five services? A sequence diagram per path (happy path plus compensation), not one diagram for all.
  5. Now the system is event-driven. What diagram helps most? Event flow / sequence diagrams with topics as participants, plus a state diagram of the main entity.

Task: Draw a Mermaid class diagram for Example 2's Order, using all six relationship types.

Solution 
classDiagram
    Customer <|-- PremiumCustomer
    Notifier <|.. SmsNotifier
    Order *-- OrderLine : lines
    Order o-- Product : suggestions
    Order --> Customer : customer
    Order ..> Notifier : confirm()
    Order ..> LocalDate : confirm()

docs.title: 19. Practice
docs.text:
• Draw the class diagram for Example 1 of the OOP Refresher. ??? tip "Hint" One interface, two implementations, both realising it.
  • Add an Audit component to Example 3 that Checkout calls after payment, and check the new diagram. ??? tip "Hint" Create a traced Audit interface and call it inside the checkout lambda.
  • Add a "Returned" state to the order state diagram: from Delivered, within 24 hours. ??? tip "Hint" Delivered --> Returned : returned within 24h and Returned --> [*].

docs.title: 20. Quick Revision Card
docs.text:
Remember in 30 seconds

  • Box = class; <<interface>>, <<abstract>>; + public, - private, # protected.
  • Triangle = inheritance (solid) or realisation (dashed), on the parent's side.
  • Diamond = composition (filled, owns) or aggregation (hollow, shares), on the whole's side.
  • Arrow = association (solid, field) or dependency (dashed, parameter).
  • Sequence: calls down the page; dashed returns; x for failures.
classDiagram
    Parent <|-- Child
    Interface <|.. Impl
    Whole *-- Part
    Group o-- Member
    A --> B
    A ..> Helper

docs.text:

  • OMG Unified Modeling Language specification

docs.title: What Are Design Patterns
docs.text:
L0 ⚪ Orientation · ⏱ 15 min read · Prerequisites: none

TL;DR

A design pattern is a named, proven solution to a design problem that keeps coming back, described so you can adapt it rather than copy it. The classic catalogue is the Gang of Four's 23 patterns, grouped into creational, structural and behavioural. Learn them to recognise problems faster and to talk about designs in a few words.

docs.title: 1. What It Is
docs.text:
Plain English. When experienced developers solve the same kind of problem many times, the good solutions start to look alike. A design pattern writes one of those solutions down, gives it a name ("Strategy", "Observer", "Adapter"), and explains when it helps and what it costs.

Precise definition. The GoF book defines design patterns as "descriptions of communicating objects and classes that are customized to solve a general design problem in a particular context." A pattern is not a library or a piece of code to paste: it's a description of the roles (classes, interfaces) and how they collaborate. Your implementation will differ every time.

New terms on this page:

  • Intent: the one-sentence summary of what the pattern does.
  • Participants: the roles in the pattern (for Strategy: context, strategy, concrete strategy).
  • Consequences: the trade-offs the pattern brings.
  • Idiom: a pattern specific to one language (for example Java's try-with-resources or the lazy holder idiom).

docs.title: 2. Why It Exists
docs.text:
The architect Christopher Alexander described patterns for towns and buildings in A Pattern Language (1977). Kent Beck and Ward Cunningham applied the idea to software in 1987, and in 1994 Erich Gamma, Richard Helm, Ralph Johnson and John Vlissides (the "Gang of Four", or GoF) published Design Patterns: Elements of Reusable Object-Oriented Software.

Before shared catalogues, every team reinvented the same solutions, often badly, and had no short way to describe them. Without patterns you still get structure, but it's accidental: a "notification manager" that turns out to be a half-finished Observer, or a 500-line switch that should have been a Strategy.

docs.title: 3. Mental Model / Analogy
docs.text:
Analogy. A recipe card for "white sauce" doesn't say which pan or brand of butter to use. It tells a cook the proven combination (fat + flour + milk, whisked over heat) and what can go wrong (lumps). A cook adapts it for lasagne or mac and cheese. A design pattern is a recipe card for code structure.

Technical model. Think of a pattern as a small graph: roles (nodes) and the calls between them (edges), plus a list of forces it balances (flexibility vs. simplicity, for example). When you see that shape in a problem, the pattern tells you a tested way to arrange your classes.

docs.title: 4. How It Works
docs.text:
You use a pattern in four steps: recognise the problem, pick a candidate pattern, map its roles onto your classes, and check the consequences are acceptable.

flowchart LR
    A["Recurring problem in your code"] --> B["Recognise the forces"]
    B --> C{"Matches a known pattern?"}
    C -- "yes" --> D["Map roles to your classes"]
    D --> E["Check consequences and trade-offs"]
    E --> F["Implement and name it in code and docs"]
    C -- "no" --> G["Keep the simplest design that works"]

Each GoF pattern is documented with the same sections, which is also how you should read one:

Section What it tells you Name and classification What to call it and whether it's creational, structural or behavioural Intent One sentence: what it does Also known as Other names (Strategy is also called Policy) Motivation A concrete scenario showing the problem Applicability When to use it Structure A class diagram of the roles Participants and collaborations Who does what, and who calls whom Consequences The benefits and the costs Implementation and sample code Hints, variations and example code Known uses Real systems that use it Related patterns Similar or complementary patterns

docs.title: Christopher Alexander and the GoF book (1994)
docs.text:
• Description: Patterns started in architecture. Alexander wrote that each pattern "describes a problem which occurs over and over again in our environment, and then describes the core of the solution to that problem, in such a way that you can use this solution a million times over, without ever doing it the same way twice." The GoF book brought the idea to object-oriented design with 23 patterns and examples in C++ and Smalltalk.
  • How to use it: read the GoF introduction (chapter 1) once; its two principles, program to an interface and favour composition over inheritance, matter more than any single pattern.
  • Best practice: treat the book as a catalogue to look things up in, not a novel to memorise.
  • Gotcha: the book's examples predate Java; several patterns are much shorter in modern Java (see Patterns in Modern Java).

docs.title: Anatomy of a pattern: intent, problem, solution, consequences
docs.text:
• Description: Every pattern has four essential parts, named in the GoF book: a name, the problem (when to apply it), the solution (the roles and collaborations) and the consequences (trade-offs).
  • How to use it: before using a pattern, write one line for each of the four parts in your design note or pull request description.
  • Best practice: read Consequences first. It tells you what the pattern costs.
  • Gotcha: copying the Structure diagram exactly, including roles you don't need.

docs.title: Creational, structural and behavioural categories
docs.text:
• Description: Creational patterns deal with how objects are created (Factory Method, Builder). Structural patterns deal with how classes and objects are composed into bigger structures (Adapter, Decorator). Behavioural patterns deal with how objects distribute responsibility and communicate (Strategy, Observer).
  • How to use it: when stuck, ask which kind of problem you have: "creating things", "fitting things together" or "who does what and who tells whom". That narrows 23 patterns to about 5–11.
  • Best practice: learn two or three patterns from each category first (this playbook's L1 does exactly that).
  • Gotcha: the GoF also classify patterns by scope (class vs. object); it matters less day to day than the three purposes.

docs.title: Patterns vs. idioms vs. architectural styles vs. principles
docs.text:
• Description: A principle is a guideline (SOLID, DRY). A design pattern is a solution at the level of a few classes. An idiom is a pattern tied to one language (Java's lazy holder idiom). An architectural pattern or style shapes a whole application (layered, hexagonal, microservices).
  • How to use it: use principles to judge designs, design patterns to structure classes, architectural patterns to structure systems.
  • Pros: clear vocabulary avoids talking past each other in reviews.
  • Cons: the boundaries are fuzzy; MVC is called both a design pattern and an architectural pattern.
  • Best practice: say which level you mean ("Repository as in DDD, not Spring Data's interface").
  • Gotcha: treating a principle as a pattern ("we implemented SOLID") or a pattern as a principle ("always use factories").

docs.title: The 23 GoF patterns at a glance
docs.text:
• Description: the full catalogue, with where each is covered in this playbook.
Creational (5) Structural (7) Behavioural (11) Abstract Factory Adapter Chain of Responsibility Builder Bridge Command Factory Method Composite Interpreter Prototype Decorator Iterator Singleton Facade Mediator Flyweight Memento Proxy Observer State Strategy Template Method Visitor
  • Best practice: learn the most common ones first: Strategy, Observer, Factory Method, Builder, Adapter, Decorator, Facade, Template Method.
  • Gotcha: some (Interpreter, Flyweight, Memento) are rare in business code; know them, don't force them.

docs.title: Example 1: Minimal (L0)
docs.text:
Scenario: FreshCart sends "Order placed" messages by SMS and email, and the product team wants push notifications next. Compare a switch that must be edited for every channel with the Strategy pattern, where a new channel is a new class.

Code / Config:

NotifierDemo.java
import java.util.Map;

public class NotifierDemo {

    // ---- Without a pattern: every new channel means editing this method ----
    static String notifyWithSwitch(String channel, String customer, String message) {
        switch (channel) {
            case "sms":   return "SMS to " + customer + ": " + message;
            case "email": return "Email to " + customer + ": " + message;
            default: throw new IllegalArgumentException("Unknown channel: " + channel);
        }
    }

    // ---- With the Strategy pattern: each channel is an object behind one interface ----
    interface Notifier {                                              // (1)!
        String send(String customer, String message);
    }

    static final class SmsNotifier implements Notifier {              // (2)!
        public String send(String customer, String message) { return "SMS to " + customer + ": " + message; }
    }

    static final class EmailNotifier implements Notifier {
        public String send(String customer, String message) { return "Email to " + customer + ": " + message; }
    }

    static final class PushNotifier implements Notifier {             // (3)!
        public String send(String customer, String message) { return "Push to " + customer + ": " + message; }
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println(notifyWithSwitch("sms", "Asha", "Order placed"));

        Map<String, Notifier> notifiers = Map.of(
                "sms", new SmsNotifier(), "email", new EmailNotifier(), "push", new PushNotifier());
        for (String channel : new String[] {"sms", "email", "push"}) {
            System.out.println(notifiers.get(channel).send("Asha", "Order placed"));  // (4)!
        }
    }
}
  1. The strategy role: one interface for "how to send".
  2. A concrete strategy. Each channel is its own small class.
  3. Push was added without touching SMS, email or the calling code.
  4. The context (here, main) picks a strategy and calls it without knowing which one it is.

Run it:

java NotifierDemo.java

Output:

SMS to Asha: Order placed
SMS to Asha: Order placed
Email to Asha: Order placed
Push to Asha: Order placed

What to notice:

  • Both versions print the same result; the difference is how they change.
  • The pattern is visible from the names alone: anyone who knows Strategy understands Notifier instantly.
  • For two channels that never change, the switch would be fine. Patterns pay off when variation is real.

docs.title: Example 2: Realistic (in FreshCart grocery delivery)
docs.text:
Scenario: One FreshCart flow touches all three categories: choosing a delivery type (creational), booking a rider through a partner SDK whose API doesn't match ours (structural), and telling the app and the store when an order's status changes (behavioural).

Code / Config:

ThreeCategoriesDemo.java
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.function.Consumer;

public class ThreeCategoriesDemo {

    // ===== Creational: Factory Method decides WHICH object to create =====
    interface Delivery { String describe(); }
    record StandardDelivery(String slot) implements Delivery {
        public String describe() { return "standard delivery in slot " + slot; }
    }
    record ExpressDelivery(int minutes) implements Delivery {
        public String describe() { return "express delivery within " + minutes + " min"; }
    }

    static Delivery createDelivery(boolean express, String slot) {          // (1)!
        return express ? new ExpressDelivery(30) : new StandardDelivery(slot);
    }

    // ===== Structural: Adapter makes a third-party API fit OUR interface =====
    /** Pretend this class comes from a rider-partner SDK we can't change. */
    static final class PartnerRiderApi {
        String requestCourier(double lat, double lon, String ref) {
            return "partner courier booked for " + ref + " at " + lat + "," + lon;
        }
    }

    interface RiderDispatch { String dispatch(String orderId, String address); }

    static final class PartnerRiderAdapter implements RiderDispatch {       // (2)!
        private final PartnerRiderApi api = new PartnerRiderApi();
        public String dispatch(String orderId, String address) {
            // Real code would geocode the address; this example uses a fixed point.
            return api.requestCourier(12.97, 77.59, orderId);
        }
    }

    // ===== Behavioural: Observer tells interested parties about changes =====
    static final class OrderStatus {
        private final List<Consumer<String>> listeners = new ArrayList<>();
        void subscribe(Consumer<String> listener) { listeners.add(listener); }
        void change(String orderId, String status) {                        // (3)!
            listeners.forEach(l -> l.accept(orderId + " is now " + status));
        }
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("Creational:  " + createDelivery(false, "18:00-19:00").describe());
        System.out.println("Creational:  " + createDelivery(true, "ignored").describe());
        System.out.println("Structural:  " + new PartnerRiderAdapter().dispatch("FC-1001", "12 MG Road"));

        OrderStatus status = new OrderStatus();
        status.subscribe(msg -> System.out.println("Behavioural: app push   -> " + msg));
        status.subscribe(msg -> System.out.println("Behavioural: store desk -> " + msg));
        status.change("FC-1001", "PACKED");
    }
}
  1. Factory Method (creational): callers ask for "a delivery" and the method decides which class to create.
  2. Adapter (structural): wraps the partner API behind our own RiderDispatch interface.
  3. Observer (behavioural): every subscriber hears about the change; the order doesn't know who they are.

Run it:

java ThreeCategoriesDemo.java

Output:

Creational:  standard delivery in slot 18:00-19:00
Creational:  express delivery within 30 min
Structural:  partner courier booked for FC-1001 at 12.97,77.59
Behavioural: app push   -> FC-1001 is now PACKED
Behavioural: store desk -> FC-1001 is now PACKED

What to notice:

  • Each pattern solves a different kind of problem, which is exactly what the three categories mean.
  • The Adapter keeps the partner's odd method signature (requestCourier(lat, lon, ref)) out of the rest of the code.
  • The Observer uses Consumer<String> lambdas: in modern Java many patterns don't need a named class per role.

docs.title: Example 3: Production-grade
docs.text:
Scenario: A small checkout combines three patterns the way real code does. Orders are built with a Builder that reports all validation problems at once, delivery is priced by a Strategy, and receipts, loyalty and metrics listen as Observers. A failing listener (the loyalty service is down) must not stop the order or the other listeners.

Code / Config:

CheckoutDemo.java
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Objects;

/** Three patterns working together in one small, production-shaped checkout. */
public class CheckoutDemo {

    // ---------- Builder (creational): a valid, immutable Order or nothing ----------
    record Order(String id, String customer, long basketInCents, boolean express) {
        static Builder builder() { return new Builder(); }

        static final class Builder {                                        // (1)!
            private String id;
            private String customer;
            private long basketInCents = -1;
            private boolean express;

            Builder id(String id) { this.id = id; return this; }
            Builder customer(String customer) { this.customer = customer; return this; }
            Builder basketInCents(long cents) { this.basketInCents = cents; return this; }
            Builder express(boolean express) { this.express = express; return this; }

            Order build() {
                List<String> problems = new ArrayList<>();
                if (id == null || id.isBlank()) problems.add("id is required");
                if (customer == null || customer.isBlank()) problems.add("customer is required");
                if (basketInCents <= 0) problems.add("basket must be positive");
                if (!problems.isEmpty()) throw new IllegalStateException("Invalid order: " + String.join(", ", problems));
                return new Order(id, customer, basketInCents, express);
            }
        }
    }

    // ---------- Strategy (behavioural): how delivery is priced ----------
    interface FeeStrategy { long feeInCents(Order order); }                 // (2)!

    static final FeeStrategy STANDARD = order -> order.basketInCents() >= 5_000 ? 0 : 499;
    static final FeeStrategy EXPRESS = order -> STANDARD.feeInCents(order) + 300;

    // ---------- Observer (behavioural): who hears about a placed order ----------
    interface CheckoutListener { void orderPlaced(Order order, long totalInCents); }

    static final class Checkout {
        private final List<CheckoutListener> listeners = new ArrayList<>();

        void addListener(CheckoutListener listener) { listeners.add(Objects.requireNonNull(listener)); }

        long place(Order order) {
            FeeStrategy strategy = order.express() ? EXPRESS : STANDARD;
            long total = order.basketInCents() + strategy.feeInCents(order);
            for (CheckoutListener listener : listeners) {
                try {
                    listener.orderPlaced(order, total);
                } catch (RuntimeException e) {                              // (3)!
                    System.out.println("listener_failed order=" + order.id() + " error=\"" + e.getMessage() + "\"");
                }
            }
            return total;
        }
    }

    static String money(long cents) { return "$%d.%02d".formatted(cents / 100, cents % 100); }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Checkout checkout = new Checkout();
        checkout.addListener((o, total) -> System.out.println("receipt order=" + o.id() + " total=" + money(total)));
        checkout.addListener((o, total) -> { throw new RuntimeException("loyalty service unavailable"); });
        checkout.addListener((o, total) -> System.out.println("metric orders_placed{express=" + o.express() + "} +1"));

        checkout.place(Order.builder().id("FC-2001").customer("Asha").basketInCents(3_250).build());
        checkout.place(Order.builder().id("FC-2002").customer("Ravi").basketInCents(6_100).express(true).build());

        try {
            Order.builder().id(" ").basketInCents(0).build();
        } catch (IllegalStateException e) {
            System.out.println("rejected: " + e.getMessage());
        }
    }
}
  1. The Builder collects every problem and refuses to build an invalid Order, so the rest of the code can trust it.
  2. Strategies as lambdas: EXPRESS reuses STANDARD and adds a surcharge.
  3. Each listener is isolated: one failure is logged and the loop continues.

Run it:

java CheckoutDemo.java

Output:

receipt order=FC-2001 total=$37.49
listener_failed order=FC-2001 error="loyalty service unavailable"
metric orders_placed{express=false} +1
receipt order=FC-2002 total=$64.00
listener_failed order=FC-2002 error="loyalty service unavailable"
metric orders_placed{express=true} +1
rejected: Invalid order: id is required, customer is required, basket must be positive

What to notice:

  • Patterns combine: Builder produces the object, Strategy prices it, Observer reacts to it.
  • The failing loyalty listener shows up as a log line, and the metric listener after it still runs.
  • The rejected order lists three problems at once, which is friendlier for API clients and mobile forms than failing on the first.
  • FC-2002 is over $50, so standard delivery is free and express adds only $3.00: total $64.00.

docs.title: 7. Pros, Cons & Trade-offs
docs.text: Aspect Pros Cons Simplicity A named pattern explains a design in one word Applied without need, a pattern adds classes and indirection Performance Most patterns cost nothing measurable on the JVM Some (Proxy, Observer with many listeners) add overhead on hot paths Scalability Patterns make code easier to extend as the team grows Teams can standardise on patterns that no longer fit Operability Clear seams for logging, metrics and error isolation More layers to step through when debugging Security Proxies and facades give natural places for checks Extra indirection can hide where a check is missing Testability Most patterns introduce interfaces you can fake Over-abstracted code needs many fakes per test Cost Reusing proven designs avoids expensive mistakes Learning and reviewing pattern-heavy code takes time Learning curve A shared vocabulary speeds up onboarding 23+ patterns is a lot to learn; beginners over-apply them

docs.title: 8. When to Use / When NOT to Use
docs.text:
Use a pattern when:

  • You can name the problem it solves in your code today, not hypothetically.
  • The variation it allows (new channels, new rules, new types) is likely.
  • The team knows the pattern, so naming it helps communication.

Don't use a pattern when:

  • A simpler construct does the job: a method, a lambda, an enum, a switch over a sealed type.
  • You're adding it "in case we need it later" (see Why Patterns Matter).
  • The framework already does it for you (Spring's DI container is a factory; don't wrap it in another).

See the Decision Guide for "which pattern when".

docs.title: 9. Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Name the pattern in class names or Javadoc (PartnerRiderAdapter), because it tells readers the design in one word. (Consensus.)
  2. Start from the problem, not the pattern. (Consensus.)
  3. Read the Consequences section before implementing. (Opinion.)
  4. Prefer the smallest Java construct that expresses the pattern: a lambda before a class, a record before a hand-written class. (Opinion, common in modern Java.)
  5. Leave out roles you don't need. A Strategy with one implementation isn't a Strategy yet. (Consensus.)
  6. Document why you chose a pattern in the pull request or an architecture decision record. (Opinion.)

docs.title: 10. Pitfalls & Anti-Patterns
docs.text:
Pattern fever

Symptom: a beginner's project with AbstractNotificationFactoryProvider and five layers for one feature. Root cause: patterns used to show knowledge rather than to solve a problem. Fix: delete roles that have one implementation and no planned variation; inline until the code is boringly simple.

Name without the pattern

Symptom: a class called OrderObserver that the order calls directly with if (type == ...) branches. Root cause: pattern names used as decoration. Fix: either implement the pattern's collaboration properly or rename the class to say what it does.

One bad listener takes down checkout (production failure mode)

Symptom: orders failed with a 500 error whenever the loyalty service was slow. Root cause: the Observer loop called listeners synchronously with no error isolation, so one exception aborted the order. Fix: isolate each listener (as in Example 3), or deliver events asynchronously and retry. See Observer.

docs.title: 14. Testing It
docs.text: Patterns usually make code easier to test because each role can be tested alone and replaced with a fake. In Example 3 you can test each fee strategy with a plain assertEquals, and test Checkout by adding a listener that records what it receives. Testing Patterns covers this in depth.

docs.title: 16. Version Notes
docs.text: The GoF catalogue hasn't changed since 1994, but Java has: lambdas (Java 8) shrink Strategy, Command and Observer; records (Java 16) shrink value classes and Builders' targets; sealed types and pattern matching (Java 17–21) give an alternative to Visitor. The Java Version History for Patterns has the full list.

docs.title: 17. Expert Deep Dive
docs.text:
What a 15-year engineer knows about patterns that a 2-year engineer doesn't:

  • Patterns are discovered, not invented. A real pattern has known uses, usually in three or more independent systems. Be suspicious of a team-invented "pattern" that only exists in one code base.
  • Patterns compensate for language features. Peter Norvig's 1996 talk showed that many GoF patterns become invisible or simpler in dynamic languages with first-class functions. Java's lambdas and sealed types are doing the same thing now, so the intent outlives the structure.
  • The vocabulary is the main value. In design reviews, "put an anti-corruption layer (an Adapter) in front of the partner API" ends a 20-minute discussion. That only works if the team shares the terms, which is why seniors invest in teaching them.
  • Patterns have scale. The same idea repeats at different sizes: Strategy (classes) → plugin architecture (modules) → feature flags choosing services (systems). Recognising the shape at any scale is an expert skill.
  • Reviewing legacy code: map the existing accidental structures to named patterns first ("this is a half Observer"). It makes the refactoring plan obvious and gives you names for the tickets.

War story: the 1,800-line pricing switch

A grocery platform priced orders in one method with a switch on promotion type and nested ifs for region and customer tier. Each new campaign took a week, and twice a campaign change broke an unrelated region's prices in production, found only by customer complaints. The team traced both incidents to edits in shared branches of the switch. They introduced a Promotion Strategy interface, moved one promotion type per sprint into its own class with its own tests, and kept the old switch as the fallback until it was empty. New campaigns dropped to a day, and the cross-region bugs stopped. Lesson: the pattern wasn't clever; it simply gave each rule its own place to live and to be tested.

19. Practice
docs.text:
• For each of these, say which category it belongs to: "create a report in PDF or CSV", "make an old SOAP client look like our REST interface", "notify three services when stock runs out". ??? tip "Hint" Creational (Factory Method), structural (Adapter), behavioural (Observer).
  • Find two patterns in the JDK classes you already use. ??? tip "Hint" Iterator in collections, decorators in java.io (BufferedReader wraps a Reader).
  • Add a "store printer" listener to Example 2 that prints only when the status is PACKED. ??? tip "Hint" status.subscribe(msg -> { if (msg.endsWith("PACKED")) System.out.println(...); });

docs.title: 20. Quick Revision Card
docs.text:
Remember in 30 seconds

  • Pattern = named, proven solution to a recurring design problem.
  • Four parts: name, problem, solution, consequences.
  • GoF 1994: 23 patterns, creational (5), structural (7), behavioural (11).
  • Principles judge designs; patterns structure classes; architectural styles structure systems.
  • Use a pattern for a real, current problem; prefer the smallest Java construct.
interface Strategy { long apply(long input); }          // role
Strategy standard = in -> in >= 5_000 ? 0 : 499;        // concrete strategy (lambda)
long fee = standard.apply(basketTotal);                 // context uses it
