docs.title: Why Patterns Matter (and When They Don't)
docs.text:
L0 ⚪ Orientation · ⏱ 12 min read · Prerequisites: What Are Design Patterns

TL;DR

Patterns matter because they give teams a shared vocabulary and proven ways to keep code easy to change. They stop mattering, and start hurting, when you add them for changes that never come. Modern Java has made several patterns much smaller, so the goal is the pattern's intent, not its original class diagram.

docs.title: 1. What It Is
docs.text:
Plain English. This page is about the value of patterns: what you gain by knowing and using them, and the cost you pay when you use them in the wrong place.

Precise definition. A pattern's value is the reduction in the cost of change and communication it brings, minus the cost of the indirection it adds. Two terms you'll meet:

  • Speculative generality: abstraction added for flexibility nobody needs yet (a code smell named by Martin Fowler and Kent Beck in Refactoring).
  • Cost of change: how much code you must touch, re-test and re-deploy to make a typical change.

docs.title: 2. Why It Exists
docs.text:
Software is changed far more often than it is written. Teams that can't describe a design quickly spend review time re-explaining it, and code that isn't arranged for its likely changes turns every feature into edits across many files. Patterns address both.

But the industry also learned the opposite lesson: early-2000s enterprise Java was famous for factories of factories and layers that only delegated, which made simple changes slow. Knowing when not to use a pattern is as important as knowing the pattern.

docs.title: 3. Mental Model / Analogy
docs.text:
Analogy. Shelving in a supermarket. A few well-chosen shelves (dairy, bakery, produce) let staff restock fast and customers find things. A shelf for every single product would be "flexible", but no one could find anything and every new product would need new carpentry. Patterns are shelves: put them where things actually vary.

Technical model. Picture your code as having axes of change: places where new variants keep arriving (new promotions, new payment providers). A pattern placed on a real axis turns future edits into additions. A pattern placed where nothing varies is pure cost: more files, more indirection, no benefit.

docs.title: 4. How It Works
docs.text:
Use this loop to decide whether a pattern earns its place:

flowchart TD
    A["A change request arrives"] --> B{"Second time this kind of change has happened?"}
    B -- "no" --> C["Make the simplest change"]
    B -- "yes" --> D{"Will more of these changes come?"}
    D -- "no" --> C
    D -- "yes" --> E["Refactor toward a pattern on that axis"]
    E --> F["Next change of this kind is an addition, not an edit"]

This is the "rule of three" applied to design: write it once, tolerate the duplication twice, refactor to a pattern the third time (or the second, if you're sure more is coming).

docs.title: Shared vocabulary in code review
docs.text:
• Description: A pattern name compresses a paragraph of explanation into one word. "This is a Decorator around the repository" tells a reviewer the class structure, the call flow and the testing approach.
  • How to use it: name classes after their role (CachingProductCatalog as a Decorator, PartnerRiderAdapter) and mention the pattern in the pull request description.
  • Pros: faster reviews; easier onboarding; fewer misunderstandings.
  • Cons: only works if everyone knows the term; jargon excludes newcomers.
  • Best practice: link new team members to the relevant pattern page the first time it comes up in their review.
  • Gotcha: using the name for something that isn't the pattern misleads more than no name at all.

docs.title: Designing for change
docs.text:
• Description: Patterns let you add new behaviour by adding code instead of editing existing code (the Open/Closed Principle). That keeps changes small and reduces regressions.
  • How to use it: find the axis that changes most (for FreshCart: promotions, payment providers, delivery partners) and put an interface on it.
  • Pros: small, safe changes; each variant is testable alone; parallel work without merge conflicts.
  • Cons: you must guess the axis right; the wrong guess makes the real change harder.
  • Best practice: use history: git log on a file shows which kinds of changes actually happen.
  • Gotcha: designing for every imaginable change produces the over-engineering below.

docs.title: Pattern fever and speculative generality
docs.text:
• Description: Adding patterns because they might be useful. The code gains interfaces with one implementation, factories that build one thing, and layers that only forward calls.
  • How to use it (to fix it): inline the indirection, keep the simple version, and reintroduce the pattern when the second real variant appears.
  • Pros (of resisting it): less code, easier navigation, faster builds and onboarding.
  • Cons (of resisting it): you'll occasionally refactor later; with tests that's cheap.
  • Best practice: follow YAGNI ("you aren't gonna need it") for patterns, and keep code easy to refactor instead.
  • Gotcha: public library APIs are the exception; they can't be refactored freely, so some up-front extension points are justified (see Designing Frameworks and Libraries).

docs.title: Patterns that modern Java made smaller
docs.text:
• Description: Lambdas (Java 8), records (16), sealed types (17) and pattern matching for switch (21) express several patterns in far less code. Strategy and Command become functional interfaces, Visitor can become a switch over a sealed interface, and value objects become records.
  • How to use it: reach for the language feature first, and write the classic class-based form when you need state, multiple methods or extensibility by other teams.
  • Pros: less boilerplate; the compiler checks exhaustiveness for sealed types.
  • Cons: less discoverable than a named class; lambdas give poorer stack traces and can't hold multiple methods.
  • Best practice: give lambda strategies names (static final FeeStrategy EXPRESS = ...) so they're findable and testable.
  • Gotcha: a sealed interface is closed: other modules can't add variants. That's the point, but it's wrong for plugin-style extension.

docs.title: Example 1: Minimal (L0)
docs.text:
Scenario: A developer is asked to print a greeting. They build a Strategy and a Factory for it "to be flexible". Compare that with what the requirement needed.

Code / Config:

OverEngineeringDemo.java
public class OverEngineeringDemo {

    // ---- Pattern fever: four types to format one greeting that never varies ----
    interface GreetingStrategy { String greet(String name); }                 // (1)!
    static final class DefaultGreetingStrategy implements GreetingStrategy {
        public String greet(String name) { return "Hello, " + name + "!"; }
    }
    interface GreetingStrategyFactory { GreetingStrategy create(); }
    static final class DefaultGreetingStrategyFactory implements GreetingStrategyFactory {
        public GreetingStrategy create() { return new DefaultGreetingStrategy(); }
    }

    // ---- What the requirement actually needed ----
    static String greet(String name) { return "Hello, " + name + "!"; }        // (2)!

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        GreetingStrategyFactory factory = new DefaultGreetingStrategyFactory();
        System.out.println("over-engineered: " + factory.create().greet("Asha"));
        System.out.println("simple:          " + greet("Asha"));
    }
}
  1. Four types (two interfaces, two classes) with one implementation each, and no second greeting on the roadmap.
  2. One method does the same job.

Run it:

java OverEngineeringDemo.java

Output:

over-engineered: Hello, Asha!
simple:          Hello, Asha!

What to notice:

  • Identical behaviour, four times the code.
  • Nothing about the requirement varies, so there's no axis of change for a pattern to sit on.
  • If a second greeting arrives later, extracting an interface from greet takes a minute with an IDE.

docs.title: Example 2: Realistic (in FreshCart grocery delivery)
docs.text:
Scenario: FreshCart's marketing team launches a new promotion type almost every sprint. Version 1 handles promotions in a switch; version 2 uses the Strategy pattern. In a later sprint, marketing asks for "25¢ off every item when you buy 10 or more".

Code / Config:

PromotionDemo.java
import java.util.List;

public class PromotionDemo {

    record Basket(long totalInCents, int items) { }

    // ---- Version 1: a switch that grows with every marketing idea ----
    static long discountWithSwitch(String promo, Basket basket) {             // (1)!
        return switch (promo) {
            case "NONE" -> 0;
            case "TEN_PERCENT" -> basket.totalInCents() / 10;
            case "FLAT_5_OVER_40" -> basket.totalInCents() >= 4_000 ? 500 : 0;
            default -> throw new IllegalArgumentException("Unknown promotion " + promo);
        };
    }

    // ---- Version 2: Strategy. New promotions are new objects, nothing else changes ----
    interface Promotion {                                                      // (2)!
        String code();
        long discountInCents(Basket basket);
    }

    record PercentOff(String code, int percent) implements Promotion {
        public long discountInCents(Basket b) { return b.totalInCents() * percent / 100; }
    }

    record FlatOffOver(String code, long offInCents, long thresholdInCents) implements Promotion {
        public long discountInCents(Basket b) { return b.totalInCents() >= thresholdInCents ? offInCents : 0; }
    }

    /** Added in a later sprint WITHOUT editing any existing promotion or the checkout. */
    record BuyManySaveMore(String code, int minItems, long offPerItemInCents) implements Promotion {   // (3)!
        public long discountInCents(Basket b) { return b.items() >= minItems ? b.items() * offPerItemInCents : 0; }
    }

    static String money(long cents) { return "$%d.%02d".formatted(cents / 100, cents % 100); }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Basket basket = new Basket(4_800, 12);
        System.out.println("switch   TEN_PERCENT    -> " + money(discountWithSwitch("TEN_PERCENT", basket)));
        System.out.println("switch   FLAT_5_OVER_40 -> " + money(discountWithSwitch("FLAT_5_OVER_40", basket)));

        List<Promotion> promotions = List.of(
                new PercentOff("TEN_PERCENT", 10),
                new FlatOffOver("FLAT_5_OVER_40", 500, 4_000),
                new BuyManySaveMore("BULK_10", 10, 25));
        for (Promotion p : promotions) {
            System.out.printf("strategy %-14s -> %s%n", p.code(), money(p.discountInCents(basket)));
        }
    }
}
  1. Every new promotion means editing this method and re-testing all existing cases.
  2. The axis of change (promotion rules) gets an interface.
  3. The new requirement is one new record. No existing code was touched.

Run it:

java PromotionDemo.java

Output:

switch   TEN_PERCENT    -> $4.80
switch   FLAT_5_OVER_40 -> $5.00
strategy TEN_PERCENT    -> $4.80
strategy FLAT_5_OVER_40 -> $5.00
strategy BULK_10        -> $3.00

What to notice:

  • Here the pattern earns its place, because promotions really do change every sprint.
  • Promotions are records: the rule's parameters (percent, threshold) become data, so marketing could configure new instances without code.
  • Compare with Example 1: same pattern, opposite verdict, because the context differs.

docs.title: Example 3: Production-grade
docs.text:
Scenario: The delivery service handles four event types (rider assigned, picked up, delivered, failed) and needs several operations on them: customer push text, metrics, later audit logs. Classically this is the Visitor pattern. With Java 21, a sealed interface plus pattern matching for switch does the same job, and the compiler refuses to build if a new event type isn't handled. Invalid events must be rejected at creation.

Code / Config:

DeliveryEventsDemo.java
import java.util.EnumMap;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Map;

/**
 * The classic answer to "add operations over a fixed set of event types" is the Visitor pattern
 * (an interface with one visit method per type plus accept() on every type). With Java 21,
 * sealed interfaces and pattern matching for switch do the same job in a fraction of the code.
 */
public class DeliveryEventsDemo {

    sealed interface DeliveryEvent permits Assigned, PickedUp, Delivered, Failed { // (1)!
        String orderId();
    }
    record Assigned(String orderId, String rider) implements DeliveryEvent { }
    record PickedUp(String orderId, int etaMinutes) implements DeliveryEvent { }
    record Delivered(String orderId) implements DeliveryEvent { }
    record Failed(String orderId, String reason) implements DeliveryEvent {
        Failed {
            if (reason == null || reason.isBlank()) throw new IllegalArgumentException("Failed event needs a reason");
        }
    }

    enum Kind { ASSIGNED, PICKED_UP, DELIVERED, FAILED }

    /** Operation 1: the customer-facing push text. */
    static String customerMessage(DeliveryEvent event) {
        return switch (event) {                                                  // (2)!
            case Assigned a -> a.rider() + " is your rider for " + a.orderId();
            case PickedUp p when p.etaMinutes() <= 10 -> "Almost there! " + p.orderId() + " arrives in " + p.etaMinutes() + " min";
            case PickedUp p -> p.orderId() + " is on its way, ETA " + p.etaMinutes() + " min";
            case Delivered d -> d.orderId() + " delivered. Enjoy!";
            case Failed f -> "Sorry, " + f.orderId() + " could not be delivered: " + f.reason();
        };
    }

    /** Operation 2: the metric bucket. Adding a new event type makes BOTH switches fail to compile. */
    static Kind kind(DeliveryEvent event) {                                      // (3)!
        return switch (event) {
            case Assigned a -> Kind.ASSIGNED;
            case PickedUp p -> Kind.PICKED_UP;
            case Delivered d -> Kind.DELIVERED;
            case Failed f -> Kind.FAILED;
        };
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        List<DeliveryEvent> events = List.of(
                new Assigned("FC-3001", "Imran"),
                new PickedUp("FC-3001", 25),
                new PickedUp("FC-3001", 8),
                new Delivered("FC-3001"),
                new Failed("FC-3002", "customer not reachable"));

        Map<Kind, Integer> counts = new EnumMap<>(Kind.class);
        for (DeliveryEvent event : events) {
            System.out.println("push: " + customerMessage(event));
            counts.merge(kind(event), 1, Integer::sum);
        }
        System.out.println("metrics: " + counts);

        try {
            new Failed("FC-3003", " ");
        } catch (IllegalArgumentException e) {
            System.out.println("rejected: " + e.getMessage());                  // (4)!
        }
    }
}
  1. sealed ... permits fixes the set of event types, so switch can be checked for exhaustiveness.
  2. Pattern matching with a when guard: two cases for PickedUp depending on the ETA. No default branch is needed.
  3. A second operation over the same types without adding a method to any event (Visitor's intent).
  4. The compact constructor rejects a Failed event without a reason.

Run it:

java DeliveryEventsDemo.java

Output:

push: Imran is your rider for FC-3001
push: FC-3001 is on its way, ETA 25 min
push: Almost there! FC-3001 arrives in 8 min
push: FC-3001 delivered. Enjoy!
push: Sorry, FC-3002 could not be delivered: customer not reachable
metrics: {ASSIGNED=1, PICKED_UP=2, DELIVERED=1, FAILED=1}
rejected: Failed event needs a reason

What to notice:

  • A classic Visitor needs an interface with four visit methods plus an accept method on every event. Here it's two switch expressions.
  • Add a Cancelled record to permits and both switches stop compiling until you handle it: the safety Visitor gave you, for free.
  • EnumMap keeps the metric output in a stable order, which keeps the output deterministic.
  • This only works because the event set is closed and owned by one team; see Visitor for when the classic form is still better.

docs.title: 7. Pros, Cons & Trade-offs
docs.text: Aspect Pros Cons Simplicity Right-sized patterns make code predictable Speculative patterns make simple code hard to follow Performance Negligible cost in almost all business code Unneeded layers add allocations and calls Scalability Teams can extend code in parallel along clear axes Wrong axes force cross-cutting edits anyway Operability Pattern seams are natural places for logging and metrics More layers in stack traces Security Centralised extension points are easier to review More extension points mean more surface to review Testability Each variant is testable alone Over-abstraction needs many fakes Cost Cheaper changes on real axes of change Up-front and reading cost on imaginary ones Learning curve Shared vocabulary speeds onboarding Juniors copy patterns without the judgement

docs.title: 8. When to Use / When NOT to Use
docs.text:
Lean on patterns when:

  • The same kind of change has already happened and will keep happening.
  • Several people or teams need to extend the same code.
  • You're designing a public API or library that others will extend.

Hold back when:

  • It's the first time you've seen the requirement.
  • The variation is closed and small: use an enum or a sealed type with switch.
  • You're prototyping or writing code you'll throw away.

See Pattern Comparisons for alternatives.

docs.title: 9. Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Refactor toward a pattern on the second or third occurrence of a change, not before. (Consensus: rule of three, YAGNI.)
  2. Use change history to find real axes of change. (Opinion, widely practised.)
  3. Prefer language features (lambdas, records, sealed types) to class-heavy pattern forms when other teams don't need to extend the code. (Opinion.)
  4. Keep tests good enough that adding a pattern later is cheap. That's what makes waiting safe. (Consensus.)
  5. Remove patterns that stopped paying, the same way you remove dead code. (Opinion.)

docs.title: 10. Pitfalls & Anti-Patterns
docs.text:
Speculative generality

Symptom: interfaces with a single Impl, abstract classes with one subclass, factories returning one type. Root cause: designing for imagined future requirements. Fix: inline them. Reintroduce the abstraction when a second real case appears.

Golden hammer

Symptom: every problem in the code base is solved with the same pattern (often Strategy or an event bus). Root cause: the team learned one pattern well and stopped choosing. Fix: review designs against the Decision Guide; ask what the simplest alternative would be.

Indirection hides the bug (production failure mode)

Symptom: a discount was applied twice in production, and it took a day to find where. Root cause: the promotion went through a factory, a decorator chain and a registry that was configured in three places; the same decorator was registered twice. Fix: one composition root that wires everything in a single place, plus a startup check that rejects duplicate registrations.

docs.title: 14. Testing It
docs.text:
Strategy-style code is easy to test at its boundaries. This parameterised JUnit 5 test checks the new bulk promotion around its threshold; CI runs it with the example.

PromotionTest.java
import static org.junit.jupiter.api.Assertions.assertEquals;

import org.junit.jupiter.params.ParameterizedTest;
import org.junit.jupiter.params.provider.CsvSource;

class PromotionTest {

    @ParameterizedTest(name = "{0} items, basket {1} cents -> {2} cents off")
    @CsvSource({
            "9,  4800, 0",     // one item short of the threshold
            "10, 4800, 250",   // exactly at the threshold
            "12, 4800, 300"})
    void bulkDiscountStartsAtTheThreshold(int items, long totalInCents, long expectedDiscount) {
        var promo = new PromotionDemo.BuyManySaveMore("BULK_10", 10, 25);
        assertEquals(expectedDiscount, promo.discountInCents(new PromotionDemo.Basket(totalInCents, items)));
    }
}

docs.title: 16. Version Notes
docs.text: Java Feature Pattern it simplifies 8 Lambdas, functional interfaces Strategy, Command, Observer, Template Method 16 Records (JEP 395) Value objects, Memento, DTOs 17 Sealed classes (JEP 409) Closed hierarchies, State 21 Pattern matching for switch (JEP 441), record patterns (JEP 440) Visitor, Interpreter

docs.title: 17. Expert Deep Dive
docs.text:
• Flexibility has a carrying cost. Every abstraction is paid for on every read, review and debugging session, not just when written. Seniors estimate the probability of the change against that ongoing cost.
  • Reversibility beats prediction. You can't predict the axes of change reliably, so invest in what makes adding a pattern later cheap: tests, small modules, a single composition root. Then waiting is low-risk.
  • The open/closed decision has two sides. Polymorphism makes adding types cheap and adding operations expensive; sealed types plus switch do the reverse. Knowing which kind of change your domain sees is the core judgement (the "expression problem").
  • Organisational patterns matter too. A pattern that one team owns and evolves is healthy; a "shared framework" of patterns imposed across teams often becomes the golden hammer. See Governing Patterns Across an Organisation.
  • Migrating legacy code: don't refactor everything into patterns. Put the first pattern on the axis that caused the most incidents or the slowest changes last quarter.

War story: the plugin framework nobody plugged into

A team building a delivery-tracking service spent two months on a generic plugin framework: provider interfaces, a registry, dynamic class loading and versioned extension points, so that "any partner could be added without code changes". Two years later there were exactly two partners, both added by the same team, and the framework had caused three outages from class-loading conflicts during deployments. A new lead replaced it with two plain Adapter classes behind one interface and a switch on configuration. The code shrank by 70%, and the class-loading incidents disappeared. Lesson: design for the changes you have evidence for. The cheaper option was the simple pattern, not the general framework.

docs.title: 18. Interview Corner
19. Practice
docs.text:
• Find one interface with a single implementation in a project you know. Should it stay? ??? tip "Hint" Keep it if it's a boundary you fake in tests (database, clock, HTTP client); otherwise consider inlining it.
  • Add a "free delivery" promotion to Example 2 that returns the delivery fee as the discount. ??? tip "Hint" Pass the fee in through the record's constructor; don't make the promotion look it up.
  • Rewrite DeliveryEventsDemo.kind as a classic Visitor and compare the line count. ??? tip "Hint" You need a Visitor<R> interface with four methods and an accept method on each record.

docs.title: 20. Quick Revision Card
docs.text:
Remember in 30 seconds

  • Patterns pay off on real axes of change; elsewhere they're pure cost.
  • Rule of three: refactor to a pattern on the third occurrence.
  • Shared vocabulary is a big part of a pattern's value.
  • Modern Java (lambdas, records, sealed types, switch patterns) shrinks many patterns.
  • Good tests make it safe to wait.
sealed interface Event permits A, B { }
String handle(Event e) {
    return switch (e) { case A a -> "a"; case B b -> "b"; };   // exhaustive, no default
}

  • Joshua Kerievsky, Refactoring to Patterns (2004).
  • JEP 409: Sealed Classes and JEP 441: Pattern Matching for switch

docs.title: Adapter
docs.text:
L1 🟢 Foundations · ⏱ 35 min read · Prerequisites: SOLID Principles (Dependency Inversion), Strategy

TL;DR

Adapter makes an existing class (a vendor SDK, a legacy library) usable through the interface your code expects, by wrapping it and translating calls, data and errors. It's the everyday tool for integrating third parties without letting their types, units and error codes leak into your domain. Prefer object adapters (composition); test every adapter against one shared contract.

docs.title: 1. What It Is
docs.text:
Plain English. FreshCart's code sends SMS through an interface called SmsSender. The SMS vendor's SDK has a different method name, different argument order and returns numeric codes. Instead of changing all our code to fit the vendor, we write a small class that looks like SmsSender on the outside and calls the vendor SDK on the inside: a travel plug adapter, in code.

Precise definition (GoF intent). "Convert the interface of a class into another interface clients expect. Adapter lets classes work together that couldn't otherwise because of incompatible interfaces." Roles:

  • Target: the interface your code uses (SmsSender).
  • Adaptee: the existing class with the wrong interface (TextBlastApi).
  • Adapter: implements the target and translates to the adaptee.
  • Client: your code, which only knows the target.

Also known as wrapper. At system boundaries, a set of adapters forms an anti-corruption layer (a DDD term).

docs.title: 2. Why It Exists
docs.text: Third-party and legacy code rarely matches your model: different names, units (rupee strings vs cents), time types (Date vs Instant), error styles (codes vs exceptions), nulls. If you use them directly, those details spread through your codebase, and switching vendors means editing everything. An adapter confines each vendor's details to one class, so your domain depends on your own interface (Dependency Inversion).

docs.title: 3. Mental Model / Analogy
docs.text:
Analogy. A FreshCart store buys a scale from a supplier that reports weight in grams on a serial port. The billing counter expects kilograms. A small converter box between them (the adapter) turns grams into kilograms; neither the scale nor the counter changes. Buy a different scale tomorrow, and you only swap the box.

Technical model. An adapter is a class that implements the target interface and holds (or extends) the adaptee, translating each call: arguments in, results and errors out.

docs.title: 4. How It Works
docs.text:
classDiagram
    class SmsSender {
        <<interface>>
        +send(phone, text) boolean
    }
    class TextBlastSmsSender {
        -api TextBlastApi
        +send(phone, text) boolean
    }
    class TextBlastApi {
        +sendMessage(senderId, body, msisdn) int
    }
    class Checkout
    SmsSender <|.. TextBlastSmsSender
    TextBlastSmsSender o-- TextBlastApi : adapts
    Checkout ..> SmsSender : uses
sequenceDiagram
    participant C as Checkout
    participant A as TextBlastSmsSender
    participant V as TextBlastApi
    C->>A: send(+919876543210, text)
    A->>A: phone to msisdn
    A->>V: sendMessage(FRSHCT, text, 919876543210)
    V-->>A: 200
    A-->>C: true

docs.title: Object adapter
docs.text:
Description. The adapter implements the target interface and holds a reference to the adaptee (composition). This is the standard, flexible form: it works with final classes, can adapt any subclass of the adaptee, and can combine several adaptees.

Advantages / features. Loose coupling; adaptee replaceable in tests; translation logic in one place.

ObjectAdapterDemo.java
/** Object adapter: wrap a third-party client and expose OUR interface. Composition, not inheritance. */
public class ObjectAdapterDemo {

    // ===================== Our interface (the "target") =====================
    record Location(double lat, double lng, int etaMinutes) { }
    interface RiderTracker { Location locate(String orderId); }                             // (1)!

    // ===================== Third-party client we can't change (the "adaptee") =====================
    static final class ParcelGoClient {
        /** Returns "lat;lng;etaSeconds" or "NOT_FOUND". */
        String fetchPosition(String shipmentRef) {
            return shipmentRef.equals("PG-77") ? "18.5204;73.8567;540" : "NOT_FOUND";
        }
    }

    // ===================== The adapter =====================
    static final class ParcelGoTracker implements RiderTracker {
        private final ParcelGoClient client;                                              // (2)!
        private final java.util.Map<String, String> shipmentRefs;
        ParcelGoTracker(ParcelGoClient client, java.util.Map<String, String> refs) { this.client = client; this.shipmentRefs = refs; }

        public Location locate(String orderId) {
            String ref = shipmentRefs.get(orderId);                                       // (3)!
            if (ref == null) throw new IllegalArgumentException("no ParcelGo shipment for " + orderId);
            String raw = client.fetchPosition(ref);
            if (raw.equals("NOT_FOUND")) throw new IllegalStateException("ParcelGo lost track of " + ref);
            String[] p = raw.split(";");
            return new Location(Double.parseDouble(p[0]), Double.parseDouble(p[1]), (Integer.parseInt(p[2]) + 59) / 60);   // (4)!
        }
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        RiderTracker tracker = new ParcelGoTracker(new ParcelGoClient(), java.util.Map.of("FC-1701", "PG-77", "FC-1702", "PG-99"));
        System.out.println("FC-1701 -> " + tracker.locate("FC-1701"));
        for (String id : new String[]{"FC-1702", "FC-1703"}) {
            try { tracker.locate(id); } catch (RuntimeException e) { System.out.println(id + " -> " + e.getMessage()); }
        }
    }
}
  1. Our target interface, in our terms: order IDs and a Location record.
  2. The adapter has the vendor client (composition).
  3. Translating identifiers: our order ID to the vendor's shipment reference.
  4. Translating data and units: a string to numbers, seconds to minutes (rounded up).

Run it: java ObjectAdapterDemo.java

FC-1701 -> Location[lat=18.5204, lng=73.8567, etaMinutes=9]
FC-1702 -> ParcelGo lost track of PG-99
FC-1703 -> no ParcelGo shipment for FC-1703
Pros Cons Works with final or third-party classes One more class per integration Adaptee replaceable and mockable Delegation code for every method you need Can adapt several adaptees together Translation bugs hide in the adapter

Use it by default for any integration. Avoid adapting when you own both sides; change one of them instead. Real-world Java: java.io.InputStreamReader (adapts a byte InputStream to a character Reader), Arrays.asList (array to List), Spring MVC's HandlerAdapter. Best practice: name adapters after vendor and role (ParcelGoTracker). Gotcha: an adapter that also adds caching, retries and business rules is no longer an adapter; split those into decorators or services.

docs.title: Class adapter
docs.text:
Description. The adapter extends the adaptee and implements the target. Java has single class inheritance, so this works only when the adaptee is a non-final class and the target is an interface.

Advantages / features. No delegation boilerplate; access to the adaptee's protected members; overriding adaptee behaviour is possible.

ClassAdapterDemo.java
import java.math.BigDecimal;
import java.math.RoundingMode;

/** Class adapter: the adapter EXTENDS the adaptee and IMPLEMENTS the target. Java allows this only for one class. */
public class ClassAdapterDemo {

    interface Scale { BigDecimal weightKg(); }                                             // target

    /** Old store hardware SDK: grams as int, plus a tare step. */
    static class LegacyWeighingMachine {
        protected int tareGrams = 0;
        void tare(int grams) { tareGrams = grams; }
        int readGrams() { return 1_250; }                                                 // simulated sensor
    }

    static final class LegacyScaleAdapter extends LegacyWeighingMachine implements Scale {   // (1)!
        public BigDecimal weightKg() {
            int net = readGrams() - tareGrams;                                            // (2)!
            return BigDecimal.valueOf(net).divide(BigDecimal.valueOf(1_000), 3, RoundingMode.HALF_UP);
        }
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        LegacyScaleAdapter scale = new LegacyScaleAdapter();
        scale.tare(50);                                                                   // (3)!
        Scale target = scale;
        System.out.println("net weight: " + target.weightKg() + " kg");
        System.out.println("price at 120/kg: " + target.weightKg().multiply(BigDecimal.valueOf(120)).setScale(2, RoundingMode.HALF_UP));
    }
}
  1. Extends the legacy class and implements our interface.
  2. Uses inherited state and methods directly.
  3. The adapter still exposes the adaptee's own methods, like tare.

Run it: java ClassAdapterDemo.java

net weight: 1.200 kg
price at 120/kg: 144.00
Object adapter Class adapter Mechanism Composition Inheritance Works with final adaptee Yes No Adapts subclasses of the adaptee Yes No, fixed to one class Exposes adaptee's API too No (cleaner) Yes (leaky) Delegation code Needed Not needed

Use it rarely: when you must reach protected members of a legacy class. Avoid it in general; the object adapter is safer. Real-world Java: uncommon in modern libraries; you'll see it in legacy codebases extending old SDK base classes. Best practice: prefer composition. Gotcha: callers can still use the adaptee's methods through the adapter, bypassing your translation.

docs.title: Two-way adapter
docs.text:
Description. One class implements both interfaces (old and new), so it can be used by old and new clients at once. It's mainly a migration tool: route all calls into one implementation while callers move over gradually.

Advantages / features. Gradual migration; one implementation, so behaviour can't diverge.

TwoWayAdapterDemo.java
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;

/** Two-way adapter: one object usable through the OLD and the NEW interface, so a migration can be gradual. */
public class TwoWayAdapterDemo {

    // Old interface, used by 40 legacy call sites: amounts as rupee strings, boolean results
    interface LegacyPayments { boolean pay(String customer, String amountRupees); }

    // New interface, used by new code: cents and a result record
    record Charge(String id, long cents, boolean ok) { }
    interface Payments { Charge charge(String customerId, long cents); }

    /** Implements BOTH. Every call ends up in the new implementation, so behaviour is identical either way. */
    static final class PaymentsBridge implements Payments, LegacyPayments {             // (1)!
        final List<String> ledger = new ArrayList<>();
        private int seq;

        public Charge charge(String customerId, long cents) {
            if (cents <= 0) return new Charge("rejected", cents, false);
            String id = "ch_" + (++seq);
            ledger.add(id + " " + customerId + " " + cents);
            return new Charge(id, cents, true);
        }

        public boolean pay(String customer, String amountRupees) {                       // (2)!
            long cents = new java.math.BigDecimal(amountRupees).movePointRight(2).longValueExact();
            return charge(customer, cents).ok();
        }
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        PaymentsBridge bridge = new PaymentsBridge();
        LegacyPayments oldCheckout = bridge;                                              // (3)!
        Payments newCheckout = bridge;

        System.out.println("legacy pay 499.50 -> " + oldCheckout.pay("cust-1", "499.50"));
        System.out.println("new charge 12000 -> " + newCheckout.charge("cust-2", 12_000));
        System.out.println("legacy pay 0 -> " + oldCheckout.pay("cust-3", "0"));
        System.out.println("one ledger for both: " + bridge.ledger);
    }
}
  1. Implements the old and the new interface.
  2. The old API is translated into the new one, so there's one code path.
  3. Old and new callers share one object.

Run it: java TwoWayAdapterDemo.java

legacy pay 499.50 -> true
new charge 12000 -> Charge[id=ch_2, cents=12000, ok=true]
legacy pay 0 -> false
one ledger for both: [ch_1 cust-1 49950, ch_2 cust-2 12000]
Pros Cons Old and new callers work during migration Class has two responsibilities until migration ends Single source of truth for behaviour Easy to leave in place forever Callers migrate one at a time Conversions in both directions to test

Use it for planned migrations with a deadline. Avoid keeping it after the last old caller moves; delete the old interface. Real-world Java: migration layers such as old java.util.Date APIs alongside java.time via Date.from(Instant) and date.toInstant(). Best practice: track remaining old callers (a deprecation warning or metric) and remove the bridge. Gotcha: BigDecimal.longValueExact throws on fractional cents; decide how legacy strings with more decimals are handled.

docs.title: Adapting legacy and third-party APIs
docs.text:
Description. Real adapters translate more than method names: old JDK types (Enumeration, Date), null returns, checked exceptions, vendor codes and units. The adapter turns them into your model's types: Iterator, Instant, Optional, enums.

Advantages / features. Your domain code never sees the legacy quirks; one place to fix vendor surprises.

LegacyApiAdapterDemo.java
import java.util.Collections;
import java.util.Date;
import java.util.Enumeration;
import java.util.Iterator;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Optional;
import java.util.Vector;

/** Adapting legacy and third-party APIs: old JDK types, nulls, checked exceptions and vendor codes into our model. */
public class LegacyApiAdapterDemo {

    // ---- a legacy inventory library we must keep using ----
    static final class LegacyInventory {
        Enumeration<String> skus() { return new Vector<>(List.of("MILK", "EGGS", "RICE")).elements(); }
        Date lastCount() { return new Date(1_793_520_000_000L); }
        String stockCode(String sku) { return switch (sku) { case "MILK" -> "A"; case "EGGS" -> "L"; default -> null; }; }   // A=available, L=low, null=unknown
        int reserve(String sku, int qty) throws java.io.IOException {
            if (sku.equals("RICE")) throw new java.io.IOException("socket closed");
            return qty;
        }
    }

    enum Stock { AVAILABLE, LOW, UNKNOWN }

    /** Our clean API. */
    interface Inventory {
        Iterator<String> skus();
        java.time.Instant lastCount();
        Stock stock(String sku);
        Optional<Integer> tryReserve(String sku, int qty);
    }

    static final class LegacyInventoryAdapter implements Inventory {
        private final LegacyInventory legacy;
        LegacyInventoryAdapter(LegacyInventory legacy) { this.legacy = legacy; }

        public Iterator<String> skus() { return legacy.skus().asIterator(); }            // (1)!
        public java.time.Instant lastCount() { return legacy.lastCount().toInstant(); }   // (2)!
        public Stock stock(String sku) {
            String code = legacy.stockCode(sku);
            if (code == null) return Stock.UNKNOWN;                                       // (3)!
            return switch (code) { case "A" -> Stock.AVAILABLE; case "L" -> Stock.LOW; default -> Stock.UNKNOWN; };
        }
        public Optional<Integer> tryReserve(String sku, int qty) {
            try { return Optional.of(legacy.reserve(sku, qty)); }
            catch (java.io.IOException e) { return Optional.empty(); }                    // (4)!
        }
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Inventory inv = new LegacyInventoryAdapter(new LegacyInventory());
        Iterator<String> it = inv.skus();
        while (it.hasNext()) {
            String sku = it.next();
            System.out.println(sku + ": " + inv.stock(sku) + ", reserve 2 -> " + inv.tryReserve(sku, 2).map(String::valueOf).orElse("failed"));
        }
        System.out.println("last count: " + inv.lastCount());
        System.out.println("JDK's own adapters: " + Collections.list(new Vector<>(List.of(1, 2)).elements()) + ", " + java.util.Arrays.asList("a", "b"));
    }
}
  1. Enumeration to Iterator: the JDK ships this adapter as asIterator() (Java 9).
  2. Date to Instant.
  3. null and single-letter codes become an enum with an explicit UNKNOWN.
  4. A checked IOException becomes an empty Optional for callers.

Run it: java LegacyApiAdapterDemo.java

MILK: AVAILABLE, reserve 2 -> 2
EGGS: LOW, reserve 2 -> 2
RICE: UNKNOWN, reserve 2 -> failed
last count: 2026-11-01T08:00:00Z
JDK's own adapters: [1, 2], [a, b]
Legacy or vendor style Adapt to Enumeration, arrays Iterator, List, Stream Date, Calendar, epoch numbers Instant, LocalDate, ZonedDateTime null for "not found" Optional or a domain UNKNOWN Checked exceptions Domain exceptions or result types Codes and magic strings Enums Units (rupee strings, grams) Your units (cents, kilograms), typed

Use it at every boundary with code you don't own. Avoid "pass-through" adapters that return vendor types unchanged. Real-world Java: Collections.list(Enumeration), Date.toInstant(), Arrays.asList, InputStreamReader. Best practice: map unknown codes to an explicit UNKNOWN and count them. Gotcha: swallowing exceptions into Optional.empty() loses the reason; log or count it.

docs.title: Adapter vs. Facade vs. Decorator
docs.text:
Description. All three wrap something. Adapter changes an interface to match what clients expect. Decorator keeps the same interface and adds behaviour. Facade offers one simpler interface over several subsystems.

Advantages of knowing the difference. You name classes accurately, and you don't overload one wrapper with three jobs.

AdapterVsFacadeVsDecoratorDemo.java
/** Same "wrapper" shape, three intents: Adapter changes the interface, Facade simplifies many, Decorator adds behaviour. */
public class AdapterVsFacadeVsDecoratorDemo {

    interface Notifier { String send(String to, String text); }

    /** A vendor SDK with a different interface. */
    static final class TextBlastSdk { int blast(String body, String[] numbers) { return numbers.length; } }

    // Adapter: SAME capability, DIFFERENT interface -> our interface
    static final class TextBlastAdapter implements Notifier {                             // (1)!
        private final TextBlastSdk sdk = new TextBlastSdk();
        public String send(String to, String text) { return "sent to " + sdk.blast(text, new String[]{to}) + " number"; }
    }

    // Decorator: SAME interface, EXTRA behaviour
    static final class QuietHoursNotifier implements Notifier {                           // (2)!
        private final Notifier inner; private final int hour;
        QuietHoursNotifier(Notifier inner, int hour) { this.inner = inner; this.hour = hour; }
        public String send(String to, String text) { return hour >= 22 || hour < 7 ? "held until 07:00" : inner.send(to, text); }
    }

    // Facade: ONE simple entry point over SEVERAL subsystems
    static final class OrderUpdates {                                                     // (3)!
        private final Notifier sms; private final java.util.List<String> audit = new java.util.ArrayList<>();
        OrderUpdates(Notifier sms) { this.sms = sms; }
        String outForDelivery(String orderId, String phone, String rider) {
            String r = sms.send(phone, "Order " + orderId + " is on the way with " + rider);
            audit.add(orderId + " notified");
            return r + ", audit=" + audit;
        }
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Notifier adapter = new TextBlastAdapter();
        System.out.println("adapter:   " + adapter.send("+919800000001", "hi"));
        System.out.println("decorator: " + new QuietHoursNotifier(adapter, 23).send("+919800000001", "hi"));
        System.out.println("facade:    " + new OrderUpdates(adapter).outForDelivery("FC-1801", "+919800000001", "Ravi"));
    }
}
  1. Adapter: the vendor's blast becomes our send.
  2. Decorator: same Notifier interface, plus quiet-hours behaviour.
  3. Facade: one simple method that coordinates several parts.

Run it: java AdapterVsFacadeVsDecoratorDemo.java

adapter:   sent to 1 number
decorator: held until 07:00
facade:    sent to 1 number, audit=[FC-1801 notified]
Adapter Decorator Facade Interface in vs out Different Same New, simpler Wraps One adaptee One component of the same type Several subsystems Purpose Make it fit Add behaviour Make it easy Stackable Rarely Yes No

Use each for its own purpose. Avoid one class that adapts, retries, caches and orchestrates. Real-world Java: InputStreamReader (adapter), BufferedInputStream (decorator), javax.faces.context.FacesContext or a Spring service layer (facade). Best practice: compose them: an adapter wrapped in decorators, used by a facade. Gotcha: calling everything a "wrapper" hides intent in reviews.

docs.title: Example 1: Minimal (L1)
docs.text:
Scenario: Checkout sends SMS through SmsSender. The vendor SDK takes a sender ID, the body and a number without +, and returns HTTP-style codes.

SmsVendorAdapterDemo.java
/** Minimal Adapter: our code depends on SmsSender; a vendor SDK with a different shape is wrapped to fit. */
public class SmsVendorAdapterDemo {

    interface SmsSender { boolean send(String phone, String text); }                     // (1)!

    /** Vendor SDK (can't change): different method name, argument order, and int status codes. */
    static final class TextBlastApi {
        int sendMessage(String senderId, String body, String msisdn) {
            if (!msisdn.startsWith("91")) return 400;
            return body.length() > 160 ? 413 : 200;
        }
    }

    static final class TextBlastSmsSender implements SmsSender {
        private final TextBlastApi api = new TextBlastApi();
        public boolean send(String phone, String text) {
            String msisdn = phone.replace("+", "");                                       // (2)!
            return api.sendMessage("FRSHCT", text, msisdn) == 200;
        }
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        SmsSender sms = new TextBlastSmsSender();
        System.out.println("+919876543210 -> " + sms.send("+919876543210", "Your order is packed"));
        System.out.println("+447700900123 -> " + sms.send("+447700900123", "Your order is packed"));
        System.out.println("long text     -> " + sms.send("+919876543210", "x".repeat(200)));
    }
}
  1. Our interface: phone and text, true or false.
  2. Translating the phone format and argument order is the adapter's whole job.

Run it: java SmsVendorAdapterDemo.java

Output:

+919876543210 -> true
+447700900123 -> false
long text     -> false

What to notice:

  • Checkout never sees status codes like 400 or 413.
  • Switching SMS vendors means one new adapter class.

docs.title: Example 2: Realistic (in FreshCart grocery delivery)
docs.text:
Scenario: Two couriers send tracking webhooks in different formats: QuickDrop uses numeric codes and epoch seconds; ParcelGo uses key-value text, words for states and ISO timestamps. The app needs one tracking model.

CourierStatusAdapterDemo.java
import java.time.Instant;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Map;

/** Realistic Adapter: two couriers report tracking in different formats; adapters translate both into one model. */
public class CourierStatusAdapterDemo {

    enum Status { PICKED_UP, IN_TRANSIT, DELIVERED, FAILED, UNKNOWN }
    record TrackingUpdate(String orderId, Status status, Instant at, String courier) { }

    interface TrackingSource { TrackingUpdate translate(String rawPayload); }             // (1)!

    /** QuickDrop: "orderId|statusCode|epochSeconds", codes 10/20/30/90. */
    static final class QuickDropAdapter implements TrackingSource {
        private static final Map<Integer, Status> CODES = Map.of(10, Status.PICKED_UP, 20, Status.IN_TRANSIT, 30, Status.DELIVERED, 90, Status.FAILED);
        public TrackingUpdate translate(String raw) {
            String[] f = raw.split("\\|");
            Status s = CODES.getOrDefault(Integer.parseInt(f[1]), Status.UNKNOWN);       // (2)!
            return new TrackingUpdate(f[0], s, Instant.ofEpochSecond(Long.parseLong(f[2])), "QuickDrop");
        }
    }

    /** ParcelGo: "ref=..;state=..;time=ISO", states as words, refs prefixed "PG-". */
    static final class ParcelGoAdapter implements TrackingSource {
        public TrackingUpdate translate(String raw) {
            Map<String, String> f = new java.util.HashMap<>();
            for (String kv : raw.split(";")) { String[] p = kv.split("=", 2); f.put(p[0], p[1]); }
            Status s = switch (f.get("state")) {
                case "COLLECTED" -> Status.PICKED_UP;
                case "ON_ROUTE", "NEAR_YOU" -> Status.IN_TRANSIT;                         // (3)!
                case "HANDED_OVER" -> Status.DELIVERED;
                case "RETURNED", "CUSTOMER_UNREACHABLE" -> Status.FAILED;
                default -> Status.UNKNOWN;
            };
            return new TrackingUpdate(f.get("ref").substring(3), s, Instant.parse(f.get("time")), "ParcelGo");   // (4)!
        }
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        TrackingSource qd = new QuickDropAdapter(), pg = new ParcelGoAdapter();
        List<TrackingUpdate> updates = List.of(
                qd.translate("FC-1901|20|1793606400"),
                pg.translate("ref=PG-FC-1902;state=NEAR_YOU;time=2026-11-02T10:05:00Z"),
                qd.translate("FC-1903|55|1793606700"),
                pg.translate("ref=PG-FC-1904;state=CUSTOMER_UNREACHABLE;time=2026-11-02T10:12:00Z"));
        updates.forEach(System.out::println);
        System.out.println("needs review (unknown codes): " + updates.stream().filter(u -> u.status() == Status.UNKNOWN).map(TrackingUpdate::orderId).toList());
    }
}
  1. One target interface for every courier.
  2. Unknown codes map to UNKNOWN instead of crashing or guessing.
  3. Several vendor states can map to one of ours.
  4. Vendor-specific identifiers (the PG- prefix) are removed here and nowhere else.

Run it: java CourierStatusAdapterDemo.java

Output:

TrackingUpdate[orderId=FC-1901, status=IN_TRANSIT, at=2026-11-02T08:00:00Z, courier=QuickDrop]
TrackingUpdate[orderId=FC-1902, status=IN_TRANSIT, at=2026-11-02T10:05:00Z, courier=ParcelGo]
TrackingUpdate[orderId=FC-1903, status=UNKNOWN, at=2026-11-02T08:05:00Z, courier=QuickDrop]
TrackingUpdate[orderId=FC-1904, status=FAILED, at=2026-11-02T10:12:00Z, courier=ParcelGo]
needs review (unknown codes): [FC-1903]

What to notice:

  • The app shows the same statuses for both couriers.
  • QuickDrop's new code 55 (not in the docs) didn't break anything; it was flagged for review.

docs.title: Example 3: Production-grade
docs.text:
Scenario: Integrating a payment provider SDK. FreshCart's checkout works in cents and expects a sealed result: approved, declined (with a reason the app can show) or failed (retryable or not). The SDK uses rupee strings, its own error codes and a checked exception. The adapter must pass our idempotency key so retries never double-charge, map every known code, and flag unknown ones. A contract test runs the same checks against the real adapter and the in-memory fake.

PaymentProviderAdapterDemo.java
import java.math.BigDecimal;
import java.util.HashMap;
import java.util.Map;

/**
 * Production-grade Adapter (an anti-corruption layer for a payment SDK):
 * - our PaymentGateway interface uses cents, our IDs and a sealed result type
 * - the vendor SDK uses rupee strings, its own codes and a CHECKED exception
 * - the adapter validates, converts units, passes our idempotency key, maps every vendor code,
 *   and never lets a vendor type escape
 */
public class PaymentProviderAdapterDemo {

    // ===================== Our model =====================
    record ChargeRequest(String orderId, String customerId, long amountCents, String idempotencyKey) { }
    enum DeclineReason { INSUFFICIENT_FUNDS, CARD_EXPIRED, SUSPECTED_FRAUD, OTHER }
    sealed interface ChargeResult permits Approved, Declined, Failed { }
    record Approved(String paymentId) implements ChargeResult { }
    record Declined(DeclineReason reason) implements ChargeResult { }
    record Failed(String detail, boolean retryable) implements ChargeResult { }

    interface PaymentGateway { ChargeResult charge(ChargeRequest request); }

    // ===================== Vendor SDK (can't change) =====================
    static final class PayLinkException extends Exception {
        final String code;
        PayLinkException(String code, String msg) { super(msg); this.code = code; }
    }
    static final class PayLinkSdk {
        private final Map<String, String> seenKeys = new HashMap<>();
        private int seq = 500;
        /** amount like "499.50"; returns txn id. */
        String createPayment(String merchantRef, String amount, String customer, String requestId) throws PayLinkException {
            if (seenKeys.containsKey(requestId)) return seenKeys.get(requestId);           // vendor dedupes by requestId
            if (customer.equals("broke")) throw new PayLinkException("E51", "insufficient balance");
            if (customer.equals("old-card")) throw new PayLinkException("E54", "expired");
            if (customer.equals("timeout")) throw new PayLinkException("E91", "issuer timeout");
            if (customer.equals("weird")) throw new PayLinkException("E77", "undocumented");
            String id = "plk_" + (++seq);
            seenKeys.put(requestId, id);
            return id;
        }
    }

    // ===================== The adapter =====================
    static final class PayLinkGateway implements PaymentGateway {
        private static final Map<String, DeclineReason> DECLINES = Map.of(                // (1)!
                "E51", DeclineReason.INSUFFICIENT_FUNDS, "E54", DeclineReason.CARD_EXPIRED, "E59", DeclineReason.SUSPECTED_FRAUD);
        private static final java.util.Set<String> RETRYABLE = java.util.Set.of("E91", "E96");
        private final PayLinkSdk sdk;
        final Map<String, Integer> unmappedCodes = new HashMap<>();

        PayLinkGateway(PayLinkSdk sdk) { this.sdk = sdk; }

        public ChargeResult charge(ChargeRequest r) {
            if (r.amountCents() <= 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("amount must be positive");   // (2)!
            String rupees = BigDecimal.valueOf(r.amountCents()).movePointLeft(2).toPlainString();      // (3)!
            try {
                return new Approved(sdk.createPayment(r.orderId(), rupees, r.customerId(), r.idempotencyKey()));   // (4)!
            } catch (PayLinkException e) {                                                // (5)!
                DeclineReason reason = DECLINES.get(e.code);
                if (reason != null) return new Declined(reason);
                if (RETRYABLE.contains(e.code)) return new Failed("PayLink " + e.code, true);
                unmappedCodes.merge(e.code, 1, Integer::sum);
                return new Failed("PayLink " + e.code + " (unmapped)", false);
            }
        }
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        PayLinkGateway gateway = new PayLinkGateway(new PayLinkSdk());
        String[][] cases = {{"FC-2001", "cust-1", "49950"}, {"FC-2002", "broke", "12000"}, {"FC-2003", "old-card", "8000"},
                {"FC-2004", "timeout", "8000"}, {"FC-2005", "weird", "8000"}};
        for (String[] c : cases) {
            ChargeResult result = gateway.charge(new ChargeRequest(c[0], c[1], Long.parseLong(c[2]), "idem-" + c[0]));
            String text = switch (result) {                                               // callers handle OUR types only
                case Approved a -> "approved " + a.paymentId();
                case Declined d -> "declined: " + d.reason();
                case Failed f -> "failed: " + f.detail() + (f.retryable() ? ", retry later" : ", do not retry");
            };
            System.out.println(c[0] + " -> " + text);
        }
        ChargeResult retry = gateway.charge(new ChargeRequest("FC-2001", "cust-1", 49_950, "idem-FC-2001"));
        System.out.println("retry of FC-2001 with same key -> " + retry + " (no double charge)");
        System.out.println("unmapped vendor codes to investigate: " + gateway.unmappedCodes);
        try { gateway.charge(new ChargeRequest("FC-2006", "cust-1", 0, "idem-FC-2006")); } catch (IllegalArgumentException e) { System.out.println("rejected: " + e.getMessage()); }
    }
}
  1. Vendor decline codes mapped to our reasons, in one table.
  2. Validate in our terms before calling the vendor.
  3. Unit conversion with BigDecimal, never double, for money.
  4. Our idempotency key becomes the vendor's request ID: retries return the same payment.
  5. The checked vendor exception never escapes; it becomes one of our result types.

Run it: java PaymentProviderAdapterDemo.java

Output:

FC-2001 -> approved plk_501
FC-2002 -> declined: INSUFFICIENT_FUNDS
FC-2003 -> declined: CARD_EXPIRED
FC-2004 -> failed: PayLink E91, retry later
FC-2005 -> failed: PayLink E77 (unmapped), do not retry
retry of FC-2001 with same key -> Approved[paymentId=plk_501] (no double charge)
unmapped vendor codes to investigate: {E77=1}
rejected: amount must be positive

What to notice:

  • Checkout's switch handles only FreshCart types; PayLink could be replaced without touching it.
  • The retry of FC-2001 returned the same payment ID: no double charge.
  • E77 isn't in the vendor's docs; it's treated as non-retryable and counted for investigation.

docs.title: 7. Pros, Cons & Trade-offs
docs.text: Aspect Pros Cons Simplicity Domain code stays clean Extra layer and mapping code Coupling Vendor details in one class Adapter must track vendor API changes Performance Negligible Data copying for large payloads Operability One place to log, count and map vendor errors Mapping gaps appear only in production Testability Domain tested with fakes; contract tests per adapter Real adapters need integration tests with sandboxes Learning curve Simple idea Knowing what to translate (units, errors) needs care

docs.title: 8. When to Use / When NOT to Use
docs.text:
Use it when:

  • integrating any third-party SDK, API or legacy library;
  • you may switch vendors, or support several at once;
  • an old interface must keep working while you migrate.

Don't use it when:

  • you own both sides and can just change one;
  • you want to simplify many subsystems: use Facade;
  • you want to add behaviour without changing the interface: use Decorator.

docs.title: 9. Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Define the target interface in your domain's terms first, then adapt vendors to it. (Consensus.)
  2. Never let vendor types escape the adapter (classes, exceptions, codes). (Consensus.)
  3. Map unknown values explicitly and count them. (Consensus.)
  4. Write one contract test suite and run it against every adapter and fake. (Consensus.)
  5. Use BigDecimal or integer minor units for money conversions. (Consensus.)
  6. Keep adapters thin: put retries, caching and metrics in decorators. (Opinion.)
  7. Pass idempotency keys through to vendors that support them. (Consensus for payments.)

docs.title: 10. Pitfalls & Anti-Patterns
docs.text:
Leaky adapter

Symptom: PayLinkException appears in checkout code; vendor codes in the database. Root cause: the adapter re-threw or returned vendor types. Fix: map everything to your own types inside the adapter.

Lost paise (production failure mode)

Symptom: reconciliation found thousands of payments off by one paisa. Root cause: the adapter converted cents to rupees with double arithmetic (499.5 became 499.49999). Fix: BigDecimal.movePointLeft(2) or integer arithmetic, and a contract test with awkward amounts.

Silent default mapping

Symptom: new courier status "RETURN_TO_ORIGIN" shown to customers as "Delivered". Root cause: default -> DELIVERED in the mapping switch. Fix: default to UNKNOWN, alert on it, and add mappings deliberately.

God adapter

Symptom: a 2,000-line VendorAdapter with caching, retries, business rules and reporting. Root cause: every vendor-related concern added to the adapter. Fix: thin adapter + decorators (retry, cache) + domain services.

docs.title: 11. Configuration & Tuning
docs.text: Setting Default What it does When to change it Risk of changing Code mapping tables In code Vendor codes to domain values Vendor adds codes Wrong mapping shows wrong status or retries permanent errors Retryable code set E91, E96 Which failures may be retried Vendor guidance changes Retrying declines causes duplicate attempts and fraud flags Sender ID (Example 1) FRSHCT Shown as SMS sender Brand or regulatory change Messages blocked by carriers

docs.title: 12. Security Considerations
docs.text:
• Adapters handle raw vendor payloads: validate and size-limit them, especially webhooks (Example 2).
  • Don't log full vendor requests or responses containing card data, tokens or personal data; redact in the adapter.
  • Verify webhook signatures in the adapter before translating anything.

docs.title: 13. Performance & Scalability
docs.text: Translation costs are tiny compared to network calls. Watch for adapters that convert large payloads repeatedly (parsing a big JSON per field access) and for adapters creating a new vendor client per call; vendor clients usually hold connection pools and must be shared (see Singleton and Factory Method).

docs.title: 14. Testing It
docs.text:
One contract, two implementations: the real adapter (over a stub SDK here, a vendor sandbox in integration tests) and the fake used by checkout tests. If the fake passes the same contract, tests that use it can be trusted.

PaymentGatewayContractTest.java
import static org.junit.jupiter.api.Assertions.assertEquals;
import static org.junit.jupiter.api.Assertions.assertInstanceOf;
import static org.junit.jupiter.api.Assertions.assertThrows;

import java.util.HashMap;
import java.util.Map;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;

/** One contract, run against every adapter: the real PayLink adapter and the in-memory fake used by other tests. */
abstract class PaymentGatewayContractTest {

    abstract PaymentProviderAdapterDemo.PaymentGateway gateway();

    private PaymentProviderAdapterDemo.ChargeRequest request(String customer, long cents, String key) {
        return new PaymentProviderAdapterDemo.ChargeRequest("o-" + key, customer, cents, key);
    }

    @Test
    void approvesAValidCharge() {
        assertInstanceOf(PaymentProviderAdapterDemo.Approved.class, gateway().charge(request("cust-1", 1_000, "k1")));
    }

    @Test
    void sameIdempotencyKeyNeverChargesTwice() {
        var g = gateway();
        var first = (PaymentProviderAdapterDemo.Approved) g.charge(request("cust-1", 1_000, "k2"));
        var second = (PaymentProviderAdapterDemo.Approved) g.charge(request("cust-1", 1_000, "k2"));
        assertEquals(first.paymentId(), second.paymentId());
    }

    @Test
    void insufficientFundsIsADeclineNotAFailure() {
        assertEquals(new PaymentProviderAdapterDemo.Declined(PaymentProviderAdapterDemo.DeclineReason.INSUFFICIENT_FUNDS),
                gateway().charge(request("broke", 1_000, "k3")));
    }

    @Test
    void rejectsNonPositiveAmounts() {
        assertThrows(IllegalArgumentException.class, () -> gateway().charge(request("cust-1", 0, "k4")));
    }
}

class PayLinkGatewayContractTest extends PaymentGatewayContractTest {
    PaymentProviderAdapterDemo.PaymentGateway gateway() {
        return new PaymentProviderAdapterDemo.PayLinkGateway(new PaymentProviderAdapterDemo.PayLinkSdk());
    }
}

class FakeGatewayContractTest extends PaymentGatewayContractTest {
    PaymentProviderAdapterDemo.PaymentGateway gateway() {
        Map<String, String> byKey = new HashMap<>();
        return r -> {
            if (r.amountCents() <= 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("amount must be positive");
            if (r.customerId().equals("broke")) return new PaymentProviderAdapterDemo.Declined(PaymentProviderAdapterDemo.DeclineReason.INSUFFICIENT_FUNDS);
            return new PaymentProviderAdapterDemo.Approved(byKey.computeIfAbsent(r.idempotencyKey(), k -> "fake_" + byKey.size()));
        };
    }
}

docs.title: 15. Observability & Operations
docs.text: Log and count per vendor and per mapped outcome: approvals, each decline reason, retryable failures and unmapped codes. Alert on any unmapped code and on sudden shifts in the mix (for example, "suspected fraud" declines doubling), which often signal a vendor-side change before they announce it.

docs.title: 16. Version Notes
docs.text: Java Change relevant to Adapter 1.1 InputStreamReader, OutputStreamWriter (byte/char adapters) 1.2 Arrays.asList, Collections.enumeration and Collections.list 8 Date.from(Instant), date.toInstant() to adapt legacy dates 9 Enumeration.asIterator() 17 Sealed result types for adapters' outputs 21 Pattern matching for switch over adapter results

docs.title: 17. Expert Deep Dive
docs.text:
• Anti-corruption layer. In DDD, a set of adapters and translators protects a bounded context from another system's model. Seniors treat it as a deliberate boundary with its own tests, not just a few wrapper classes.
  • Ports and adapters (hexagonal architecture). The domain defines ports (interfaces like PaymentGateway); infrastructure provides adapters. The whole architecture is the Adapter pattern applied systematically (see Architectural Patterns).
  • Contract tests as the safety net. Consumer-driven contract tests (Pact) and shared adapter contracts catch vendor changes before customers do.
  • Versioned mappings. Vendors add codes without notice. Keep mappings data-driven where possible and monitored, so a new code is a dashboard alert, not an incident.

War story: the courier that invented a status

A delivery platform mapped courier statuses with a default -> IN_TRANSIT branch. The courier quietly introduced HELD_AT_HUB for parcels stuck because of address problems. For three weeks, customers saw "in transit" for orders that were going nowhere, and support tickets piled up. After the incident, the adapter mapped unknown statuses to UNKNOWN, alerted on them, and showed customers "We're checking on your order". Lesson: an adapter's default branch is a business decision; make it a safe and visible one.

docs.title: 20. Quick Revision Card
docs.text:
Remember in 30 seconds

  • Intent: make an existing class fit the interface clients expect.
  • Object adapter (composition) by default; class adapter rarely.
  • Translate names, units, types, nulls, exceptions, codes and IDs; never leak vendor types.
  • Unknown codes → explicit UNKNOWN, alert, count.
  • One contract test for every adapter and fake.
final class TextBlastSmsSender implements SmsSender {
    public boolean send(String phone, String text) { return api.sendMessage("FRSHCT", text, phone.replace("+", "")) == 200; }
}
