docs.title: Singleton
docs.text:
L1 🟢 Foundations · ⏱ 45 min read · Prerequisites: OOP Refresher, SOLID Principles

TL;DR

Singleton guarantees a class has exactly one instance and gives global access to it. In Java the safest forms are an enum or the lazy holder idiom. Use it sparingly: global state hurts testing and hides dependencies, so in most applications you want one instance created in the composition root and injected, not the Singleton pattern itself.

docs.title: 1. What It Is
docs.text:
Plain English. Some things should exist only once in a running program: the app's settings, a metrics registry, a connection pool. Singleton is a class that makes sure only one object of it can ever be created, and offers a static method (or field) to reach that object from anywhere.

Precise definition (GoF intent). "Ensure a class only has one instance, and provide a global point of access to it." It's a creational pattern with two parts:

  • Controlled construction: a private constructor so no one else can call new.
  • Global access: a static accessor (getInstance()) or an enum constant (INSTANCE).

New terms: class initialisation is when the JVM runs a class's static initialisers, on its first active use. Safe publication means other threads are guaranteed to see a fully constructed object.

docs.title: 2. Why It Exists
docs.text:
Some resources are expensive or must be coordinated: a thread pool, a cache, a hardware device, the configuration loaded at startup. Before the pattern, programs used global variables, which anyone could reassign, and which were created in an unpredictable order. Singleton gave one controlled place for creation, and lazy creation for expensive objects.

What goes wrong without any single-instance control: two caches that disagree, two connection pools each sized for the whole database (so twice the connections), or two clients for a payment provider each with its own rate limit.

docs.title: 3. Mental Model / Analogy
docs.text:
Analogy. A FreshCart store has one master key cabinet. There's a single cabinet (one instance), it's in a known place everyone can reach (global access), and nobody is allowed to build a second one (private constructor). The downside is the same as in code: because everyone uses it directly, you can't easily swap it for a test cabinet, and you can't see from a staff member's job description that they depend on it.

Technical model. A Singleton is a static field holding the only instance, plus rules that make sure the field is set exactly once, safely across threads, and can't be bypassed by reflection, serialization or cloning.

docs.title: 4. How It Works
docs.text:
classDiagram
    class AppSettings {
        <<enum>>
        INSTANCE
        -region String
        -maxBasketItems int
        +region() String
        +maxBasketItems() int
    }
    class Checkout
    class Delivery
    Checkout ..> AppSettings : AppSettings.INSTANCE
    Delivery ..> AppSettings : AppSettings.INSTANCE
sequenceDiagram
    participant A as Thread A
    participant B as Thread B
    participant C as ProductCatalog.Holder
    A->>C: getInstance() first use
    Note over C: JVM initialises Holder once, under the class-init lock
    B->>C: getInstance() at the same time
    Note over B,C: B waits for initialisation to finish
    C-->>A: the instance
    C-->>B: the same instance

The JVM guarantees that a class is initialised only once, and that the result is visible to every thread (JLS §12.4.2). The enum and lazy holder forms reuse that guarantee, which is why they need no explicit locking.

docs.title: 5. Subtopics
docs.text: Each implementation gets a deep dive with a runnable example, pros and cons, and when to use it.

docs.title: Eager initialisation
docs.text:
Description. The instance is created in a static final field initialiser. It's simple and thread-safe because class initialisation is. "Eager" means when the class is initialised (its first active use), which is not the same as program start.

Advantages / features. Simplest correct form; thread-safe without locks; failures in construction surface early and loudly.

EagerSingletonDemo.java
import java.util.Map;

/** Eager initialisation: the instance is created when the class is initialised. */
public class EagerSingletonDemo {

    static final class FeatureFlags {
        private static final FeatureFlags INSTANCE = new FeatureFlags();            // (1)!

        private final Map<String, Boolean> flags;

        private FeatureFlags() {                                                     // (2)!
            System.out.println("FeatureFlags created");
            flags = Map.of("express-delivery", true, "upi-payments", false);
        }

        static FeatureFlags getInstance() { return INSTANCE; }

        boolean isOn(String flag) {
            Boolean value = flags.get(flag);
            if (value == null) throw new IllegalArgumentException("unknown flag: " + flag);  // (3)!
            return value;
        }
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("main started");
        FeatureFlags a = FeatureFlags.getInstance();
        FeatureFlags b = FeatureFlags.getInstance();
        System.out.println("same instance: " + (a == b));
        System.out.println("express-delivery: " + a.isOn("express-delivery"));
        try { a.isOn("drone-delivery"); } catch (IllegalArgumentException e) { System.out.println("rejected: " + e.getMessage()); }
    }
}
  1. Created once, when FeatureFlags is initialised.
  2. private: nobody else can call new FeatureFlags().
  3. Unknown flags fail loudly instead of silently returning false.

Run it: java EagerSingletonDemo.java

main started
FeatureFlags created
same instance: true
express-delivery: true
rejected: unknown flag: drone-delivery

Notice "FeatureFlags created" prints after "main started": the nested class was initialised on first use.

Pros Cons Simplest correct implementation Created even if only a static constant of the class is used Thread-safe through class initialisation Construction errors become ExceptionInInitializerError No locking on access Can't pass parameters to the constructor

Use it for cheap objects that are always needed. Avoid it when construction is expensive and often unused, or needs runtime parameters. Real-world Java: java.lang.Runtime.getRuntime() returns an eagerly created instance. Best practice: keep the constructor cheap and free of I/O. Gotcha: an exception in the initialiser makes the class unusable for the rest of the JVM's life (NoClassDefFoundError on later access).

docs.title: Lazy holder idiom
docs.text:
Description. The instance lives in a private static nested Holder class. The holder is only initialised when getInstance() first touches it, so creation is lazy, and the JVM's class-initialisation lock makes it thread-safe. Also called initialization-on-demand holder.

Advantages / features. Lazy and lock-free on every access after the first; no volatile; easy to read.

LazyHolderDemo.java
import java.util.Map;

/** Initialization-on-demand holder: lazy, thread-safe, no locks. */
public class LazyHolderDemo {

    static final class ProductCatalog {
        private final Map<String, Long> prices;

        private ProductCatalog() {
            System.out.println("  loading catalog (expensive)...");
            prices = Map.of("MILK-1L", 129L, "BREAD-WHT", 249L);
        }

        private static final class Holder {                                           // (1)!
            static final ProductCatalog INSTANCE = new ProductCatalog();
        }

        static ProductCatalog getInstance() { return Holder.INSTANCE; }               // (2)!

        static String describe() { return "ProductCatalog (no loading needed for this)"; }  // (3)!

        long priceOf(String sku) {
            Long p = prices.get(sku);
            if (p == null) throw new IllegalArgumentException("unknown sku " + sku);
            return p;
        }
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("1. calling a static helper: " + ProductCatalog.describe());
        System.out.println("2. first getInstance():");
        long milk = ProductCatalog.getInstance().priceOf("MILK-1L");
        System.out.println("   milk = " + milk);
        System.out.println("3. second getInstance(): no loading line below");
        System.out.println("   bread = " + ProductCatalog.getInstance().priceOf("BREAD-WHT"));
    }
}
  1. The nested class holds the instance and isn't initialised until it's used.
  2. First call initialises Holder; later calls just read the field.
  3. Other static members of the outer class don't trigger loading.

Run it: java LazyHolderDemo.java

1. calling a static helper: ProductCatalog (no loading needed for this)
2. first getInstance():
  loading catalog (expensive)...
   milk = 129
3. second getInstance(): no loading line below
   bread = 249
Pros Cons Lazy creation for expensive objects Slightly more code than eager Thread-safe with no explicit locking No constructor parameters No cost on access after initialisation A failing constructor still breaks the class permanently

Use it when the object is expensive and may not be needed. Avoid it when you need to reset or replace the instance (tests). Real-world Java: a common idiom for loggers' and libraries' internal registries. Best practice: prefer this over double-checked locking for static singletons. Gotcha: it only works for static instances, not for per-object lazy fields.

docs.title: Enum singleton
docs.text:
Description. An enum with a single constant. The JVM guarantees one instance, and Java's serialization and reflection rules protect enums specifically. Joshua Bloch calls a single-element enum "often the best way to implement a singleton" (Effective Java, Item 3).

Advantages / features. Shortest code; serialization-safe; reflection-safe; thread-safe.

EnumSingletonDemo.java
import java.io.ByteArrayInputStream;
import java.io.ByteArrayOutputStream;
import java.io.ObjectInputStream;
import java.io.ObjectOutputStream;
import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicLong;

/** Enum singleton: serialization-safe and reflection-safe for free (Effective Java, Item 3). */
public class EnumSingletonDemo {

    enum OrderNumbers {                                                               // (1)!
        INSTANCE;

        private final AtomicLong next = new AtomicLong(1000);

        String nextOrderId() { return "FC-" + next.incrementAndGet(); }               // (2)!
    }

    @SuppressWarnings("unchecked")
    static <T> T roundTrip(T value) throws Exception {
        ByteArrayOutputStream bytes = new ByteArrayOutputStream();
        try (ObjectOutputStream out = new ObjectOutputStream(bytes)) { out.writeObject(value); }
        try (ObjectInputStream in = new ObjectInputStream(new ByteArrayInputStream(bytes.toByteArray()))) {
            return (T) in.readObject();
        }
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        System.out.println(OrderNumbers.INSTANCE.nextOrderId());
        System.out.println(OrderNumbers.INSTANCE.nextOrderId());

        OrderNumbers copy = roundTrip(OrderNumbers.INSTANCE);                         // (3)!
        System.out.println("same after serialization: " + (copy == OrderNumbers.INSTANCE));

        try {
            var ctor = OrderNumbers.class.getDeclaredConstructor(String.class, int.class);
            ctor.setAccessible(true);
            ctor.newInstance("SECOND", 1);
        } catch (IllegalArgumentException e) {
            System.out.println("reflection blocked: " + e.getMessage());               // (4)!
        }
    }
}
  1. One constant, one instance.
  2. State inside a singleton must be thread-safe: AtomicLong here.
  3. Deserialising an enum returns the existing constant, never a copy.
  4. The JDK refuses to create enum instances through reflection.

Run it: java EnumSingletonDemo.java

FC-1001
FC-1002
same after serialization: true
reflection blocked: Cannot reflectively create enum objects
Pros Cons Shortest correct code Can't extend another class Safe against serialization and reflection attacks Eager (initialised with the enum class) Thread-safe creation Looks unusual to some readers Works naturally with switch and EnumMap Still global state: same testing problems

Use it when you really need a static singleton. Avoid it when the instance needs constructor arguments known only at runtime, or when tests need to replace it. Real-world Java: java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit constants and java.math.RoundingMode are enum instances used as shared singletons. Best practice: keep enum singletons stateless or use thread-safe state. Gotcha: mutable state in an enum is still shared mutable global state.

docs.title: Double-checked locking with volatile
docs.text:
Description. Check without a lock, lock only if the instance is missing, check again inside the lock, then create. The field must be volatile; without it, another thread can see a non-null reference to an object whose fields aren't initialised yet (the classic broken DCL, fixed by the Java 5 memory model, JSR-133).

Advantages / features. Lazy; locking only on the first access; supports constructor arguments read at runtime.

DclSingletonDemo.java
import java.util.Set;
import java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap;
import java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch;
import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService;
import java.util.concurrent.Executors;
import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger;

/** Double-checked locking: lazy, with a lock only on the first call. `volatile` is essential. */
public class DclSingletonDemo {

    static final class PaymentGatewayClient {
        static final AtomicInteger constructions = new AtomicInteger();
        private static volatile PaymentGatewayClient instance;                         // (1)!

        private final String endpoint;

        private PaymentGatewayClient(String endpoint) {
            constructions.incrementAndGet();
            this.endpoint = endpoint;
        }

        static PaymentGatewayClient getInstance() {
            PaymentGatewayClient local = instance;                                     // (2)!
            if (local == null) {
                synchronized (PaymentGatewayClient.class) {
                    local = instance;
                    if (local == null) {                                               // (3)!
                        local = new PaymentGatewayClient(System.getProperty("pg.endpoint", "https://pg.example/v1"));
                        instance = local;
                    }
                }
            }
            return local;
        }

        String endpoint() { return endpoint; }
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        int threads = 64;
        Set<PaymentGatewayClient> seen = ConcurrentHashMap.newKeySet();
        CountDownLatch start = new CountDownLatch(1);
        try (ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(threads)) {
            for (int i = 0; i < threads; i++) {
                pool.submit(() -> { start.await(); seen.add(PaymentGatewayClient.getInstance()); return null; });
            }
            start.countDown();                                                         // (4)!
        }
        System.out.println("threads: " + threads);
        System.out.println("distinct instances seen: " + seen.size());
        System.out.println("constructor calls: " + PaymentGatewayClient.constructions.get());
        System.out.println("endpoint: " + PaymentGatewayClient.getInstance().endpoint());
    }
}
  1. volatile makes publication safe across threads.
  2. Read the field once into a local: one volatile read on the fast path.
  3. The second check prevents a second construction by a thread that waited for the lock.
  4. All 64 threads start at once to stress the race.

Run it: java DclSingletonDemo.java

threads: 64
distinct instances seen: 1
constructor calls: 1
endpoint: https://pg.example/v1
Pros Cons Lazy, with no lock after initialisation Easy to get subtly wrong (volatile, local copy) Can read runtime configuration More code than holder or enum Works for instance fields too (lazy per object) Reviewers must know the memory model to verify it

Use it for lazy instance fields, or when the holder idiom doesn't fit. Avoid it for static singletons; the holder idiom is simpler. Real-world Java: used inside JDK and library classes for lazily computed fields. Best practice: copy the pattern exactly, including the local variable. Gotcha: dropping volatile produces a bug that almost never shows up in tests.

docs.title: Breaking singletons: reflection, serialization, class loaders
docs.text:
Description. A private constructor isn't a guarantee. Reflection can call it with setAccessible(true). Serialization creates a new object on readObject unless the class defines readResolve. Class loaders: each class loader that loads the class gets its own static field, so application servers, plugin systems and some test runners can end up with "one singleton per class loader". Cloning creates a copy if the class implements Cloneable.

Advantages of knowing this. You can harden singletons that matter (security, licensing, payment clients), and you can recognise "two instances" bugs in app servers.

BreakingSingletonDemo.java
import java.io.ByteArrayInputStream;
import java.io.ByteArrayOutputStream;
import java.io.ObjectInputStream;
import java.io.ObjectOutputStream;
import java.io.Serial;
import java.io.Serializable;
import java.lang.reflect.Constructor;

/** How classic singletons break, and the defences. */
public class BreakingSingletonDemo {

    /** A naive singleton: private constructor, nothing else. */
    static final class NaiveSettings implements Serializable {
        @Serial private static final long serialVersionUID = 1L;
        static final NaiveSettings INSTANCE = new NaiveSettings();
        private NaiveSettings() { }
    }

    /** Hardened: refuses a second construction and keeps identity on deserialization. */
    static final class HardenedSettings implements Serializable {
        @Serial private static final long serialVersionUID = 1L;
        private static boolean created;
        static final HardenedSettings INSTANCE = new HardenedSettings();

        private HardenedSettings() {
            synchronized (HardenedSettings.class) {
                if (created) throw new IllegalStateException("HardenedSettings is a singleton");   // (1)!
                created = true;
            }
        }

        @Serial private Object readResolve() { return INSTANCE; }                       // (2)!
    }

    static Object roundTrip(Object value) throws Exception {
        ByteArrayOutputStream bytes = new ByteArrayOutputStream();
        try (ObjectOutputStream out = new ObjectOutputStream(bytes)) { out.writeObject(value); }
        try (ObjectInputStream in = new ObjectInputStream(new ByteArrayInputStream(bytes.toByteArray()))) { return in.readObject(); }
    }

    static Object viaReflection(Class<?> type) throws Exception {
        Constructor<?> ctor = type.getDeclaredConstructor();
        ctor.setAccessible(true);                                                      // (3)!
        return ctor.newInstance();
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        System.out.println("naive, reflection:      second instance = " + (viaReflection(NaiveSettings.class) != NaiveSettings.INSTANCE));
        System.out.println("naive, serialization:   second instance = " + (roundTrip(NaiveSettings.INSTANCE) != NaiveSettings.INSTANCE));

        try {
            viaReflection(HardenedSettings.class);
        } catch (java.lang.reflect.InvocationTargetException e) {
            System.out.println("hardened, reflection:   blocked (" + e.getCause().getMessage() + ")");
        }
        System.out.println("hardened, serialization: same instance = " + (roundTrip(HardenedSettings.INSTANCE) == HardenedSettings.INSTANCE));
    }
}
  1. A guard in the constructor turns a reflective second construction into an error.
  2. readResolve replaces the deserialised copy with the real instance.
  3. Reflection bypasses private unless the module system or a guard prevents it.

Run it: java BreakingSingletonDemo.java

naive, reflection:      second instance = true
naive, serialization:   second instance = true
hardened, reflection:   blocked (HardenedSettings is a singleton)
hardened, serialization: same instance = true
Defence Protects against Cost Use an enum Reflection and serialization Can't extend a class Constructor guard Reflection Extra code; must be thread-safe readResolve() Serialization Must remember it; fields should be transient Don't implement Cloneable Cloning None Strong encapsulation (JPMS modules) Reflection from other modules Requires modular build

Use these defences when a second instance would be a security or correctness problem. Don't bother for ordinary in-house singletons; prefer DI instead. Real-world Java: enums are protected in java.lang.reflect.Constructor.newInstance, which throws "Cannot reflectively create enum objects". Best practice: if you need the guarantees, use an enum. Gotcha: in an application server with several web apps, each app's class loader has its own "singleton".

docs.title: Singleton vs. dependency-injected single instance
docs.text:
Description. Often what you really need is one instance per application, not a class that enforces one instance and exposes it globally. Create the object once in the composition root (or let Spring create it; Spring beans are singleton-scoped by default) and pass it to whoever needs it through their constructor.

Advantages / features. Dependencies are visible in constructors; tests create their own instance (or a fake); no global state; you can still have exactly one instance at runtime.

DiSingletonDemo.java
import java.time.Clock;
import java.time.Instant;
import java.time.ZoneOffset;
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;

/** "Single instance" without the Singleton pattern: create one object in the composition root and inject it. */
public class DiSingletonDemo {

    // ===================== BEFORE: a static singleton hidden inside the service =====================
    static final class AuditLogStatic {
        static final AuditLogStatic INSTANCE = new AuditLogStatic();
        final List<String> lines = new ArrayList<>();
        void write(String line) { lines.add(Instant.now() + " " + line); }            // (1)!
    }

    static final class RefundServiceBefore {
        void refund(String orderId) { AuditLogStatic.INSTANCE.write("refund " + orderId); }   // (2)!
    }

    // ===================== AFTER: an interface, one instance, injected =====================
    interface AuditLog { void write(String line); }

    static final class ListAuditLog implements AuditLog {
        private final Clock clock;
        final List<String> lines = new ArrayList<>();
        ListAuditLog(Clock clock) { this.clock = clock; }
        public void write(String line) { lines.add(clock.instant() + " " + line); }
    }

    static final class RefundService {
        private final AuditLog audit;
        RefundService(AuditLog audit) { this.audit = audit; }                          // (3)!
        void refund(String orderId) { audit.write("refund " + orderId); }
    }

    static final class SupportDesk {
        private final AuditLog audit;
        SupportDesk(AuditLog audit) { this.audit = audit; }
        void escalate(String ticket) { audit.write("escalate " + ticket); }
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        new RefundServiceBefore().refund("FC-1");
        System.out.println("before: static log has " + AuditLogStatic.INSTANCE.lines.size() + " line(s), timestamp is real time, can't be reset between tests");

        // Composition root: exactly ONE AuditLog, shared by everyone who needs it.
        ListAuditLog audit = new ListAuditLog(Clock.fixed(Instant.parse("2026-11-02T10:00:00Z"), ZoneOffset.UTC));  // (4)!
        RefundService refunds = new RefundService(audit);
        SupportDesk support = new SupportDesk(audit);

        refunds.refund("FC-2");
        support.escalate("T-77");
        audit.lines.forEach(line -> System.out.println("after:  " + line));
    }
}
  1. The static version uses the real clock and accumulates state across tests.
  2. The dependency is hidden: nothing in RefundServiceBefore's constructor tells you it writes an audit log.
  3. The dependency is explicit and replaceable.
  4. One instance, created once, shared by both services.

Run it: java DiSingletonDemo.java

before: static log has 1 line(s), timestamp is real time, can't be reset between tests
after:  2026-11-02T10:00:00Z refund FC-2
after:  2026-11-02T10:00:00Z escalate T-77
Static Singleton DI single instance Number of instances at runtime One One Dependency visible in constructors No Yes Replace in tests Hard (global state) Easy (pass a fake) Thread safety of creation Must be designed in Composition root creates it once Works with Spring Fights the container Default bean scope

Use DI in applications, especially with Spring, Micronaut, Quarkus or Dagger. Use a static singleton only in libraries or low-level code with no composition root, or for truly stateless constants. Real-world Java: Spring @Service and @Component beans are single instances managed by the container, not GoF singletons. Best practice: "single instance" is a wiring decision, so make it in the composition root. Gotcha: a Spring bean that also has a static getInstance() gives you two ways to reach it, and they can diverge.

docs.title: Example 1: Minimal (L1)
docs.text:
Scenario: FreshCart's checkout needs app-wide settings (the region and the basket limit) that are read once at startup and never change.

AppSettingsDemo.java
/** The smallest useful singleton: one settings object for the whole app, as an enum. */
public class AppSettingsDemo {

    enum AppSettings {
        INSTANCE;                                                                       // (1)!

        private final String region = System.getProperty("freshcart.region", "IN-MH");
        private final int maxBasketItems = Integer.getInteger("freshcart.maxBasketItems", 50);

        String region() { return region; }
        int maxBasketItems() { return maxBasketItems; }
    }

    static String checkBasket(int items) {
        int max = AppSettings.INSTANCE.maxBasketItems();                                 // (2)!
        return items <= max ? "ok (" + items + "/" + max + ")" : "too many items (" + items + "/" + max + ")";
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("region: " + AppSettings.INSTANCE.region());
        System.out.println("basket of 12: " + checkBasket(12));
        System.out.println("basket of 80: " + checkBasket(80));
    }
}
  1. One enum constant: one settings object, created safely by the JVM.
  2. Any class can read settings without passing them around.

Run it:

java AppSettingsDemo.java
java -Dfreshcart.maxBasketItems=100 AppSettingsDemo.java   # the 80-item basket is now ok

Output:

region: IN-MH
basket of 12: ok (12/50)
basket of 80: too many items (80/50)

What to notice:

  • No locking code at all; the enum handles thread safety.
  • Settings are read once; changing the system property later has no effect, which is usually what you want for startup configuration.
  • checkBasket hides a dependency on AppSettings: fine in a tiny program, a testing problem in a large one (see Example 3).

docs.title: Example 2: Realistic (in FreshCart grocery delivery)
docs.text:
Scenario: Checkout and Delivery both count business events (orders placed, deliveries completed or failed). Operations wants one registry to read all counters from, and the counters must be correct when many requests update them at once.

MetricsRegistryDemo.java
import java.util.Map;
import java.util.TreeMap;
import java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap;
import java.util.concurrent.atomic.LongAdder;

/** One process-wide metrics registry that every FreshCart component writes to. */
public class MetricsRegistryDemo {

    enum Metrics {
        INSTANCE;

        private final Map<String, LongAdder> counters = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();       // (1)!

        void increment(String name) {
            if (!name.matches("[a-z_.]+")) throw new IllegalArgumentException("bad metric name: " + name);
            counters.computeIfAbsent(name, n -> new LongAdder()).increment();            // (2)!
        }

        Map<String, Long> snapshot() {
            Map<String, Long> copy = new TreeMap<>();
            counters.forEach((k, v) -> copy.put(k, v.sum()));
            return copy;                                                                 // (3)!
        }
    }

    static final class Checkout {
        void place(String orderId) { Metrics.INSTANCE.increment("checkout.orders_placed"); }
    }

    static final class Delivery {
        void deliver(String orderId, boolean ok) {
            Metrics.INSTANCE.increment(ok ? "delivery.completed" : "delivery.failed");
        }
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Checkout checkout = new Checkout();
        Delivery delivery = new Delivery();
        for (int i = 1; i <= 3; i++) checkout.place("FC-" + i);
        delivery.deliver("FC-1", true);
        delivery.deliver("FC-2", true);
        delivery.deliver("FC-3", false);
        System.out.println(Metrics.INSTANCE.snapshot());
        try { Metrics.INSTANCE.increment("Delivery Failed!"); } catch (IllegalArgumentException e) { System.out.println("rejected: " + e.getMessage()); }
    }
}
  1. Thread-safe map, because every request thread writes to the singleton.
  2. LongAdder handles heavy concurrent increments better than AtomicLong.
  3. Return a copy so callers can't modify the registry's state.

Run it: java MetricsRegistryDemo.java

Output:

{checkout.orders_placed=3, delivery.completed=2, delivery.failed=1}
rejected: bad metric name: Delivery Failed!

What to notice:

  • A metrics registry is one of the few places a static singleton is common in production code (Micrometer has Metrics.globalRegistry).
  • All state inside the singleton is thread-safe; that's mandatory, not optional.
  • Metric names are validated, so a malformed name (spaces, capitals) fails fast instead of creating a counter no dashboard queries.

docs.title: Example 3: Production-grade
docs.text:
Scenario: FreshCart's slot service caches each store's open delivery slots for five minutes. There must be one cache per service so app and web requests share it, entries must expire, the database must be called as little as possible, a database outage should serve stale data rather than fail, and tests must be able to create a fresh cache and control time. That rules out a static singleton; the answer is one instance created in the composition root and injected.

SlotCacheDemo.java
import java.time.Clock;
import java.time.Duration;
import java.time.Instant;
import java.time.ZoneId;
import java.time.ZoneOffset;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Map;
import java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap;
import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger;
import java.util.function.Function;

/**
 * Production shape: ONE shared cache instance for the whole service, created in the composition root and
 * injected. Thread-safe, time-based expiry with an injected Clock, and hit/miss/load-failure metrics.
 */
public class SlotCacheDemo {

    record Slots(String storeId, List<String> open) { }

    /** Thread-safe, single shared instance. Not a static singleton: tests create their own. */
    static final class SlotCache {
        private record Entry(Slots slots, Instant loadedAt) { }

        private final Map<String, Entry> entries = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();           // (1)!
        private final Function<String, Slots> loader;
        private final Duration ttl;
        private final Clock clock;
        final AtomicInteger hits = new AtomicInteger(), misses = new AtomicInteger(), loadFailures = new AtomicInteger();

        SlotCache(Function<String, Slots> loader, Duration ttl, Clock clock) {
            if (ttl.isNegative() || ttl.isZero()) throw new IllegalArgumentException("ttl must be positive");
            this.loader = loader; this.ttl = ttl; this.clock = clock;
        }

        Slots get(String storeId) {
            Instant now = clock.instant();
            Entry current = entries.get(storeId);
            if (current != null && now.isBefore(current.loadedAt().plus(ttl))) {
                hits.incrementAndGet();
                return current.slots();
            }
            misses.incrementAndGet();
            try {
                Entry fresh = new Entry(loader.apply(storeId), now);
                entries.put(storeId, fresh);
                return fresh.slots();
            } catch (RuntimeException e) {
                loadFailures.incrementAndGet();
                if (current != null) return current.slots();                            // (2)!
                throw new IllegalStateException("slots unavailable for " + storeId, e);
            }
        }

        String stats() { return "hits=" + hits + " misses=" + misses + " loadFailures=" + loadFailures; }
    }

    /** A clock tests (and this demo) can move forward. */
    static final class MutableClock extends Clock {
        private Instant now;
        MutableClock(Instant start) { now = start; }
        void advance(Duration d) { now = now.plus(d); }
        @Override public Instant instant() { return now; }
        @Override public ZoneId getZone() { return ZoneOffset.UTC; }
        @Override public Clock withZone(ZoneId zone) { return this; }
    }

    // ---- Two request handlers that share the single cache instance ----
    record AppHandler(SlotCache cache) { String show(String store) { return "app sees " + cache.get(store).open(); } }
    record WebHandler(SlotCache cache) { String show(String store) { return "web sees " + cache.get(store).open(); } }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        MutableClock clock = new MutableClock(Instant.parse("2026-11-02T09:00:00Z"));
        AtomicInteger dbCalls = new AtomicInteger();
        boolean[] dbDown = {false};
        Function<String, Slots> database = store -> {
            dbCalls.incrementAndGet();
            if (dbDown[0]) throw new RuntimeException("db timeout");
            return new Slots(store, dbCalls.get() == 1 ? List.of("12:00", "18:00") : List.of("18:00"));
        };

        SlotCache cache = new SlotCache(database, Duration.ofMinutes(5), clock);          // (3)!
        AppHandler app = new AppHandler(cache);
        WebHandler web = new WebHandler(cache);

        System.out.println(app.show("pune-01"));
        System.out.println(web.show("pune-01") + "  (same cache, no db call)");
        clock.advance(Duration.ofMinutes(6));
        System.out.println(app.show("pune-01") + "  (expired, reloaded)");
        clock.advance(Duration.ofMinutes(6));
        dbDown[0] = true;
        System.out.println(web.show("pune-01") + "  (db down, served stale)");
        try { app.show("mumbai-02"); } catch (IllegalStateException e) { System.out.println("rejected: " + e.getMessage()); }
        System.out.println("db calls: " + dbCalls.get() + ", " + cache.stats());
    }
}
  1. ConcurrentHashMap: the single instance is shared by every request thread.
  2. On a load failure, serve the last known value if there is one (stale-if-error).
  3. The composition root creates exactly one cache and hands it to both handlers.

Run it: java SlotCacheDemo.java

Output:

app sees [12:00, 18:00]
web sees [12:00, 18:00]  (same cache, no db call)
app sees [18:00]  (expired, reloaded)
web sees [18:00]  (db down, served stale)
rejected: slots unavailable for mumbai-02
db calls: 4, hits=1 misses=4 loadFailures=2

What to notice:

  • The web request after the app request didn't call the database: one shared instance.
  • Expiry is tested by moving an injected clock, not by sleeping.
  • The database was down for the fourth request, yet customers still saw slots; only a store with no cached value failed.
  • Hit, miss and load-failure counters are what you'd export to your metrics system.

docs.title: 7. Pros, Cons & Trade-offs
docs.text: Aspect Pros Cons Simplicity One well-known place to get the object Hidden dependencies: callers reach for it from anywhere Performance Expensive resources created once Contention if the singleton's state is synchronised badly Scalability Shared pools and caches use memory efficiently Global state becomes a bottleneck and a coupling point Operability One place to configure and observe Hard to reconfigure at runtime without a restart Security Enum form resists reflection and serialization attacks A mutable global is reachable by all code Testability — Hard to replace, state leaks between tests, order-dependent tests Cost Little code Refactoring away from singletons later is expensive Learning curve Easy to understand Thread-safe lazy variants are easy to get wrong

docs.title: 8. When to Use / When NOT to Use
docs.text:
Use a static Singleton when:

  • there's genuinely one of something per JVM and no DI container (a library's internal registry, a process-wide metrics registry);
  • the object is stateless or immutable (constants, pure functions grouped in an enum).

Use a DI-managed single instance instead when:

  • you're in an application with a composition root or a container (Spring, Quarkus, Micronaut, Dagger);
  • the object has dependencies, configuration, or state that tests need to control.

Don't use either for: per-user or per-request data, or anything you'll need more than one of later (multi-tenant, multi-region). Compare alternatives in Pattern Comparisons.

docs.title: 9. Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Prefer DI for single instances in applications. (Consensus in modern Java.)
  2. If you need a static singleton, use an enum or the lazy holder idiom. (Consensus: Effective Java Item 3.)
  3. Make all state inside a singleton thread-safe or immutable. (Consensus.)
  4. Keep constructors cheap and free of I/O, so initialisation failures don't poison the class. (Consensus.)
  5. Never store per-user or per-request data in a singleton. (Consensus.)
  6. Hide the singleton behind an interface if other code depends on it, so tests can substitute it. (Opinion.)
  7. Write volatile double-checked locking only when profiling shows the simpler forms don't fit. (Opinion.)

docs.title: 10. Pitfalls & Anti-Patterns
docs.text:
Singletonitis

Symptom: OrderService.getInstance(), PaymentService.getInstance(), UserService.getInstance() everywhere; tests need a specific run order. Root cause: Singleton used as a convenient way to reach things instead of passing dependencies. Fix: convert to constructor injection one service at a time; create instances in the composition root.

Customer data shown to the wrong customer (production failure mode)

Symptom: under load, some users saw another customer's basket total in the app. Root cause: a singleton CheckoutContext stored the "current customer" in a field, and concurrent requests overwrote each other. Fix: per-request data goes in request-scoped objects or method parameters, never in a singleton's fields.

Broken double-checked locking

Symptom: rare NullPointerExceptions inside a freshly created singleton, only on multi-core production machines. Root cause: the field wasn't volatile, so another thread saw a reference to a partially constructed object. Fix: add volatile, or switch to the lazy holder idiom.

Poisoned class

Symptom: every request fails with NoClassDefFoundError: Could not initialize class ... after a startup hiccup. Root cause: the singleton's static initialiser threw once (database down at startup), and the JVM never retries class initialisation. Fix: don't do I/O in static initialisers; create the resource lazily with retries, or in the composition root.

docs.title: 11. Configuration & Tuning
docs.text: Setting Default What it does When to change it Risk of changing Eager vs lazy Eager (enum/static field) When the instance is built Expensive and often unused objects Lazy hides startup failures until first use Cache TTL (Example 3) 5 minutes How long cached data is served Data changes faster or slower Too long: stale data; too short: database load Stale-if-error On Serve the last value when loading fails Data must never be stale (prices at payment) Off: outages surface to customers

docs.title: 12. Security Considerations
docs.text:
• Use an enum for security-sensitive singletons (licence checks, crypto key holders) so reflection and serialization can't create a second instance.
  • Never keep secrets in a singleton's toString(), and don't keep per-user tokens in singleton fields.
  • With JPMS, don't opens the package containing security singletons, so other modules can't reflect into them.

docs.title: 13. Performance & Scalability
docs.text: Access to an enum, eager or holder singleton is just a static field read after initialisation; the JIT often constant-folds it. The real performance risk is contention: a synchronized method on a singleton serialises every request. Use concurrent data structures (ConcurrentHashMap, LongAdder) inside singletons, and measure with JMH before optimising (see Performance Cost of Patterns).

docs.title: 14. Testing It
docs.text:
Each test creates its own cache instance and controls time, which a static singleton would make impossible:

SlotCacheTest.java
import static org.junit.jupiter.api.Assertions.assertEquals;
import static org.junit.jupiter.api.Assertions.assertSame;

import java.time.Duration;
import java.time.Instant;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;

class SlotCacheTest {

    private final SlotCacheDemo.MutableClock clock = new SlotCacheDemo.MutableClock(Instant.parse("2026-11-02T09:00:00Z"));
    private final AtomicInteger loads = new AtomicInteger();

    /** Each test gets its OWN cache: impossible with a static singleton. */
    private SlotCacheDemo.SlotCache newCache() {
        return new SlotCacheDemo.SlotCache(s -> { loads.incrementAndGet(); return new SlotCacheDemo.Slots(s, List.of("18:00")); },
                Duration.ofMinutes(5), clock);
    }

    @Test
    void servesFromCacheUntilTheTtlExpires() {
        var cache = newCache();
        var first = cache.get("s1");
        clock.advance(Duration.ofMinutes(4).plusSeconds(59));
        assertSame(first, cache.get("s1"));
        clock.advance(Duration.ofSeconds(1));
        cache.get("s1");
        assertEquals(2, loads.get());
    }

    @Test
    void handlersShareOneInstance() {
        var cache = newCache();
        new SlotCacheDemo.AppHandler(cache).show("s1");
        new SlotCacheDemo.WebHandler(cache).show("s1");
        assertEquals(1, loads.get());
        assertEquals(1, cache.hits.get());
    }
}

If you must test code that uses a static singleton, add a package-private reset method for tests, or better, refactor the caller to accept an interface.

docs.title: 15. Observability & Operations
docs.text: Singletons that own resources (pools, caches, clients) should expose metrics: size, hit rate, load failures, and for pools active versus idle connections. Log once at creation with the effective configuration, so you can see in production what the single instance was built with. Alert on a rising load-failure count before it becomes customer-visible.

docs.title: 16. Version Notes
docs.text:
Java Change relevant to Singleton 5 New memory model (JSR-133) makes volatile double-checked locking correct; enums introduced 9 Modules (JPMS) can block reflective access to private constructors from other modules 16 Records: handy for immutable values held by singletons 21 Virtual threads: avoid synchronized blocks around blocking I/O inside shared singletons, since they pin the carrier thread in Java 21

Verify against the official docs

The pinning behaviour of synchronized with virtual threads was improved in later JDK releases (JEP 491, JDK 24). Check the release notes for the JDK you run.

docs.title: 17. Expert Deep Dive
docs.text:
• "One per what?" Seniors ask what the uniqueness scope really is: per JVM, per class loader, per tenant, per region, per request? A GoF Singleton answers "per class loader" whether you meant it or not. In multi-tenant systems, most "singletons" turn out to be "one per tenant".
  • Singletons are global variables with better manners. They create hidden coupling, which shows up as tests that must run in a specific order and features that can't be split into modules. In design reviews, ask: "how would a test replace this?"
  • Container scope is the modern answer. Spring's singleton scope, Dagger's @Singleton and Guice's @Singleton give one instance per container, visible in constructors, replaceable in tests.
  • Initialisation order bugs. Static singletons that depend on each other can deadlock during class initialisation if two threads initialise them in opposite orders. Avoid singleton-to-singleton dependencies in static initialisers.
  • Migrating legacy code: keep getInstance() working, but make it return an instance that the composition root installs. Move callers to constructor injection one by one; delete getInstance() when it has no callers.

War story: the singleton that knew too much

A grocery platform's mobile backend had a SessionManager.getInstance() singleton that cached "the current store" for pricing. It worked for years because each JVM served one city. When the team consolidated cities onto shared instances to cut costs, customers in Pune occasionally saw Mumbai prices. The cause took a week to find: the singleton's "current store" was being overwritten by concurrent requests from different cities. The fix was to remove the field, pass the store through the request, and replace the singleton with an injected, stateless PricingService. Lesson: a singleton's uniqueness assumption ("one city per JVM") is a hidden architectural constraint; write it down or design it out.

docs.title: 18. Interview Corner
19. Practice
docs.text:
• Convert EagerSingletonDemo.FeatureFlags to an enum and check the output is unchanged. ??? tip "Hint" enum FeatureFlags { INSTANCE; private final Map<String, Boolean> flags = ...; }
  • Remove volatile from DclSingletonDemo and explain why the test probably still passes. ??? tip "Hint" The bug depends on instruction reordering and CPU memory visibility; x86 hides many such bugs. The code is still wrong.
  • Add a maxEntries limit to SlotCache that evicts the oldest store. ??? tip "Hint" Track insertion order, or use a LinkedHashMap with removeEldestEntry behind a lock.
  • Find every getInstance() in a project you know and classify each as "keep" or "inject". ??? tip "Hint" Keep stateless or process-wide infrastructure; inject anything with dependencies or business state.

docs.title: 20. Quick Revision Card
docs.text:
Remember in 30 seconds

  • Intent: one instance + global access. Creational.
  • Best static forms: enum (safest) or lazy holder (lazy, lock-free).
  • Double-checked locking needs volatile and a local copy.
  • Breakers: reflection, serialization (readResolve), cloning, class loaders.
  • In applications, prefer one instance created in the composition root and injected.
enum Settings { INSTANCE; int maxItems() { return 50; } }

final class Catalog {
    private Catalog() { }
    private static final class Holder { static final Catalog I = new Catalog(); }
    static Catalog get() { return Holder.I; }
}
