docs.title: Mediator
docs.text:
L2 🔵 Practitioner · ⏱ 35 min read · Prerequisites: Observer, Facade

TL;DR

Mediator puts the coordination between several objects into one place. Instead of every object knowing and calling the others (a web of n² links), each "colleague" talks only to the mediator, which decides who should react. Typical uses: UI screens where fields affect each other, dispatchers matching orders with riders, and in-process buses that route requests to handlers. Keep each mediator focused on one workflow, or it becomes a god class.

docs.title: 1. What It Is
docs.text:
Plain English. On FreshCart's checkout screen, changing the address must reload delivery slots, clear the chosen slot, and disable the "Place order" button until a slot and payment are chosen again. If each widget called the others directly, every widget would know about every other one. Instead, each widget tells the screen "I changed", and the screen (the mediator) decides what happens next.

Definition (GoF). "Define an object that encapsulates how a set of objects interact. Mediator promotes loose coupling by keeping objects from referring to each other explicitly, and it lets you vary their interaction independently." Parts:

  • Mediator: an interface for colleagues to report events (changed(widget), orderPacked(id)).
  • Concrete mediator: knows the colleagues and contains the coordination rules.
  • Colleagues: objects that do their own job and report to the mediator instead of calling each other.

docs.title: 2. Why It Exists
docs.text: When objects interact directly, each new rule adds links: n objects can need up to n × (n − 1) references, and the rules end up scattered across all of them. Changing a rule ("clear the payment method when the address has no slots") means finding which classes know about which. A mediator turns that many-to-many web into many-to-one, with the rules in one class that can be read, tested and changed in one place. The colleagues become reusable because they no longer know their neighbours.

docs.title: 3. Mental Model / Analogy
docs.text:
Analogy. An airport control tower. Planes don't negotiate runway use with each other; each talks to the tower, which tells them when to land or wait. Adding a new plane doesn't require it to know every other plane.

Technical model. A hub-and-spoke graph. Colleagues hold a reference to the mediator (often through a narrow interface) and call it on events. The mediator holds references to the colleagues and updates them according to its rules.

docs.title: 4. How It Works
docs.text:
classDiagram
    class CheckoutMediator {
        <<interface>>
        +changed(widget)
    }
    class CheckoutScreen {
        +changed(widget)
    }
    class AddressField
    class SlotPicker
    class PaymentSelector
    class PlaceOrderButton
    CheckoutMediator <|.. CheckoutScreen
    CheckoutScreen o-- AddressField
    CheckoutScreen o-- SlotPicker
    CheckoutScreen o-- PaymentSelector
    CheckoutScreen o-- PlaceOrderButton
    AddressField ..> CheckoutMediator : reports
    SlotPicker ..> CheckoutMediator : reports
    PaymentSelector ..> CheckoutMediator : reports
sequenceDiagram
    participant A as AddressField
    participant M as CheckoutScreen
    participant S as SlotPicker
    participant B as PlaceOrderButton
    A->>M: changed(address)
    M->>S: load slots for 560001, clear choice
    M->>B: disable (no slot chosen)
    S->>M: changed(slot)
    M->>B: enable if payment chosen

docs.title: Mediator and colleagues
docs.text:
Description. Colleagues report events to the mediator; the mediator holds the rules that involve several colleagues and updates them. Colleagues don't reference each other at all.

Advantages / features. Rules are centralised and readable; colleagues are simpler and reusable; adding a widget affects only the mediator.

Before: the address field would hold references to the slot picker, payment selector and button, and each of those would hold references back. After:

MediatorColleaguesDemo.java
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Map;

/** Mediator: widgets on the checkout screen talk to one coordinator instead of to each other. */
public class MediatorColleaguesDemo {

    interface CheckoutMediator { void changed(Object widget); }                                    // (1)!

    static final class AddressField {
        private final CheckoutMediator m; String pincode;
        AddressField(CheckoutMediator m) { this.m = m; }
        void enter(String pin) { pincode = pin; m.changed(this); }                                 // (2)!
    }
    static final class SlotPicker {
        private final CheckoutMediator m; List<String> options = List.of(); String chosen;
        SlotPicker(CheckoutMediator m) { this.m = m; }
        void choose(String slot) { chosen = slot; m.changed(this); }
    }
    static final class PaymentSelector {
        private final CheckoutMediator m; String method;
        PaymentSelector(CheckoutMediator m) { this.m = m; }
        void select(String method) { this.method = method; m.changed(this); }
    }
    static final class PlaceOrderButton { boolean enabled; }

    static final class CheckoutScreen implements CheckoutMediator {                                 // (3)!
        final AddressField address = new AddressField(this);
        final SlotPicker slots = new SlotPicker(this);
        final PaymentSelector payment = new PaymentSelector(this);
        final PlaceOrderButton button = new PlaceOrderButton();
        private final Map<String, List<String>> slotsByArea = Map.of("560034", List.of("10-11", "11-12"), "560001", List.of("18-19"));

        public void changed(Object widget) {
            if (widget == address) {
                slots.options = slotsByArea.getOrDefault(address.pincode, List.of());
                slots.chosen = null;                                                                  // a new address invalidates the slot
                payment.method = slots.options.isEmpty() ? null : payment.method;
            }
            button.enabled = slots.chosen != null && payment.method != null;                        // (4)!
            System.out.println("  after " + widget.getClass().getSimpleName() + ": slots=" + slots.options + " chosen=" + slots.chosen + " pay=" + payment.method + " button=" + (button.enabled ? "ON" : "off"));
        }
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        CheckoutScreen s = new CheckoutScreen();
        s.address.enter("560034");
        s.slots.choose("10-11");
        s.payment.select("UPI");
        s.address.enter("560001");
    }
}
  1. Colleagues see only this narrow interface.
  2. A colleague does its own job and reports the change; it never calls another widget.
  3. The screen is the mediator: it owns the widgets and the rules between them.
  4. The cross-widget rule ("button enabled only with a slot and a payment method") lives in exactly one place.

Run it: java MediatorColleaguesDemo.java

  after AddressField: slots=[10-11, 11-12] chosen=null pay=null button=off
  after SlotPicker: slots=[10-11, 11-12] chosen=10-11 pay=null button=off
  after PaymentSelector: slots=[10-11, 11-12] chosen=10-11 pay=UPI button=ON
  after AddressField: slots=[18-19] chosen=null pay=UPI button=off
Pros Cons n² links become n The mediator can grow very large Interaction rules in one place One more class to read to understand behaviour Colleagues reusable and testable Colleagues' changes all funnel through one method

Use it when several objects have rules about each other (forms, dashboards, dispatch). Avoid it when two objects interact simply; a direct call is clearer. Real-world Java: Swing/JavaFX controllers coordinating form fields; java.util.Timer coordinating tasks; Spring's DispatcherServlet coordinating handler mappings, adapters and view resolvers. Best practice: give colleagues a narrow mediator interface, not the concrete class. Gotcha: a mediator that updates a colleague, which reports back, which triggers another update, can loop; make updates from the mediator not trigger reports (or guard re-entry).

docs.title: Event bus as a mediator
docs.text:
Description. An in-process event bus is a generic mediator: publishers post events to the bus, subscribers register for event types, and neither knows the other. Unlike a hand-written mediator, the bus has no business rules; it only routes.

Advantages / features. Very loose coupling; new reactions added without touching publishers; failures in one subscriber can be isolated.

EventBusMediatorDemo.java
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.HashMap;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Map;
import java.util.function.Consumer;

/** An in-process event bus is a mediator: publishers and subscribers only know the bus, never each other. */
public class EventBusMediatorDemo {

    record OrderPlaced(String orderId, List<String> skus) { }
    record OrderCancelled(String orderId) { }

    static final class EventBus {
        private final Map<Class<?>, List<Consumer<Object>>> subs = new HashMap<>();
        @SuppressWarnings("unchecked")
        <E> void subscribe(Class<E> type, Consumer<? super E> handler) {                              // (1)!
            subs.computeIfAbsent(type, t -> new ArrayList<>()).add(e -> handler.accept((E) e));
        }
        void publish(Object event) {
            for (Consumer<Object> h : subs.getOrDefault(event.getClass(), List.of())) {
                try { h.accept(event); }
                catch (RuntimeException ex) { System.out.println("  subscriber failed: " + ex.getMessage() + " (others still run)"); }   // (2)!
            }
        }
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        EventBus bus = new EventBus();
        bus.subscribe(OrderPlaced.class, e -> System.out.println("  inventory: reserve " + e.skus()));
        bus.subscribe(OrderPlaced.class, e -> { throw new IllegalStateException("analytics endpoint down"); });
        bus.subscribe(OrderPlaced.class, e -> System.out.println("  notifications: SMS for " + e.orderId()));
        bus.subscribe(OrderCancelled.class, e -> System.out.println("  inventory: release " + e.orderId()));

        System.out.println("checkout publishes OrderPlaced:");
        bus.publish(new OrderPlaced("FC-9401", List.of("MILK-1L", "BREAD")));                          // (3)!
        System.out.println("support publishes OrderCancelled:");
        bus.publish(new OrderCancelled("FC-9401"));
    }
}
  1. Subscribers register by event type; the bus keeps the list.
  2. A failing subscriber is isolated so the others still run.
  3. Checkout publishes one event and knows nothing about inventory, analytics or notifications.

Run it: java EventBusMediatorDemo.java

checkout publishes OrderPlaced:
  inventory: reserve [MILK-1L, BREAD]
  subscriber failed: analytics endpoint down (others still run)
  notifications: SMS for FC-9401
support publishes OrderCancelled:
  inventory: release FC-9401
Pros Cons Publishers and subscribers fully decoupled Flow is hard to follow ("who reacts to this?") Easy to add reactions Ordering and error handling are implicit Good for cross-module notifications Overuse turns a codebase into "event spaghetti"

Use a bus for notifications that several modules care about. Avoid it for request/response flows where the caller needs a result. Real-world Java: Spring ApplicationEventPublisher and @EventListener (with @TransactionalEventListener for after-commit), Guava EventBus, Vert.x event bus. Best practice: document events like an API (name, fields, who publishes). Gotcha: Spring events are synchronous by default; a slow listener slows the publisher unless you use @Async.

docs.title: Mediator vs. Observer
docs.text:
Description. Both decouple objects. In Observer, a subject broadcasts changes and each observer decides independently what to do; the subject has no coordination logic. In Mediator, the mediator contains the logic that involves several colleagues ("if stock is low and a promo is active, pause the promo and reorder more").

Advantages / features (of knowing the difference). Put multi-party rules in a mediator and single-party reactions in observers.

MediatorVsObserverDemo.java
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.function.Consumer;

/** Observer broadcasts and each listener decides alone; a Mediator holds the coordination rule that involves several parties. */
public class MediatorVsObserverDemo {

    // ===================== Observer: stock broadcasts; listeners react independently =====================
    static final class Stock {
        final List<Consumer<Integer>> listeners = new ArrayList<>();
        void update(int units) { listeners.forEach(l -> l.accept(units)); }                          // (1)!
    }

    // ===================== Mediator: the rule needs stock AND promo AND buyer, so it lives in one place =====================
    static final class Promo { boolean active = true; void pause() { active = false; System.out.println("  promo paused"); } }
    static final class Buyer { void reorder(int qty) { System.out.println("  buyer: reorder " + qty + " units"); } }

    static final class StockPromoMediator {                                                          // (2)!
        private final Promo promo; private final Buyer buyer;
        StockPromoMediator(Promo promo, Buyer buyer) { this.promo = promo; this.buyer = buyer; }
        void stockChanged(int units) {
            if (units < 20 && promo.active) { promo.pause(); buyer.reorder(200); }                   // (3)!
            else if (units < 20) buyer.reorder(100);
        }
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Stock mangoes = new Stock();
        mangoes.listeners.add(u -> System.out.println("  dashboard shows " + u + " units"));
        mangoes.listeners.add(u -> { if (u < 20) System.out.println("  app shows 'only a few left'"); });
        System.out.println("observer:");
        mangoes.update(15);

        System.out.println("mediator:");
        StockPromoMediator m = new StockPromoMediator(new Promo(), new Buyer());
        m.stockChanged(15);
        m.stockChanged(12);
    }
}
  1. Observer: the subject just notifies; it doesn't know what listeners do.
  2. Mediator: knows the promo and the buyer, and coordinates them.
  3. The rule needs information about several parties, so it can't live in any single listener.

Run it: java MediatorVsObserverDemo.java

observer:
  dashboard shows 15 units
  app shows 'only a few left'
mediator:
  promo paused
  buyer: reorder 200 units
  buyer: reorder 100 units
Observer Mediator Direction One-to-many broadcast Many-to-many via a hub Logic location In each observer In the mediator Knows the others Subject doesn't know observers' types Mediator knows all colleagues Typical use "Something happened" "Coordinate these parties"

Use Observer for independent reactions; Mediator for rules spanning several objects. Avoid chains of observers that trigger each other to implement a multi-party rule; that's a hidden mediator. Real-world Java: Observer: PropertyChangeListener, Spring events; Mediator: controllers, dispatchers, workflow coordinators. Best practice: combine them: the mediator can be an observer of colleagues' events. Gotcha: an event bus with one subscriber that contains all the rules is a mediator in disguise; name it as one.

docs.title: Avoiding the god mediator
docs.text:
Description. Because all coordination flows into the mediator, it tends to grow until it knows every colleague and handles every event: a god class that every team edits. The fix is to split mediators by workflow or use case, each with only the colleagues it needs.

Advantages / features. Small mediators are readable, testable, and owned by one team; changes have a smaller blast radius.

GodMediatorDemo.java
import java.util.List;

/** A mediator that coordinates everything becomes a god class. Split by workflow, each with only the colleagues it needs. */
public class GodMediatorDemo {

    // ===================== Before: one mediator, every event, every colleague =====================
    static final class StoreMediator {                                                               // (1)!
        static final List<String> COLLEAGUES = List.of("cart", "slots", "payment", "inventory", "riders", "sms", "promos", "analytics", "refunds");
        static final List<String> EVENTS = List.of("cartChanged", "slotChosen", "paid", "packed", "riderFree", "delivered", "cancelled", "stockLow", "refundRequested");
        void on(String event) { /* a 400-line switch lives here */ }
    }

    // ===================== After: one mediator per workflow =====================
    record Mediator(String name, List<String> colleagues, List<String> events) { }                 // (2)!

    static final List<Mediator> SPLIT = List.of(
            new Mediator("CheckoutMediator", List.of("cart", "slots", "payment"), List.of("cartChanged", "slotChosen", "paid")),
            new Mediator("DispatchMediator", List.of("inventory", "riders", "sms"), List.of("packed", "riderFree", "delivered")),
            new Mediator("AfterSalesMediator", List.of("refunds", "sms", "inventory"), List.of("cancelled", "refundRequested")),
            new Mediator("MerchandisingMediator", List.of("promos", "inventory", "analytics"), List.of("stockLow")));

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("before: 1 mediator, " + StoreMediator.COLLEAGUES.size() + " colleagues, " + StoreMediator.EVENTS.size() + " events");
        SPLIT.forEach(m -> System.out.println("after:  " + m.name() + " -> " + m.colleagues().size() + " colleagues, " + m.events().size() + " event" + (m.events().size() == 1 ? "" : "s")));
        for (String colleague : List.of("refunds", "inventory")) {                                   // (3)!
            List<String> users = SPLIT.stream().filter(m -> m.colleagues().contains(colleague)).map(Mediator::name).toList();
            System.out.println("a change to '" + colleague + "' touches " + users + " (before: StoreMediator, which every team edits)");
        }
    }
}
  1. Before: one mediator, nine colleagues, nine events, one giant switch.
  2. After: one mediator per workflow, each with three colleagues.
  3. A change to refunds now touches one small class; shared colleagues like inventory are used by several mediators, which is fine.

Run it: java GodMediatorDemo.java

before: 1 mediator, 9 colleagues, 9 events
after:  CheckoutMediator -> 3 colleagues, 3 events
after:  DispatchMediator -> 3 colleagues, 3 events
after:  AfterSalesMediator -> 3 colleagues, 2 events
after:  MerchandisingMediator -> 3 colleagues, 1 event
a change to 'refunds' touches [AfterSalesMediator] (before: StoreMediator, which every team edits)
a change to 'inventory' touches [DispatchMediator, AfterSalesMediator, MerchandisingMediator] (before: StoreMediator, which every team edits)
Signal of a god mediator Fix More than ~7 colleagues Split by workflow Many unrelated events in one method One mediator per use case Several teams edit the same mediator Split along team/bounded-context lines Hard to test without everything Narrow interfaces for colleagues

Use one mediator per screen, workflow or bounded context. Avoid "application-wide" mediators. Real-world Java: large Spring controllers or "manager" services that coordinate everything are the common god mediators. Best practice: name mediators after the workflow (CheckoutMediator, DispatchCoordinator), not the app. Gotcha: splitting can create mediators that call each other; if two mediators coordinate constantly, they may be one workflow, or need events between them.

docs.title: Example 1: Minimal (L2)
docs.text:
Scenario: packers and riders send messages through the store desk, which routes them by role.

StoreDeskDemo.java
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;

/** Minimal Mediator: packers and riders don't call each other; the store desk routes messages by role. */
public class StoreDeskDemo {

    record Staff(String name, String role) { }

    static final class StoreDesk {                                                                  // (1)!
        private final List<Staff> staff = new ArrayList<>();
        void join(Staff s) { staff.add(s); }
        void send(Staff from, String toRole, String text) {
            staff.stream().filter(s -> s.role().equals(toRole))
                    .forEach(s -> System.out.println("  " + from.name() + " -> " + s.name() + ": " + text));   // (2)!
        }
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        StoreDesk desk = new StoreDesk();
        Staff priya = new Staff("Priya", "packer"), arjun = new Staff("Arjun", "rider"), meena = new Staff("Meena", "rider");
        desk.join(priya); desk.join(arjun); desk.join(meena);
        desk.send(priya, "rider", "FC-9501 is packed at bay 2");
        desk.send(arjun, "packer", "picking up FC-9501");
    }
}
  1. The desk is the mediator: staff join it and send through it.
  2. Routing by role: senders don't know who's on shift.

Run it: java StoreDeskDemo.java

Output:

  Priya -> Arjun: FC-9501 is packed at bay 2
  Priya -> Meena: FC-9501 is packed at bay 2
  Arjun -> Priya: picking up FC-9501

What to notice:

  • Priya didn't need to know which riders were working.

docs.title: Example 2: Realistic (in FreshCart grocery delivery)
docs.text:
Scenario: packing stations finish orders and riders become free at unpredictable times. A dispatcher matches them: a packed order goes to a waiting rider, or waits for the next free one.

DispatchMediatorDemo.java
import java.util.ArrayDeque;
import java.util.Deque;

/** Realistic Mediator: the dispatcher coordinates packed orders and free riders; neither side knows about the other. */
public class DispatchMediatorDemo {

    interface Dispatcher { void orderPacked(String orderId); void riderFree(String riderId); }   // (1)!

    static final class StoreDispatcher implements Dispatcher {
        private final Deque<String> waitingOrders = new ArrayDeque<>(), freeRiders = new ArrayDeque<>();
        public void orderPacked(String orderId) {
            if (freeRiders.isEmpty()) { waitingOrders.add(orderId); System.out.println("  " + orderId + " waits (no free rider)"); }
            else assign(orderId, freeRiders.poll());
        }
        public void riderFree(String riderId) {
            if (waitingOrders.isEmpty()) { freeRiders.add(riderId); System.out.println("  " + riderId + " waits (no packed order)"); }
            else assign(waitingOrders.poll(), riderId);                                              // (2)!
        }
        private void assign(String order, String rider) { System.out.println("  assign " + order + " -> " + rider); }   // (3)!
    }

    // Colleagues: they only report what happened to them
    record PackingStation(Dispatcher d) { void finished(String orderId) { d.orderPacked(orderId); } }
    record RiderApp(Dispatcher d, String riderId) { void tapAvailable() { d.riderFree(riderId); } }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Dispatcher d = new StoreDispatcher();
        PackingStation station = new PackingStation(d);
        RiderApp arjun = new RiderApp(d, "R-42"), meena = new RiderApp(d, "R-43");
        station.finished("FC-9601");
        station.finished("FC-9602");
        arjun.tapAvailable();
        meena.tapAvailable();
        meena.tapAvailable();
        station.finished("FC-9603");
    }
}
  1. Colleagues report only what happened to them.
  2. The matching rule works from both sides: a free rider takes the oldest waiting order.
  3. One place assigns; it's also where you'd add rules (bulky orders, rider capacity).

Run it: java DispatchMediatorDemo.java

Output:

  FC-9601 waits (no free rider)
  FC-9602 waits (no free rider)
  assign FC-9601 -> R-42
  assign FC-9602 -> R-43
  R-43 waits (no packed order)
  assign FC-9603 -> R-43

What to notice:

  • Neither the packing station nor the rider app knows the other exists.
  • Orders were matched first-in, first-out from both directions.

docs.title: Example 3: Production-grade
docs.text:
Scenario: controllers in the order service shouldn't depend on dozens of services. They send requests (PlaceOrder, GetOrderStatus) to an in-process mediator that routes each to exactly one handler, and handlers publish notifications (OrderPlaced) that any number of listeners handle. Requirements: missing or duplicate handlers fail at startup; cross-cutting behaviours (logging, validation) wrap every request; a failing listener doesn't break the others and is reported.

InProcessMediatorDemo.java
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.HashMap;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Map;
import java.util.function.Function;

/**
 * Production-grade in-process mediator (the idea behind MediatR / Spring's ApplicationEventPublisher):
 * - REQUESTS have exactly one handler (validated at startup: none missing, no duplicates)
 * - NOTIFICATIONS have zero or more handlers; one failing handler doesn't stop the others, failures are reported
 * - pipeline behaviours (logging, validation) wrap every request, so handlers stay focused
 * - callers depend only on the Mediator interface: no handler imports anywhere in controllers
 */
public class InProcessMediatorDemo {

    interface Request<R> { }
    interface Notification { }
    interface RequestHandler<Q extends Request<R>, R> { R handle(Q request); }
    interface Behaviour { Object around(Request<?> request, Function<Request<?>, Object> next); }

    record PlaceOrder(String customer, List<String> skus) implements Request<String> { }
    record GetOrderStatus(String orderId) implements Request<String> { }
    record OrderPlaced(String orderId, String customer) implements Notification { }

    static final class Mediator {
        private final Map<Class<?>, RequestHandler<?, ?>> handlers = new HashMap<>();
        private final Map<Class<?>, List<java.util.function.Consumer<Notification>>> listeners = new HashMap<>();
        private final List<Behaviour> behaviours = new ArrayList<>();
        final List<String> failures = new ArrayList<>();

        <Q extends Request<R>, R> Mediator handle(Class<Q> type, RequestHandler<Q, R> h) {
            if (handlers.putIfAbsent(type, h) != null) throw new IllegalStateException("two handlers for " + type.getSimpleName());   // (1)!
            return this;
        }
        @SuppressWarnings("unchecked")
        <N extends Notification> Mediator on(Class<N> type, java.util.function.Consumer<N> l) {
            listeners.computeIfAbsent(type, t -> new ArrayList<>()).add(n -> l.accept((N) n));
            return this;
        }
        Mediator behaviour(Behaviour b) { behaviours.add(b); return this; }

        Mediator validate(List<Class<? extends Request<?>>> requestTypes) {                        // (2)!
            List<String> missing = requestTypes.stream().filter(t -> !handlers.containsKey(t)).map(Class::getSimpleName).toList();
            if (!missing.isEmpty()) throw new IllegalStateException("no handler for " + missing);
            return this;
        }

        @SuppressWarnings({"unchecked", "rawtypes"})
        <R> R send(Request<R> request) {
            RequestHandler handler = handlers.get(request.getClass());
            if (handler == null) throw new IllegalStateException("no handler for " + request.getClass().getSimpleName());
            Function<Request<?>, Object> call = q -> handler.handle(q);
            for (int i = behaviours.size() - 1; i >= 0; i--) {                                       // (3)!
                Behaviour b = behaviours.get(i); Function<Request<?>, Object> next = call;
                call = q -> b.around(q, next);
            }
            return (R) call.apply(request);
        }

        void publish(Notification n) {
            for (var l : listeners.getOrDefault(n.getClass(), List.of())) {
                try { l.accept(n); }
                catch (RuntimeException e) { failures.add(n.getClass().getSimpleName() + ": " + e.getMessage()); }   // (4)!
            }
        }
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        List<String> log = new ArrayList<>();
        Mediator[] holder = new Mediator[1];
        Mediator mediator = new Mediator()
                .behaviour((q, next) -> {
                    String name = q.getClass().getSimpleName();
                    log.add("start " + name);
                    try { Object r = next.apply(q); log.add("end " + name); return r; }
                    catch (RuntimeException e) { log.add("failed " + name); throw e; }
                })
                .behaviour((q, next) -> {
                    if (q instanceof PlaceOrder p && p.skus().isEmpty()) throw new IllegalArgumentException("empty order");
                    return next.apply(q);
                })
                .handle(PlaceOrder.class, q -> {
                    String id = "FC-9701";
                    holder[0].publish(new OrderPlaced(id, q.customer()));                            // (5)!
                    return id;
                })
                .handle(GetOrderStatus.class, q -> q.orderId() + " is being packed")
                .on(OrderPlaced.class, n -> log.add("sms to " + n.customer()))
                .on(OrderPlaced.class, n -> { throw new IllegalStateException("loyalty service down"); })
                .on(OrderPlaced.class, n -> log.add("reserve stock for " + n.orderId()))
                .validate(List.of(PlaceOrder.class, GetOrderStatus.class));
        holder[0] = mediator;

        String id = mediator.send(new PlaceOrder("asha", List.of("MILK-1L")));
        System.out.println("placed " + id + "; " + mediator.send(new GetOrderStatus(id)));
        try { mediator.send(new PlaceOrder("ravi", List.of())); } catch (IllegalArgumentException e) { System.out.println("validation behaviour: " + e.getMessage()); }
        System.out.println("log: " + log);
        System.out.println("notification failures: " + mediator.failures);

        try { new Mediator().validate(List.of(PlaceOrder.class)); } catch (IllegalStateException e) { System.out.println("startup: " + e.getMessage()); }
        try { new Mediator().handle(GetOrderStatus.class, q -> "a").handle(GetOrderStatus.class, q -> "b"); } catch (IllegalStateException e) { System.out.println("startup: " + e.getMessage()); }
    }
}
  1. Exactly one handler per request type; a second registration is a startup error.
  2. Startup validation finds request types without handlers before traffic arrives.
  3. Behaviours wrap the handler like a filter chain, in registration order.
  4. Listener failures are collected (and in production, logged and alerted), not thrown at the publisher.
  5. Handlers publish notifications through the mediator; they don't call listeners directly.

Run it: java InProcessMediatorDemo.java

Output:

placed FC-9701; FC-9701 is being packed
validation behaviour: empty order
log: [start PlaceOrder, sms to asha, reserve stock for FC-9701, end PlaceOrder, start GetOrderStatus, end GetOrderStatus, start PlaceOrder, failed PlaceOrder]
notification failures: [OrderPlaced: loyalty service down]
startup: no handler for [PlaceOrder]
startup: two handlers for GetOrderStatus

What to notice:

  • The loyalty listener failed, but the SMS and stock listeners still ran and the order was placed.
  • The empty order was rejected by the validation behaviour before reaching the handler, and the logging behaviour recorded the failure.
  • Configuration mistakes (missing or duplicate handlers) surfaced at startup.

docs.title: 7. Pros, Cons & Trade-offs
docs.text: Aspect Pros Cons Coupling Colleagues don't know each other Everything depends on the mediator Readability Rules in one place Flow hidden behind indirection Change Rule changes in one class God mediator risk Reuse Colleagues reusable elsewhere Mediators rarely reusable Testability Rules testable with fake colleagues Mediator tests need many colleagues Extensibility New colleagues via the mediator Mediator grows with each colleague

docs.title: 8. When to Use / When NOT to Use
docs.text:
Use it when:

  • several objects have interaction rules that involve more than two of them;
  • the web of direct references between objects is growing;
  • you want the coordination logic visible and testable in one place.

Don't use it when:

  • two objects interact simply (call directly);
  • reactions are independent (use Observer/events);
  • the mediator would coordinate unrelated workflows (split first).

docs.title: 9. Best Practices
docs.text:
1. One mediator per workflow or screen. (Consensus.)
  2. Narrow interfaces for colleagues to report through. (Consensus.)
  3. Keep business rules in the mediator, not in an event bus. (Opinion, widely shared.)
  4. Isolate listener failures and report them. (Consensus.)
  5. Validate handler registration at startup. (Consensus.)
  6. Guard against re-entrant update loops. (Consensus.)

docs.title: 10. Pitfalls & Anti-Patterns
docs.text:
Re-entrant update loop (production failure mode)

Symptom: the checkout screen froze on some phones when customers changed their address. Root cause: the mediator cleared the slot picker, which reported "changed" back to the mediator, which reloaded slots, which cleared the picker again, recursively. Fix: mediator updates set colleague state directly without triggering reports (or a re-entry flag); a test that changing the address triggers exactly one slot reload.

God mediator

Symptom: a 3,000-line OrderCoordinator with merge conflicts every sprint. Root cause: every new workflow added a case to the same mediator. Fix: split by workflow; colleagues stay shared.

Event spaghetti

Symptom: nobody can explain what happens after OrderPlaced; a change broke refunds two modules away. Root cause: dozens of listeners triggering further events, with rules spread across them. Fix: put multi-step rules in an explicit mediator or saga; document events and their consumers.

Synchronous listener slows publishers

Symptom: placing an order took 3 seconds during an analytics outage. Root cause: a synchronous @EventListener called a slow external service. Fix: @Async or an outbox for slow work; timeouts on external calls.

docs.title: 11. Configuration & Tuning
docs.text: Setting Default What it does When to change it Risk of changing Spring event listeners synchronous Listeners run in the publisher's thread Slow listeners: @Async Lost events on crash; ordering changes @TransactionalEventListener(phase) AFTER_COMMIT Runs listener after the transaction Side effects that must not run on rollback Listener failures don't roll back the transaction @Order on listeners unordered Listener order When order matters (rarely should) Hidden coupling between listeners Async executor size SimpleAsyncTaskExecutor (unbounded threads) in plain Spring Threads for async listeners Always configure a bounded executor Unbounded threads under load

docs.title: 12. Security Considerations
docs.text:
• A mediator that routes requests must still enforce authorisation per request type (a behaviour is a good place).
  • Event payloads may be logged or sent to many listeners: keep personal data minimal (IDs, not addresses).
  • Don't let external input choose which handler runs by class name.

docs.title: 13. Performance & Scalability
docs.text: A mediator adds an indirection per interaction, which is negligible. The real costs come from what it coordinates: synchronous listeners add their latency to the publisher; a single mediator instance can become a contention point if it holds locks. For high throughput, keep mediators stateless or partition their state (one dispatcher per store), and move slow reactions to asynchronous processing.

docs.title: 14. Testing It
docs.text:
Test routing, behaviour order, listener isolation and startup validation:

InProcessMediatorTest.java
import static org.junit.jupiter.api.Assertions.assertEquals;
import static org.junit.jupiter.api.Assertions.assertThrows;

import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;

class InProcessMediatorTest {

    @Test
    void requestGoesToItsSingleHandler() {
        var m = new InProcessMediatorDemo.Mediator().handle(InProcessMediatorDemo.GetOrderStatus.class, q -> "status of " + q.orderId());
        assertEquals("status of FC-1", m.send(new InProcessMediatorDemo.GetOrderStatus("FC-1")));
    }

    @Test
    void behavioursWrapInRegistrationOrder() {
        List<String> log = new ArrayList<>();
        var m = new InProcessMediatorDemo.Mediator()
                .behaviour((q, next) -> { log.add("outer"); return next.apply(q); })
                .behaviour((q, next) -> { log.add("inner"); return next.apply(q); })
                .handle(InProcessMediatorDemo.GetOrderStatus.class, q -> { log.add("handler"); return "x"; });
        m.send(new InProcessMediatorDemo.GetOrderStatus("FC-1"));
        assertEquals(List.of("outer", "inner", "handler"), log);
    }

    @Test
    void oneFailingListenerDoesNotStopOthers() {
        List<String> got = new ArrayList<>();
        var m = new InProcessMediatorDemo.Mediator()
                .on(InProcessMediatorDemo.OrderPlaced.class, n -> { throw new IllegalStateException("down"); })
                .on(InProcessMediatorDemo.OrderPlaced.class, n -> got.add(n.orderId()));
        m.publish(new InProcessMediatorDemo.OrderPlaced("FC-1", "asha"));
        assertEquals(List.of("FC-1"), got);
        assertEquals(1, m.failures.size());
    }

    @Test
    void startupValidationFindsMissingHandlers() {
        assertThrows(IllegalStateException.class,
                () -> new InProcessMediatorDemo.Mediator().validate(List.of(InProcessMediatorDemo.PlaceOrder.class)));
    }
}

docs.title: 15. Observability & Operations
docs.text: Log each request type with timing via a behaviour (one place for all handlers). Count notification-listener failures by listener and alert on them. Spring Boot's ApplicationStartup and listener logging help identify slow listeners. Keep a generated list of event types and their listeners in documentation.

docs.title: 16. Version Notes
docs.text: Version Change relevant to Mediator Java 1.1 Event model in AWT; controllers mediating components Spring 4.2 @EventListener and @TransactionalEventListener Java 8 Lambdas: concise listeners and handlers Java 17/21 Sealed request/notification types; pattern-matching dispatch Spring Modulith 1.x Application events between modules with an event publication registry

docs.title: 17. Expert Deep Dive
docs.text:
• Mediator at architecture scale. An orchestrator in a saga is a mediator across services; choreography (events only) is the observer style. Orchestration makes flows visible; choreography reduces coupling. See Distributed Data Patterns.
  • CQRS buses. Command buses (one handler) and event buses (many handlers) are mediators; pipeline behaviours give cross-cutting concerns without AOP.
  • Modular monoliths. Spring Modulith uses application events as mediators between modules, with a publication registry that retries listeners after failures, so in-process events become reliable.
  • When the mediator should be a state machine. If the mediator's rules depend on "where we are in the process", model that explicitly with State.

War story: the coordinator nobody owned

A grocery company's "OrderCoordinator" started as a small mediator between checkout, payments and inventory. Over three years it gained dispatch, refunds, loyalty, promotions and analytics, about 4,000 lines and 22 injected services. A promotions change broke refunds on a holiday weekend because both shared a private helper in the coordinator. Fixes: the team split it into workflow mediators (checkout, dispatch, after-sales, merchandising) with module boundaries checked in CI, and cross-workflow reactions moved to documented events. Merge conflicts dropped, and each mediator got one owning team. Lesson: a mediator should coordinate one workflow; when it starts coordinating the company, split it.

docs.title: 18. Interview Corner
19. Practice
docs.text:
• Add a "delivery tip" widget to MediatorColleaguesDemo that is hidden for pickup orders. ??? tip "Hint" Add a delivery-mode colleague; the rule lives in the mediator.
  • Give DispatchMediatorDemo a rule: bulky orders only go to riders with vans. ??? tip "Hint" Keep free riders by vehicle type; match by order size.
  • Add an authorisation behaviour to InProcessMediatorDemo that rejects PlaceOrder for blocked customers. ??? tip "Hint" Check q instanceof PlaceOrder p and a blocked set.
  • Find a "manager" or "coordinator" class with more than 10 dependencies and sketch how to split it. ??? tip "Hint" Group its methods by workflow; each group becomes a mediator.

docs.title: 20. Quick Revision Card
docs.text:
Remember in 30 seconds

  • Intent: centralise how objects interact; colleagues talk to the mediator, not each other.
  • n² links become n; rules live in one place.
  • Event bus = generic mediator; Observer = broadcast without coordination logic.
  • Split mediators by workflow; guard against update loops; isolate listener failures.
  • Production: one handler per request, behaviours around requests, startup validation.
interface CheckoutMediator { void changed(Object widget); }
class AddressField { void enter(String pin) { this.pin = pin; mediator.changed(this); } }

docs.title: Memento
docs.text:
L2 🔵 Practitioner · ⏱ 30 min read · Prerequisites: Prototype, Command

TL;DR

Memento captures an object's state as a snapshot, without exposing its internals, so the object can be restored later: undo, "discard changes", checkpoints before risky operations, and drafts saved for later. The object (originator) creates and restores its own snapshots; another object (caretaker) stores them without looking inside. In Java, a deeply immutable record is a natural memento. Watch the memory cost: big state with small changes may be better served by storing changes (Command) instead of full copies.

docs.title: 1. What It Is
docs.text:
Plain English. A FreshCart customer taps "Add all recipe ingredients" and six items land in the cart. They change their mind. The app saved a checkpoint of the cart just before the bulk add, so one tap restores exactly the earlier cart, including the delivery fee it had. That checkpoint is a memento.

Definition (GoF). "Without violating encapsulation, capture and externalize an object's internal state so that the object can be restored to this state later." Parts:

  • Originator: the object whose state is saved (Cart); it creates mementos and restores from them.
  • Memento: the snapshot; opaque to everyone except the originator.
  • Caretaker: keeps mementos (a history stack, a draft store) but never reads or changes their contents.

docs.title: 2. Why It Exists
docs.text: To undo or roll back, someone needs the old state. If outside code copies an object's fields through getters, encapsulation breaks: every caller must know every field, copies are easily shallow (sharing mutable lists), and adding a field silently breaks restoring. Memento puts the knowledge of "what makes up my state" inside the object itself, and gives everyone else an opaque token they can store and hand back.

docs.title: 3. Mental Model / Analogy
docs.text:
Analogy. A game's save point. The game decides what goes into a save file; you only see "Save slot 3, Tuesday 10:42" and can load it. You don't edit the save file, and a new game version knows how to read old saves.

Technical model. originator.save() returns an immutable value capturing the state; originator.restore(memento) replaces the current state with it. The caretaker holds mementos in some structure (stack, map, database) and decides when to discard them.

docs.title: 4. How It Works
docs.text:
classDiagram
    class Cart {
        -lines Map~String, Integer~
        -coupon String
        +save() Memento
        +restore(Memento)
    }
    class Memento {
        -lines Map~String, Integer~
        -coupon String
    }
    class History {
        -stack Deque~Memento~
        +push(Memento)
        +pop() Memento
    }
    Cart ..> Memento : creates and reads
    History o-- Memento : stores, never reads
sequenceDiagram
    participant U as UI (caretaker)
    participant C as Cart (originator)
    U->>C: save()
    C-->>U: memento
    U->>U: push to history
    U->>C: add items, apply coupon
    U->>C: restore(history.pop())
    C->>C: replace lines and coupon

docs.title: Originator, memento and caretaker
docs.text:
Description. The originator knows its own fields and is the only class that creates or reads mementos. In Java, a private nested class (or a record with package-private access) keeps the memento's contents hidden from caretakers. The caretaker just stores and returns mementos.

Advantages / features. Encapsulation stays intact; adding a field means updating save/restore in one class; caretakers are generic.

Before (caller copies internals) and after (originator-made mementos):

OriginatorMementoCaretakerDemo.java
import java.util.ArrayDeque;
import java.util.Collections;
import java.util.Deque;
import java.util.LinkedHashMap;
import java.util.Map;

/** Memento: capture an object's state without exposing its internals, so it can be restored later. */
public class OriginatorMementoCaretakerDemo {

    // ===================== Before: the caller copies internals through getters =====================
    static final class CartBefore {
        Map<String, Integer> lines = new LinkedHashMap<>(); String coupon;                      // (1)!
    }

    // ===================== After: the cart makes and restores its own mementos =====================
    static final class Cart {                                                                     // originator
        private final Map<String, Integer> lines = new LinkedHashMap<>();
        private String coupon;

        void add(String sku, int qty) { lines.merge(sku, qty, Integer::sum); }
        void applyCoupon(String c) { coupon = c; }

        static final class Memento {                                                               // (2)!
            private final Map<String, Integer> lines; private final String coupon;
            private Memento(Map<String, Integer> lines, String coupon) { this.lines = Collections.unmodifiableMap(new LinkedHashMap<>(lines)); this.coupon = coupon; }
        }
        Memento save() { return new Memento(lines, coupon); }                                      // (3)!
        void restore(Memento m) { lines.clear(); lines.putAll(m.lines); coupon = m.coupon; }
        public String toString() { return lines + (coupon == null ? "" : " coupon=" + coupon); }
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        CartBefore b = new CartBefore(); b.lines.put("MILK", 1);
        Map<String, Integer> copy = b.lines;                                                       // "saved" - but it's the same map
        b.lines.put("BREAD", 1);
        System.out.println("before: the 'saved' copy changed too: " + copy);

        Cart cart = new Cart();
        Deque<Cart.Memento> history = new ArrayDeque<>();                                           // (4)!
        cart.add("MILK", 2); cart.add("BREAD", 1);
        history.push(cart.save());
        cart.add("CAKE", 1); cart.applyCoupon("BDAY20");
        System.out.println("after edits: " + cart);
        cart.restore(history.pop());
        System.out.println("restored:    " + cart);
    }
}
  1. Before: public mutable fields; the "saved copy" is the same map, so it changes with the cart.
  2. A nested memento with a private constructor and private fields: only Cart can create or read it.
  3. The cart copies its own state into the memento, so the snapshot is independent.
  4. The caretaker (a history stack) stores mementos without knowing what's inside.

Run it: java OriginatorMementoCaretakerDemo.java

before: the 'saved' copy changed too: {MILK=1, BREAD=1}
after edits: {MILK=2, BREAD=1, CAKE=1} coupon=BDAY20
restored:    {MILK=2, BREAD=1}
Pros Cons Encapsulation preserved Full copies cost memory and time Restore logic lives with the state Caretaker can't inspect or diff mementos Works for any kind of change Restoring external side effects isn't possible

Use it for undo, cancel/discard, checkpoints and drafts. Avoid it for state that can't be captured (open connections, sent emails). Real-world Java: javax.swing.text undoable edits store state needed to revert; IDE "local history"; serialisation-based checkpoints. Best practice: include derived state (totals, fees) or recompute it on restore, consistently. Gotcha: a memento that holds references to mutable objects isn't a snapshot; always copy.

docs.title: Immutable snapshots with records
docs.text:
Description. A Java record is a concise, immutable carrier, which makes it a natural memento, but records are only shallowly immutable. A record holding a List keeps a reference to that list; if the originator later changes the list, the "snapshot" changes too. Copy collections in the compact constructor (List.copyOf, Map.copyOf).

Advantages / features. Short to write, equals for comparing snapshots, safe to share between threads once deeply immutable.

RecordSnapshotDemo.java
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;

/** Records make good mementos, but only if they are DEEPLY immutable: copy mutable collections in the constructor. */
public class RecordSnapshotDemo {

    record ShallowSnapshot(String title, List<String> items) { }                                // (1)!

    record Snapshot(String title, List<String> items) {
        Snapshot { items = List.copyOf(items); }                                                    // (2)!
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        List<String> banner = new ArrayList<>(List.of("Mango 20% off"));
        ShallowSnapshot shallow = new ShallowSnapshot("Summer sale", banner);
        Snapshot deep = new Snapshot("Summer sale", banner);

        banner.add("Free delivery");                                                                // the editor keeps changing its list
        System.out.println("shallow snapshot changed by later edits: " + shallow.items());
        System.out.println("deep snapshot stayed as saved:          " + deep.items());
        try { deep.items().add("hack"); } catch (UnsupportedOperationException e) { System.out.println("and nobody can modify it: UnsupportedOperationException"); }   // (3)!
    }
}
  1. A record holding the caller's list: later edits leak into the snapshot.
  2. The compact constructor copies the list into an unmodifiable one.
  3. The copied list can't be modified by anyone, so the snapshot stays true.

Run it: java RecordSnapshotDemo.java

shallow snapshot changed by later edits: [Mango 20% off, Free delivery]
deep snapshot stayed as saved:          [Mango 20% off]
and nobody can modify it: UnsupportedOperationException
Copy method Immutable Keeps order Allows nulls List.copyOf Yes Yes No Map.copyOf Yes No (unspecified order) No Collections.unmodifiableMap(new LinkedHashMap<>(m)) Yes (wrapper over a private copy) Yes Yes new ArrayList<>(list) No Yes Yes

Use records with defensive copies for mementos. Avoid Map.copyOf when order matters (cart lines, form steps); its iteration order is unspecified and can differ between runs. Real-world Java: immutable value objects in domain models; event payloads. Best practice: copy nested mutable objects too (or make them records). Gotcha: List.copyOf throws on null elements; decide whether nulls are valid before choosing it.

docs.title: Undo history
docs.text:
Description. A caretaker that keeps snapshots in two stacks gives undo and redo: before each change push the current snapshot to undo; undo moves current to redo and pops undo; a new change clears redo. A size limit drops the oldest snapshots so memory stays bounded.

Advantages / features. Simple, general undo for any editor-like feature, with predictable memory.

UndoHistoryDemo.java
import java.util.ArrayDeque;
import java.util.Deque;

/** A caretaker with bounded undo/redo history of snapshots for a promo banner editor. */
public class UndoHistoryDemo {

    record Banner(String headline, String colour, int discount) { }                               // (1)!

    static final class History {
        private final Deque<Banner> undo = new ArrayDeque<>(), redo = new ArrayDeque<>();
        private final int limit;
        History(int limit) { this.limit = limit; }

        void saved(Banner before) {
            undo.push(before);
            if (undo.size() > limit) undo.removeLast();                                              // (2)!
            redo.clear();                                                                           // (3)!
        }
        Banner undo(Banner current) { if (undo.isEmpty()) return current; redo.push(current); return undo.pop(); }
        Banner redo(Banner current) { if (redo.isEmpty()) return current; undo.push(current); return redo.pop(); }   // (4)!
        int undoDepth() { return undo.size(); }
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        History h = new History(3);
        Banner b = new Banner("Mango mania", "yellow", 10);
        for (Banner next : new Banner[] {new Banner("Mango mania", "orange", 10), new Banner("Mango mania", "orange", 15),
                new Banner("Mango madness", "orange", 15), new Banner("Mango madness", "red", 20)}) {
            h.saved(b); b = next;
        }
        System.out.println("current: " + b + ", undo depth " + h.undoDepth() + " (limit 3, oldest dropped)");
        b = h.undo(b); b = h.undo(b);
        System.out.println("undo x2: " + b);
        b = h.redo(b);
        System.out.println("redo:    " + b);
        b = h.undo(h.undo(h.undo(b)));
        System.out.println("undo as far as possible: " + b + " (the original yellow banner was dropped)");
    }
}
  1. The whole banner is a small immutable record, so a snapshot is cheap.
  2. The history keeps at most limit snapshots; the oldest is dropped.
  3. A new edit clears redo; redoing old edits after a new one would be confusing.
  4. Redo pushes the current state back onto undo.

Run it: java UndoHistoryDemo.java

current: Banner[headline=Mango madness, colour=red, discount=20], undo depth 3 (limit 3, oldest dropped)
undo x2: Banner[headline=Mango mania, colour=orange, discount=15]
redo:    Banner[headline=Mango madness, colour=orange, discount=15]
undo as far as possible: Banner[headline=Mango mania, colour=orange, discount=10] (the original yellow banner was dropped)
Undo approach Stores Best for Memento snapshots Whole state per step Small state, complex changes Command inverses Change per step Large state, simple reversible changes Event sourcing All events forever Audit, time travel, rebuilds

Use snapshots when state is small and changes are varied. Avoid unlimited histories; users rarely undo more than a few dozen steps. Real-world Java: form editors, admin consoles, drawing tools; see Command for inverse-operation undo. Best practice: coalesce rapid edits (typing) into one undo step. Gotcha: if snapshots are taken after the change instead of before, undo jumps two steps.

docs.title: Memory cost of snapshots
docs.text:
Description. A full snapshot copies all state each time. With large state and small edits, that's mostly duplicate data. Alternatives: store deltas (the change and its inverse, i.e. commands), or use persistent data structures that share unchanged parts between versions.

Advantages / features (of measuring). You choose the right undo strategy before memory becomes a problem.

SnapshotMemoryDemo.java
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.HashMap;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Map;

/** Full snapshots copy everything every time. For big state with small edits, store changes (or share unchanged parts). */
public class SnapshotMemoryDemo {

    record PriceChange(String sku, long oldPaise, long newPaise) { }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Map<String, Long> prices = new HashMap<>();
        for (int i = 0; i < 10_000; i++) prices.put("SKU-" + i, 10_000L + i);

        long copiedEntries = 0;
        List<Map<String, Long>> fullSnapshots = new ArrayList<>();                                  // (1)!
        List<PriceChange> deltas = new ArrayList<>();                                               // (2)!
        for (int edit = 0; edit < 50; edit++) {
            fullSnapshots.add(Map.copyOf(prices)); copiedEntries += prices.size();
            String sku = "SKU-" + edit * 7;
            long old = prices.get(sku), now = old * 90 / 100;
            deltas.add(new PriceChange(sku, old, now));
            prices.put(sku, now);
        }
        System.out.println("50 edits, full snapshots: " + copiedEntries + " entries copied");
        System.out.println("50 edits, deltas:         " + deltas.size() + " small records");

        for (int i = deltas.size() - 1; i >= 0; i--) prices.put(deltas.get(i).sku(), deltas.get(i).oldPaise());   // (3)!
        System.out.println("undo all via deltas equals first snapshot: " + prices.equals(fullSnapshots.get(0)));
    }
}
  1. Full snapshots: 50 edits on 10,000 prices copy 500,000 entries.
  2. Deltas: 50 tiny records with old and new values.
  3. Applying deltas in reverse reproduces the first snapshot exactly.

Run it: java SnapshotMemoryDemo.java

50 edits, full snapshots: 500000 entries copied
50 edits, deltas:         50 small records
undo all via deltas equals first snapshot: true
Strategy Memory per step Restore cost Complexity Full snapshot O(state) O(state) Low Delta / inverse command O(change) O(steps undone) Medium: each change needs an inverse Persistent structure (structural sharing) O(change × log n) O(1) to switch versions Needs a library (e.g. Vavr, PCollections)

Use full snapshots for small state (forms, banners, carts). Avoid them for large catalogues or documents; use deltas or structural sharing. Real-world Java: Git stores snapshots with structural sharing; databases use write-ahead logs (deltas). Best practice: estimate state size × history depth before choosing. Gotcha: deltas must be applied in exact reverse order; skipping or reordering corrupts state.

docs.title: Example 1: Minimal (L2)
docs.text:
Scenario: a support agent's reply box saves a draft; an accidental "select all, delete" can be undone.

ReplyDraftDemo.java
/** Minimal Memento: a support agent's reply box can save a draft and restore it after a mistaken edit. */
public class ReplyDraftDemo {

    static final class ReplyBox {
        private String text = ""; private int cursor;
        record Draft(String text, int cursor) { }                                                   // (1)!
        void type(String s) { text = text.substring(0, cursor) + s + text.substring(cursor); cursor += s.length(); }
        void selectAllAndDelete() { text = ""; cursor = 0; }
        Draft save() { return new Draft(text, cursor); }
        void restore(Draft d) { text = d.text(); cursor = d.cursor(); }                              // (2)!
        public String toString() { return "'" + text + "' (cursor " + cursor + ")"; }
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        ReplyBox box = new ReplyBox();
        box.type("Sorry about the late delivery. ");
        ReplyBox.Draft draft = box.save();
        box.selectAllAndDelete();
        System.out.println("after accident: " + box);
        box.restore(draft);
        box.type("We've refunded the delivery fee.");
        System.out.println("restored:       " + box);
    }
}
  1. The draft is a record: text and cursor position together.
  2. Restoring puts both back, so typing continues where it was.

Run it: java ReplyDraftDemo.java

Output:

after accident: '' (cursor 0)
restored:       'Sorry about the late delivery. We've refunded the delivery fee.' (cursor 63)

What to notice:

  • The cursor position was part of the state; restoring only the text would put the cursor in the wrong place.

docs.title: Example 2: Realistic (in FreshCart grocery delivery)
docs.text:
Scenario: "Add recipe ingredients" adds several items at once, which also changes the delivery fee (free above five lines). Customers need a single "Undo" for the whole bulk add.

CartCheckpointDemo.java
import java.util.Collections;
import java.util.LinkedHashMap;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Map;

/** Realistic Memento: checkpoint the cart before "Add recipe ingredients", so one tap can undo the whole bulk change. */
public class CartCheckpointDemo {

    static final class Cart {
        private final Map<String, Integer> lines = new LinkedHashMap<>();
        private long deliveryFeePaise = 2_500;

        void add(String sku, int qty) { lines.merge(sku, qty, Integer::sum); recalcFee(); }
        private void recalcFee() { deliveryFeePaise = lines.size() >= 5 ? 0 : 2_500; }               // derived state also restored

        record Checkpoint(Map<String, Integer> lines, long fee) { }                                 // (1)!
        Checkpoint checkpoint() { return new Checkpoint(Collections.unmodifiableMap(new LinkedHashMap<>(lines)), deliveryFeePaise); }
        void rollback(Checkpoint c) { lines.clear(); lines.putAll(c.lines()); deliveryFeePaise = c.fee(); }   // (2)!
        public String toString() { return lines + " fee Rs " + deliveryFeePaise / 100; }
    }

    static void addRecipe(Cart cart, List<String> ingredients) { ingredients.forEach(i -> cart.add(i, 1)); }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Cart cart = new Cart();
        cart.add("MILK-1L", 2);
        cart.add("PANEER-200G", 1);
        System.out.println("cart:         " + cart);

        Cart.Checkpoint before = cart.checkpoint();                                                  // (3)!
        addRecipe(cart, List.of("TOMATO-1KG", "ONION-1KG", "PANEER-200G", "BUTTER-100G", "CREAM-200ML"));
        System.out.println("after recipe: " + cart);
        cart.rollback(before);
        System.out.println("undo recipe:  " + cart);
    }
}
  1. The checkpoint includes derived state (the fee), with an ordered, unmodifiable copy of the lines.
  2. Rollback restores every part of the state at once.
  3. The checkpoint is taken before the bulk change, not after.

Run it: java CartCheckpointDemo.java

Output:

cart:         {MILK-1L=2, PANEER-200G=1} fee Rs 25
after recipe: {MILK-1L=2, PANEER-200G=2, TOMATO-1KG=1, ONION-1KG=1, BUTTER-100G=1, CREAM-200ML=1} fee Rs 0
undo recipe:  {MILK-1L=2, PANEER-200G=1} fee Rs 25

What to notice:

  • Paneer was already in the cart; undo restored its quantity to 1 rather than removing it, which "remove the recipe items" logic would get wrong.
  • The delivery fee came back too.

docs.title: Example 3: Production-grade
docs.text:
Scenario: a new store's onboarding form has five steps and is often finished on another device days later. Drafts are persisted mementos. Requirements: a schema version with migration from older drafts; corruption detection; a size limit; expiry after 30 days; restore goes through the form, which validates the snapshot.

FormDraftStoreDemo.java
import java.nio.charset.StandardCharsets;
import java.time.Duration;
import java.time.Instant;
import java.util.HashMap;
import java.util.LinkedHashMap;
import java.util.Map;
import java.util.zip.CRC32;

/**
 * Production-grade persisted mementos: a new store's onboarding form (many steps) is saved as a draft so the manager can
 * resume on another device. The memento is serialised with:
 * - a schema VERSION, and a migration from older versions on restore
 * - a checksum to detect corruption, a size limit, and an expiry (drafts older than 30 days are discarded)
 * - only the form's own data; restore goes through the originator, which validates
 */
public class FormDraftStoreDemo {

    static final class OnboardingForm {                                                             // originator
        private final Map<String, String> fields = new LinkedHashMap<>();
        private int step = 1;
        void fill(String field, String value) { fields.put(field, value); }
        void next() { step++; }

        record Snapshot(int step, Map<String, String> fields) { }
        Snapshot snapshot() { return new Snapshot(step, Map.copyOf(fields)); }
        void restore(Snapshot s) {                                                                   // (1)!
            if (s.step() < 1 || s.step() > 5) throw new IllegalArgumentException("invalid step " + s.step());
            fields.clear(); fields.putAll(new java.util.TreeMap<>(s.fields())); step = s.step();
        }
        public String toString() { return "step " + step + " " + new java.util.TreeMap<>(fields); }
    }

    static final class DraftStore {                                                                  // caretaker
        static final int VERSION = 2, MAX_BYTES = 2_048;
        static final Duration TTL = Duration.ofDays(30);
        final Map<String, String> storage = new HashMap<>();                                         // pretend: a database table

        void save(String key, OnboardingForm.Snapshot s, Instant now) {
            StringBuilder body = new StringBuilder("v=" + VERSION + ";saved=" + now + ";step=" + s.step());
            new java.util.TreeMap<>(s.fields()).forEach((k, v) -> body.append(';').append(k).append('=').append(v.replace(";", ",")));
            String payload = body.toString();
            if (payload.getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8).length > MAX_BYTES) throw new IllegalArgumentException("draft too large");   // (2)!
            storage.put(key, crc(payload) + "|" + payload);
        }

        OnboardingForm.Snapshot load(String key, Instant now) {
            String raw = storage.get(key);
            if (raw == null) return null;
            String crc = raw.substring(0, raw.indexOf('|')), payload = raw.substring(raw.indexOf('|') + 1);
            if (!crc.equals(crc(payload))) throw new IllegalStateException("draft " + key + " is corrupted");   // (3)!
            Map<String, String> kv = new LinkedHashMap<>();
            for (String part : payload.split(";")) { int eq = part.indexOf('='); kv.put(part.substring(0, eq), part.substring(eq + 1)); }
            if (Instant.parse(kv.remove("saved")).plus(TTL).isBefore(now)) { storage.remove(key); return null; }   // (4)!
            int version = Integer.parseInt(kv.remove("v"));
            if (version == 1 && kv.containsKey("gst")) kv.put("gstin", kv.remove("gst"));            // (5)!
            int step = Integer.parseInt(kv.remove("step"));
            return new OnboardingForm.Snapshot(step, kv);
        }

        static String crc(String s) { CRC32 c = new CRC32(); c.update(s.getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8)); return Long.toHexString(c.getValue()); }
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Instant now = Instant.parse("2026-11-02T10:00:00Z");
        DraftStore store = new DraftStore();

        OnboardingForm phone = new OnboardingForm();
        phone.fill("storeName", "FreshCart Whitefield"); phone.next(); phone.fill("gstin", "29ABCDE1234F1Z5"); phone.next();
        store.save("store-77", phone.snapshot(), now);

        OnboardingForm laptop = new OnboardingForm();
        laptop.restore(store.load("store-77", now.plus(Duration.ofDays(2))));
        System.out.println("resumed on laptop: " + laptop);

        String v1 = "v=1;saved=" + now + ";step=2;storeName=Old Store;gst=29XYZ";
        store.storage.put("store-12", DraftStore.crc(v1) + "|" + v1);
        System.out.println("migrated v1 draft: " + store.load("store-12", now).fields());

        store.storage.put("store-13", store.storage.get("store-77").replace("Whitefield", "Whitef1eld"));
        try { store.load("store-13", now); } catch (IllegalStateException e) { System.out.println(e.getMessage()); }

        System.out.println("40-day-old draft: " + store.load("store-77", now.plus(Duration.ofDays(40))) + ", still stored: " + store.storage.containsKey("store-77"));
        try { phone.fill("notes", "x".repeat(3_000)); store.save("store-78", phone.snapshot(), now); } catch (IllegalArgumentException e) { System.out.println(e.getMessage()); }
    }
}
  1. The originator validates a snapshot before accepting it; stored data is untrusted input.
  2. A size limit stops a runaway field from filling the store.
  3. A checksum detects corrupted or tampered drafts.
  4. Expired drafts are deleted on read, as the retention policy requires.
  5. Version 1 drafts used the field gst; the loader migrates them to gstin.

Run it: java FormDraftStoreDemo.java

Output:

resumed on laptop: step 3 {gstin=29ABCDE1234F1Z5, storeName=FreshCart Whitefield}
migrated v1 draft: {storeName=Old Store, gstin=29XYZ}
draft store-13 is corrupted
40-day-old draft: null, still stored: false
draft too large

What to notice:

  • The draft saved on the phone resumed on the laptop at step 3 with both fields.
  • An old v1 draft loaded correctly after migration; a one-character corruption was detected.
  • The 40-day-old draft was discarded and removed.

docs.title: 7. Pros, Cons & Trade-offs
docs.text: Aspect Pros Cons Encapsulation Internals stay private Caretaker can't inspect snapshots Simplicity Undo for any change Full copies for every step Correctness Restores exact state, including derived values Shallow copies silently break it Memory Bounded histories are predictable Large state × deep history is expensive Persistence Drafts and checkpoints survive restarts Needs versioning and migration Side effects — Can't undo external effects (emails, payments)

docs.title: 8. When to Use / When NOT to Use
docs.text:
Use it when:

  • users need undo, "discard changes" or checkpoints;
  • you must roll back an object after a failed multi-step operation;
  • work-in-progress must be saved and resumed later (drafts).

Don't use it when:

  • state is huge and changes are small (store deltas instead);
  • the change affected external systems (use compensation);
  • a database transaction already gives you rollback.

docs.title: 9. Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Let the originator create and restore mementos. (Consensus.)
  2. Make mementos deeply immutable (records with copied collections). (Consensus.)
  3. Bound histories and coalesce rapid edits. (Consensus.)
  4. Version persisted mementos and migrate on read. (Consensus.)
  5. Validate on restore: stored snapshots are untrusted input. (Consensus.)
  6. Capture before the change, never after. (Consensus.)

docs.title: 10. Pitfalls & Anti-Patterns
docs.text:
Shallow snapshot (production failure mode)

Symptom: "Undo" on the promo editor did nothing for item lists; the banner kept the newest items. Root cause: the snapshot record held the editor's live List, so later edits changed the "saved" list too. Fix: List.copyOf in the record's compact constructor; a unit test that edits after saving and checks the snapshot.

Unbounded history

Symptom: the admin app's memory grew steadily during long editing sessions until the tab crashed. Root cause: a full catalogue snapshot was pushed on every keystroke, with no limit. Fix: coalesce typing into one step, cap history, store deltas for large state.

Old drafts break after a release

Symptom: after renaming a form field, managers resuming drafts lost their GST numbers. Root cause: persisted drafts had no version and no migration. Fix: schema versions and migration on load, as in Example 3; tests with real old drafts.

Restoring part of the state

Symptom: after undo, the cart showed old items but the new delivery fee. Root cause: the memento didn't include derived state, and restore didn't recompute it. Fix: include it or recompute on restore, consistently.

docs.title: 11. Configuration & Tuning
docs.text: Setting Default What it does When to change it Risk of changing History limit 20–100 steps typical Max undo depth Large state: lower Too low frustrates users Coalescing window ~500 ms–1 s Groups rapid edits into one step Text editing Too long: undo jumps too far Draft TTL 30 days (example) Retention of saved drafts Legal/retention policy Too short loses work; too long keeps personal data Max draft size a few KB Protects storage Large forms Too low rejects real drafts

docs.title: 12. Security Considerations
docs.text:
• Persisted mementos may hold personal data (addresses, tax IDs): encrypt at rest, apply retention limits, and delete them when the user deletes their account.
  • Treat stored mementos as untrusted: validate on restore, check integrity (checksum or signature if clients can modify them).
  • Never deserialise drafts with Java native serialisation (ObjectInputStream) from untrusted sources; use a data format and explicit parsing.

docs.title: 13. Performance & Scalability
docs.text: Snapshot cost is proportional to state size, paid on every save. For small objects it's negligible; for large ones, measure. Persistent collections share structure, so "copying" a large map after one change costs only the changed path. For persisted drafts, write asynchronously and debounce (save at most every few seconds) to avoid hammering the database while users type.

docs.title: 14. Testing It
docs.text:
Test round trips, migration, corruption, expiry and validation on restore:

FormDraftStoreTest.java
import static org.junit.jupiter.api.Assertions.assertEquals;
import static org.junit.jupiter.api.Assertions.assertNull;
import static org.junit.jupiter.api.Assertions.assertThrows;

import java.time.Duration;
import java.time.Instant;
import java.util.Map;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;

class FormDraftStoreTest {

    private final Instant now = Instant.parse("2026-11-02T10:00:00Z");
    private final FormDraftStoreDemo.DraftStore store = new FormDraftStoreDemo.DraftStore();

    @Test
    void roundTripsASnapshot() {
        var snap = new FormDraftStoreDemo.OnboardingForm.Snapshot(3, Map.of("storeName", "A", "gstin", "G"));
        store.save("k", snap, now);
        assertEquals(snap, store.load("k", now));
    }

    @Test
    void migratesVersionOneFieldNames() {
        String v1 = "v=1;saved=" + now + ";step=2;gst=G";
        store.storage.put("k", FormDraftStoreDemo.DraftStore.crc(v1) + "|" + v1);
        assertEquals(Map.of("gstin", "G"), store.load("k", now).fields());
    }

    @Test
    void detectsCorruption() {
        store.save("k", new FormDraftStoreDemo.OnboardingForm.Snapshot(1, Map.of("storeName", "Abc")), now);
        store.storage.put("k", store.storage.get("k").replace("Abc", "Abd"));
        assertThrows(IllegalStateException.class, () -> store.load("k", now));
    }

    @Test
    void expiredDraftsAreDiscarded() {
        store.save("k", new FormDraftStoreDemo.OnboardingForm.Snapshot(1, Map.of()), now);
        assertNull(store.load("k", now.plus(Duration.ofDays(31))));
        assertNull(store.storage.get("k"));
    }

    @Test
    void originatorRejectsInvalidSnapshots() {
        assertThrows(IllegalArgumentException.class,
                () -> new FormDraftStoreDemo.OnboardingForm().restore(new FormDraftStoreDemo.OnboardingForm.Snapshot(9, Map.of())));
    }
}

docs.title: 15. Observability & Operations
docs.text: Track draft saves, restores, migrations by version, corruption and expiry counts. A rise in corruption points at storage or encoding bugs; old versions still being restored tell you when a migration path can be removed. For in-app undo, count undo usage per feature to tune history limits.

docs.title: 16. Version Notes
docs.text: Java Change relevant to Memento 1.1 Serialization (avoid for untrusted data) 9 List.of, Map.of; 10: List.copyOf, Map.copyOf 16 Records: concise immutable snapshots 17 Deserialization filters (JEP 415) if you must use Java serialisation 21 Sequenced collections: ordered copies are easier to reason about

docs.title: 17. Expert Deep Dive
docs.text:
• Memento vs Prototype. Both copy state. Prototype creates a new usable object; a memento is a passive snapshot that only the originator can turn back into state.
  • Event sourcing as "infinite memento". Store every event and rebuild any past state by replay; snapshots (mementos) are then an optimisation to avoid replaying from the beginning.
  • Structural sharing. Persistent data structures (hash array mapped tries, as in Clojure, Scala, Vavr) make "snapshot every step" cheap by sharing unchanged branches. This is how many modern UIs implement undo.
  • Checkpoints in long jobs. Batch jobs (Spring Batch's ExecutionContext) store checkpoints so a failed job can resume from the last committed chunk; that's Memento applied to processes.

War story: the undo that leaked prices

A grocery admin tool let category managers edit a price list and undo changes. Snapshots were records holding the live Map of prices. After an "undo", managers saw correct values on screen (re-rendered from the snapshot), but the shared map had kept the newer prices, which were saved on the next "Publish". For two days, discounts that managers believed they had undone went live. Fixes: snapshots copy the map; "Publish" shows a diff against the live catalogue; and a test edits after saving, undoes, and asserts the published values. Lesson: a memento that shares mutable state isn't a memento.

docs.title: 18. Interview Corner
19. Practice
docs.text:
• Add a coupon to CartCheckpointDemo and make sure undo restores it. ??? tip "Hint" Add it to the Checkpoint record and to rollback.
  • Replace full snapshots in SnapshotMemoryDemo with a persistent map from a library and compare memory. ??? tip "Hint" Vavr's HashMap.put returns a new map sharing structure.
  • Add a v2 → v3 migration to FormDraftStoreDemo that splits storeName into brand and area. ??? tip "Hint" Chain migrations: v1 → v2 → v3 in order.
  • Find a "cancel edits" feature in an app you know and check whether it copies state deeply. ??? tip "Hint" Look for lists or maps stored in the "original" object.

docs.title: 20. Quick Revision Card
docs.text:
Remember in 30 seconds

  • Intent: snapshot an object's state to restore later, keeping internals private.
  • Originator makes and restores; caretaker stores; memento is opaque and immutable.
  • Records + List.copyOf / ordered unmodifiable copies; never share mutable collections.
  • Undo: two stacks, a limit, new change clears redo.
  • Large state: deltas or structural sharing; persisted drafts need versions, checks and TTL.
record Checkpoint(Map<String, Integer> lines, long fee) { }
Checkpoint before = cart.checkpoint();
// ...bulk change...
cart.rollback(before);
