docs.text: Task Command Run a single-file example java StrategyDemo.java Run every example and compare output bash examples/run-all.sh Also run the JUnit tests JUNIT_JAR=/path/junit-platform-console-standalone.jar bash examples/run-all.sh Run a Maven example project mvn -q verify in its folder Serve the playbook locally mkdocs serve

docs.title: Pattern Comparisons
docs.text:
TL;DR

Many patterns look alike in a class diagram and differ only in intent. This page puts the commonly confused ones side by side, with a decision table for each group, so you can name the pattern you need and explain why not the others.

The one question that separates look-alikes: what is the wrapper or the indirection for? Converting an interface, simplifying a subsystem, adding behaviour or controlling access all produce "a class that holds another class".

docs.title: Wrappers: Adapter, Facade, Decorator, Proxy
docs.text: Adapter Facade Decorator Proxy Intent Convert an interface Simplify a subsystem Add behaviour Control access Interface vs wrapped object Different New, simpler Same Same Wraps One object Many objects One object (stackable) One object Who creates the wrapped object Caller Facade Caller Often the proxy (lazy) FreshCart example ParcelGoAdapter CheckoutFacade CachingPriceService Lazy product image, Spring @Transactional If you need to… Choose use a partner SDK through your own interface Adapter give callers one method for a multi-step process Facade add logging, caching or retries without changing the class Decorator delay creation, check permissions, or call remotely Proxy

docs.title: Families of algorithms: Strategy, State, Template Method, Command
docs.text: Strategy State Template Method Command Varies The whole algorithm Behaviour per lifecycle state Steps of a fixed algorithm Which request is executed Chosen by Caller or configuration The object itself, as state changes Subclass Whoever creates the command Mechanism Composition Composition, states know transitions Inheritance Object holding a request Lifetime Usually long-lived Replaced on transitions Fixed per subclass Created per request, can be queued Example Delivery fee rules Order: placed → packed → delivered Report jobs Cart edits with undo If… Choose the rule changes by city or campaign Strategy allowed actions depend on the current status State the process is fixed and only steps vary Template Method (or Strategy if you prefer composition) you need to queue, retry, log or undo requests Command

docs.title: Creation: Factory Method, Abstract Factory, Builder, Prototype, DI
docs.text: Factory Method Abstract Factory Builder Prototype DI Creates One product A family of products One complex product Copies of an existing object Whole object graphs Main problem solved Which class? Which family? Too many parameters Expensive or templated setup Wiring Java idiom Static factory, switch Interface with several create methods Fluent builder, records with compact constructors Copy constructor, with methods Constructor injection If… Choose the concrete class depends on input Factory Method several objects must come from the same vendor or theme Abstract Factory an object has many optional fields or cross-field validation Builder new objects start as variations of a template Prototype objects need collaborators supplied Dependency Injection

docs.title: Notification and coordination: Observer, Mediator, Pub/Sub, Chain of Responsibility
docs.text: Observer Mediator Pub/Sub Chain of Responsibility Topology One subject, many listeners Hub between peers Broker between services Linear pipeline Coupling Listeners know the subject Peers know only the mediator Only the topic and message Handlers know the next handler or the chain Process boundary In-process In-process Across processes In-process Delivery Synchronous by default Synchronous Asynchronous, durable Synchronous, stops when handled

docs.title: Trees and wrappers: Composite vs Decorator, Visitor vs pattern matching
docs.text: Composite Decorator Children Many Exactly one Purpose Treat groups like items Add behaviour Example Bundles of products Caching price service Visitor Pattern-matching switch (Java 21) Adding a new operation New visitor class New method with a switch Adding a new type Change every visitor Compiler flags non-exhaustive switches over sealed types Boilerplate accept methods everywhere None Best for Pre-Java 21 code, double dispatch in libraries Sealed hierarchies in modern Java (Patterns in Modern Java)

docs.title: Singletons: classic Singleton vs DI-managed singleton
docs.text: Classic Singleton DI container singleton Access Global static Injected Testability Hard to replace Easy (constructor parameter) Lifecycle Class loading Container start and stop Use for JDK-level registries, enums Application services

docs.title: Resilience: Timeout, Retry, Circuit Breaker, Bulkhead, Rate Limiter, Fallback
docs.text:
Pattern Protects against Without it Timeout Slow dependencies Threads wait forever Retry Transient failures Users see errors that a second try would fix Circuit breaker Persistent failures Every call waits for a dead dependency Bulkhead One dependency using all threads One slow partner takes down everything Rate limiter Exceeding a quota The partner throttles or bans you Fallback Total failure No answer at all

Order them as fallback( circuit breaker( retry( timeout( call ) ) ) ), with the bulkhead around the call. See Resilience Patterns.

docs.title: Distributed data: 2PC, Saga, Outbox, CQRS, Event Sourcing
docs.text:
Two-phase commit Saga Transactional outbox CQRS Event sourcing Solves Atomic commit across resources Long business transactions across services Reliable "save and publish" Different read and write models Full history as the source of truth Consistency Strong Eventual, with compensations Eventual Eventual between models Strong per stream Cost Locks, coordinator availability Compensation logic Relay process Two models Event schema evolution, projections Use when Rarely, inside one database cluster Orders spanning payment, stock, delivery Every event from a service with a database Read-heavy screens with complex queries Audit-critical domains

Saga styles: orchestration (a coordinator tells each step what to do; easier to follow) vs choreography (services react to each other's events; fewer central parts, harder to see the whole flow). See Distributed Data Patterns.

docs.title: Caching strategies
docs.text:
Cache-aside Read-through Write-through Write-behind Who loads Application Cache Cache Cache Write path Write DB, then invalidate n/a Write cache and DB together Write cache, DB later Staleness Until invalidated or TTL TTL Low Low in cache, DB lags Risk Stampedes, stale entries Hidden latency Slower writes Data loss on crash

See Caching Patterns.

docs.title: Architecture styles
docs.text:
Layered Hexagonal / clean Modular monolith Microservices Dependency direction Top to bottom Inward, to the domain Between modules through APIs Between services through networks Deployment One unit One unit One unit Many Team scaling Low Low to medium Medium to high High Operational cost Low Low Low High Start here when Simple CRUD Rich domain logic Most new products Many teams with clear boundaries

See Architectural Patterns and Microservice Patterns.

docs.title: Build & Tooling Configuration
docs.text:
TL;DR

The settings that most often decide whether a pattern behaves as intended: compiler flags, Spring Boot switches that change how DI and proxies work, and the defaults of the resilience, caching, pooling and messaging libraries used in this playbook. Each row gives the default, what it does, and when to change it.

Check defaults against your versions

Defaults below are for Java 21, Spring Boot 3.x, Resilience4j 2.x, Caffeine 3.x, HikariCP 5.x and Kafka clients 3.x. Library defaults change between major versions; confirm in the official docs before relying on one.

docs.title: Compiler and build
docs.text: Setting Default What it does When to change it javac --release 21 Compiler's own version Compiles against the exact API of that Java version Always set it, so you don't use newer APIs by accident javac -parameters Off Keeps parameter names in class files On for Spring 6.1+ (needed for name-based binding; Boot's parent POM enables it) javac -Xlint:all -Werror Off All warnings, fail on warnings New projects; ratchet in old ones Maven maven.compiler.release Not set Same as --release Set in every POM Surefire <version> Old default in Maven 3 JUnit 5 needs Surefire 2.22+; this playbook uses 3.5.2 Pin it explicitly junit.jupiter.execution.parallel.enabled false Parallel tests Only when tests share no mutable state Maven Shade ServicesResourceTransformer Not configured Merges META-INF/services files in fat jars Whenever you shade jars that use ServiceLoader

docs.title: Spring Boot switches that affect patterns
docs.text: Property Default What it does When to change it spring.main.allow-bean-definition-overriding false Fails if two beans share a name Keep false; overriding hides wiring mistakes spring.main.allow-circular-references false Fails on circular dependencies Keep false; fix the design (Dependency Injection) spring.main.lazy-initialization false Creates beans on first use Faster dev startup; hides startup errors in production spring.aop.proxy-target-class true Class-based (CGLIB) proxies instead of JDK interface proxies Rarely; see JVM Internals spring.threads.virtual.enabled false Virtual threads for request handling and @Async Blocking I/O-heavy services on Java 21 spring.jpa.open-in-view true (with a startup warning) Keeps the persistence context open during view rendering Set false to avoid lazy-loading queries outside services spring.jpa.properties.hibernate.jdbc.batch_size Not set (no batching) Batches inserts and updates Bulk writes

docs.title: Connection pools and HTTP clients
docs.text:
Setting Default What it does When to change it Hikari maximumPoolSize 10 Max connections Size from database capacity, not thread count Hikari connectionTimeout 30000 ms Wait for a free connection Lower (1–5 s) so overload fails fast Hikari maxLifetime 1800000 ms (30 min) Retire connections Below the database or proxy idle timeout JDK HttpClient connect timeout None Time to establish a connection Always set (for example 2 s) JDK HttpRequest.timeout None Time for the whole response Always set per call Spring RestClient / RestTemplate timeouts From the request factory (often none) Network timeouts Always configure the factory

No timeout is the most common resilience bug

Most Java HTTP clients wait forever by default. Every remote call needs a connect and a response timeout (Resilience Patterns).

docs.title: Resilience4j
docs.text: Setting Default What it does When to change it CircuitBreaker failureRateThreshold 50 (%) Failure rate that opens the circuit Lower for critical dependencies CircuitBreaker slidingWindowSize 100 Calls (or seconds) in the window Smaller for low-traffic services CircuitBreaker minimumNumberOfCalls 100 Calls before the rate is evaluated Lower for low-traffic services, or it never opens CircuitBreaker waitDurationInOpenState 60 s Time before trying half-open Match the dependency's recovery time CircuitBreaker permittedNumberOfCallsInHalfOpenState 10 Trial calls in half-open Fewer for fragile dependencies Retry maxAttempts 3 Total attempts including the first Only for idempotent operations Retry waitDuration 500 ms Fixed wait between attempts Use exponential backoff with jitter instead Bulkhead maxConcurrentCalls 25 Concurrent calls allowed Size per dependency Bulkhead maxWaitDuration 0 Wait for a permit Keep near 0 to fail fast RateLimiter limitForPeriod 50 Permits per refresh period Match the partner's quota RateLimiter limitRefreshPeriod 500 ns Period length Almost always change (for example 1 s) RateLimiter timeoutDuration 5 s Wait for a permit Lower so callers fail fast TimeLimiter timeoutDuration 1 s Timeout for async calls Per dependency SLO

docs.title: Caching (Caffeine)
docs.text: Setting Default What it does When to change it maximumSize / maximumWeight Unbounded Eviction by size Always bound caches expireAfterWrite None Entries expire after a fixed time Data with a known staleness budget expireAfterAccess None Expire idle entries Session-like data refreshAfterWrite None Refresh asynchronously while serving the old value Hot keys that must not stampede (Caching Patterns) recordStats() Off Hit/miss/eviction stats Always in production, exported to metrics executor ForkJoinPool.commonPool() Runs async loads and maintenance A dedicated executor for blocking loaders

docs.title: Messaging (Kafka clients)
docs.text:
Setting Default What it does When to change it Producer acks all (since 3.0) Waits for in-sync replicas Keep all for business events Producer enable.idempotence true (since 3.0) No duplicates from producer retries Keep on Consumer enable.auto.commit true (Spring Kafka sets false) Commits offsets periodically Commit after processing for at-least-once Consumer auto.offset.reset latest Where a new group starts earliest for new projections Consumer max.poll.records 500 Records per poll Lower when processing is slow Consumer max.poll.interval.ms 300000 Max time between polls before rebalancing Raise for slow batches, or process faster Consumer isolation.level read_uncommitted Sees aborted transactional messages read_committed with transactional producers

See Messaging Patterns and Distributed Data Patterns.

docs.title: JVM flags
docs.text: Flag Default What it does When to change it -XX:MaxRAMPercentage 25 Heap as a share of container memory Raise to 60–75 in dedicated containers -XX:+UseG1GC Default collector on server-class machines Balanced GC ZGC (-XX:+UseZGC) for low-pause, large heaps -Xlog:class+load Off Logs class loading Debugging class loaders and singletons -XX:+AutoCreateSharedArchive -XX:SharedArchiveFile=app.jsa Off Class data sharing archive Faster startup -XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError Off Heap dump on OOM Always in production -Djdk.tracePinnedThreads=full Off Reports virtual-thread pinning Debugging virtual threads before Java 24

docs.title: Architecture and API checks
docs.text:
Setting Default What it does When to change it ArchUnit archRule.failOnEmptyShould true Fails rules that match no classes Keep on; catches broken package names ArchUnit freeze.store.default.allowStoreCreation false Allows creating a baseline for frozen rules true once, when introducing a rule to old code japicmp breakBuildOnBinaryIncompatibleModifications false Fails on binary breaks Always for published libraries japicmp breakBuildBasedOnSemanticVersioning false Checks the version bump Libraries using semantic versioning

See Evolutionary Architecture and Designing Frameworks and Libraries.

docs.title: Decision Guide
docs.text:
TL;DR

"Which pattern when?" as decision trees. Start from the problem you have, not the pattern you'd like to use, and always check the first branch: maybe a plain method, a lambda or a record is enough. Each leaf links to the deep dive.

How to use these trees. Answer the questions honestly for the code in front of you today. If two leaves seem to fit, read the Pattern Comparisons for that group. If you're unsure whether a pattern pays for itself, use Choosing Patterns and Trade-offs.

docs.title: Do I need a pattern at all?
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    Q0["Is there real variation or change pressure today?"] -- No --> KISS["Write plain code. YAGNI"]
    Q0 -- Yes --> Q1["Has the same kind of change happened 3 times?"]
    Q1 -- No --> SMALL["Use the smallest tool: a method, a lambda, an enum"]
    Q1 -- Yes --> Q2["Is the change about creating, structuring or behaving?"]
    Q2 -- Creating --> CRE["See: creating objects"]
    Q2 -- Structuring --> STR["See: combining objects"]
    Q2 -- Behaving --> BEH["See: varying behaviour"]

docs.title: Creating objects
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    C0["What is hard about creating it?"] --> C1["Many optional fields or validation across fields"]
    C1 --> BUILDER["Builder, or a record with a compact constructor"]
    C0 --> C2["Which class to create depends on input"]
    C2 --> FM["Factory Method or a static factory"]
    C0 --> C3["A whole family must match, like one partner's client and parser"]
    C3 --> AF["Abstract Factory"]
    C0 --> C4["Setup is expensive, new objects are variations"]
    C4 --> PROTO["Prototype"]
    C0 --> C5["It needs collaborators"]
    C5 --> DI["Dependency Injection"]
    C0 --> C6["Only one may ever exist"]
    C6 --> SING["DI singleton scope, or an enum Singleton"]
    C0 --> C7["Creating it is very slow, like a connection"]
    C7 --> POOL["Object Pool, usually from a library"]

Links: Builder · Factory Method · Abstract Factory · Prototype · Dependency Injection · Singleton · Object Pool

docs.title: Combining objects
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    S0["What do you need from the wrapper or structure?"] --> S1["Use a class whose interface does not fit"]
    S1 --> ADAPT["Adapter"]
    S0 --> S2["One simple entry point to many services"]
    S2 --> FACADE["Facade"]
    S0 --> S3["Add optional, stackable behaviour"]
    S3 --> DECO["Decorator"]
    S0 --> S4["Control access, lazy load, or call remotely"]
    S4 --> PROXY["Proxy"]
    S0 --> S5["Treat items and groups the same way"]
    S5 --> COMP["Composite"]
    S0 --> S6["Two dimensions that vary independently"]
    S6 --> BRIDGE["Bridge"]
    S0 --> S7["Millions of objects share most of their state"]
    S7 --> FLY["Flyweight"]

Links: Adapter · Facade · Decorator · Proxy · Composite · Bridge · Flyweight

docs.title: Varying behaviour
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    B0["What varies?"] --> B1["The whole algorithm, chosen from outside"]
    B1 --> STRAT["Strategy, often a lambda"]
    B0 --> B2["Behaviour depends on the object's current status"]
    B2 --> STATE["State, or a sealed interface plus switch"]
    B0 --> B3["Some steps of a fixed process"]
    B3 --> TM["Template Method"]
    B0 --> B4["Others must react when something happens"]
    B4 --> OBS["Observer, or messaging across services"]
    B0 --> B5["A request must be queued, logged, retried or undone"]
    B5 --> CMD["Command"]
    B0 --> B6["A request passes through several checks"]
    B6 --> COR["Chain of Responsibility"]
    B0 --> B7["New operations over a fixed set of types"]
    B7 --> VIS["Pattern-matching switch, or Visitor before Java 21"]
    B0 --> B8["Business rules must be combined"]
    B8 --> SPEC["Specification"]
    B0 --> B9["Many components talk to each other"]
    B9 --> MED["Mediator"]

Links: Strategy · State · Template Method · Observer · Command · Chain of Responsibility · Visitor · Specification · Mediator

docs.title: Calling another service
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    R0["Calling a remote dependency"] --> R1["Always set a timeout"]
    R1 --> R2{"Are failures sometimes transient?"}
    R2 -- Yes --> R3{"Is the operation idempotent or keyed?"}
    R3 -- Yes --> RETRY["Retry with backoff and jitter"]
    R3 -- No --> KEY["Add an idempotency key first"]
    R2 -- No --> R4["Skip retries"]
    RETRY --> R5{"Can it fail for minutes?"}
    R4 --> R5
    R5 -- Yes --> CB["Circuit breaker"]
    R5 -- No --> R6{"Could it use all your threads?"}
    CB --> R6
    R6 -- Yes --> BULK["Bulkhead"]
    R6 -- No --> R7{"Is there a useful degraded answer?"}
    BULK --> R7
    R7 -- Yes --> FB["Fallback"]
    R7 -- No --> ERR["Fail fast with a clear error"]

Links: Resilience Patterns · API Design Patterns

docs.title: Keeping data consistent across services
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    D0["A change spans more than one service"] --> D1{"Can it live in one service and database?"}
    D1 -- Yes --> TX["Use a local transaction. Rethink the boundary"]
    D1 -- No --> D2{"Must you publish an event after saving?"}
    D2 -- Yes --> OUTBOX["Transactional outbox or CDC"]
    D2 -- No --> D3
    OUTBOX --> D3{"Several steps, each can fail?"}
    D3 -- Yes --> SAGA["Saga with compensations"]
    D3 -- No --> D4
    SAGA --> D4{"Reads need a different shape than writes?"}
    D4 -- Yes --> CQRS["CQRS read model"]
    D4 -- No --> DONE["Keep one model"]
    CQRS --> D5{"Is the full history the business record?"}
    D5 -- Yes --> ES["Event sourcing"]
    D5 -- No --> DONE2["Store current state plus an outbox"]

Every consumer of those events should be an idempotent consumer. Links: Distributed Data Patterns · Messaging Patterns

docs.title: Caching
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    K0["Reads are slow or expensive"] --> K1{"Is some staleness acceptable?"}
    K1 -- No --> NOCACHE["Optimise the query or add a read replica"]
    K1 -- Yes --> K2{"Is it the same process only?"}
    K2 -- Yes --> LOCAL["Local cache like Caffeine with size and TTL"]
    K2 -- No --> SHARED["Shared cache like Redis, cache-aside"]
    LOCAL --> K3{"Hot keys expire under load?"}
    SHARED --> K3
    K3 -- Yes --> REFRESH["Refresh-ahead or single-flight loading"]
    K3 -- No --> K4{"Writes must update the cache?"}
    REFRESH --> K4
    K4 -- Yes --> INVAL["Invalidate on write, or write-through"]
    K4 -- No --> TTL["TTL is enough"]

Links: Caching Patterns

docs.title: Structuring the system
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    A0["How many teams will work on it in a year?"] --> A1["One team"]
    A1 --> A2{"Rich business rules?"}
    A2 -- Yes --> HEX["Hexagonal modules in one deployable"]
    A2 -- No --> LAYER["Simple layered app"]
    A0 --> A3["Several teams"]
    A3 --> A4{"Clear bounded contexts and independent release needs?"}
    A4 -- No --> MODMONO["Modular monolith with enforced boundaries"]
    A4 -- Yes --> A5{"Can you run distributed systems: tracing, on-call, CI per service?"}
    A5 -- No --> MODMONO
    A5 -- Yes --> MICRO["Microservices along bounded contexts"]

Links: Architectural Patterns · DDD Strategic · Microservice Patterns · Evolutionary Architecture

docs.title: Modernising legacy code
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    L0["Legacy system must change"] --> L1{"Do you have tests around the behaviour?"}
    L1 -- No --> CHAR["Add characterisation tests and seams first"]
    L1 -- Yes --> L2
    CHAR --> L2{"Can you route traffic per feature?"}
    L2 -- Yes --> STRANGLER["Strangler fig"]
    L2 -- No --> BBA["Branch by abstraction inside the code"]
    STRANGLER --> L3{"Is the new result risky?"}
    BBA --> L3
    L3 -- Yes --> PARALLEL["Parallel run and compare"]
    L3 -- No --> TOGGLE["Feature toggle rollout"]
    PARALLEL --> TOGGLE

Links: Legacy Modernisation Patterns · Refactoring to Patterns

docs.title: Migration Guide
docs.text:
TL;DR

How to move pattern implementations from older Java and framework styles to modern Java 21 idioms: anonymous classes to lambdas, Visitor to sealed types with pattern matching, hand-written value classes to records, field injection to constructor injection, and older libraries (Hystrix, Guava Cache, java.util.Observable) to their maintained replacements. Each migration lists the safe steps.

General approach. Migrate one pattern at a time, behind tests. Write characterisation tests first if there are none, change the implementation, keep the public API until callers move, then remove the old code. See Refactoring to Patterns and Legacy Modernisation.

docs.title: Java language migrations
docs.text: From To Since Pattern pages Anonymous inner classes for one-method interfaces Lambdas and method references Java 8 Strategy, Command Hand-written immutable classes (fields, constructor, equals, hashCode, toString) Records Java 16 Builder, DDD Tactical Visitor with accept methods Sealed interfaces plus pattern-matching switch Java 21 Visitor instanceof then cast Pattern matching for instanceof Java 16 Patterns in Modern Java Type-code constants with switch statements Enums with behaviour, or sealed types Java 5 / 17 State Double-checked locking singletons Holder idiom or enum Java 5 Singleton java.util.Date / Calendar java.time Java 8 Testing Patterns (injectable Clock) Platform thread pools for blocking I/O Virtual threads Java 21 Concurrency Patterns finalize() Cleaner or try-with-resources Java 9 Object Pool java.util.Observable / Observer (deprecated in 9) Your own listener interface, java.util.concurrent.Flow, or events Java 9 Observer sun.misc.Unsafe field access VarHandle Java 9 JVM Internals

docs.title: Visitor to sealed types and pattern matching
docs.text:
1. Make the element hierarchy sealed with permits for every existing subtype.
  2. For one visitor, write a method with an exhaustive switch over the sealed type that calls the same logic.
  3. Point callers at the new method; run tests.
  4. Repeat per visitor, then delete the accept methods and the visitor interface.
// before: price.accept(new TaxVisitor())
long tax(BasketItem item) {
    return switch (item) {
        case Product p -> p.pricePaise() * 5 / 100;
        case Bundle b -> b.items().stream().mapToLong(this::tax).sum();
    };
}

docs.title: Value classes to records
docs.text:
1. Check that the class is effectively immutable and has no identity-based behaviour.
  2. Replace it with a record; move validation into the compact constructor.
  3. Replace getter calls (getSku()) with accessor calls (sku()), or keep getters temporarily as extra methods.
  4. Watch for frameworks that need no-arg constructors (older JPA); records fit DTOs and value objects, not JPA entities.

docs.title: Framework migrations
docs.text: From To Notes Field injection (@Autowired on fields) Constructor injection Final fields, testable without the container (Dependency Injection) Spring XML configuration Java @Configuration and component scanning Type-checked wiring javax.* packages jakarta.* Required by Spring Boot 3 and Jakarta EE 9+; OpenRewrite automates most of it Netflix Hystrix (maintenance mode since 2018) Resilience4j Map commands to decorators; check different defaults (Resilience Patterns) Guava CacheBuilder Caffeine Near-identical builder API, better hit rates (Caching Patterns) Spring Cloud Netflix Ribbon / Zuul Spring Cloud LoadBalancer / Spring Cloud Gateway Ribbon and Zuul 1 are in maintenance (Microservice Patterns) RestTemplate RestClient (Spring 6.1) or WebClient RestTemplate is in maintenance mode; set timeouts explicitly JUnit 4 JUnit 5 (Jupiter) Vintage engine lets both run during migration (Testing Patterns)

docs.title: Hystrix to Resilience4j
docs.text:
1. List each HystrixCommand with its timeout, thread pool size and fallback.
  2. Create a Resilience4j TimeLimiter, CircuitBreaker and Bulkhead per dependency with equivalent settings; Hystrix used a 10-second rolling window and 50% error threshold by default, so set those explicitly rather than relying on Resilience4j defaults.
  3. Wrap the call with decorators in the order fallback, circuit breaker, retry, time limiter.
  4. Compare metrics in a canary before switching all traffic.

docs.title: Architecture migrations
docs.text: From To Approach Monolith Modular monolith Enforce module boundaries with ArchUnit or JPMS first (Evolutionary Architecture) Modular monolith Microservices Extract one bounded context at a time with a strangler fig (Microservice Patterns) Dual writes Transactional outbox Add the outbox table, write to it in the same transaction, run a relay, then remove direct publishing (Distributed Data Patterns) Shared database Database per service Expand-and-contract, CDC to sync during transition, then cut access In-house API v1 v2 alongside v1 Version, publish a deprecation schedule, track usage, then retire (API Design Patterns)

docs.title: Tools that automate migrations
docs.text: Tool Helps with OpenRewrite recipes Java version upgrades, javax to jakarta, JUnit 4 to 5, Spring Boot upgrades IntelliJ IDEA inspections Anonymous class to lambda, pattern matching, records jdeprscan Finds uses of deprecated JDK APIs jdeps --jdk-internals Finds uses of JDK internal APIs before upgrading ArchUnit Proves the new boundaries hold after the migration

docs.title: Production Checklist
docs.text:
TL;DR

A go-live checklist for a Java service built with the patterns in this playbook. Tick each item or write down why it doesn't apply. It's grouped by concern, and each item links to the page that explains it.

How to use it. Copy this list into the service's launch ticket or design doc. Items marked (must) are blockers for a customer-facing FreshCart service; the rest are strongly recommended.

docs.title: Design and code
docs.text:
• (must) Dependencies are injected through constructors; no service locator or mutable singletons (Dependency Injection).
  • (must) Domain invariants are enforced inside aggregates and value objects, not only in controllers (DDD Tactical).
  • Money uses integer minor units or BigDecimal, never double (Anti-Pattern Catalogue).
  • Each pattern in use has a reason that a reviewer can state; no speculative abstractions (Choosing Patterns).
  • Module or package boundaries are enforced by ArchUnit or JPMS (Evolutionary Architecture).
  • Shared state is immutable or uses concurrent structures; no double-checked locking without volatile (Concurrency Patterns).

docs.title: Remote calls and resilience
docs.text:
• (must) Every remote call has a connect timeout and a response timeout (Resilience Patterns).
  • (must) Retries only for idempotent or keyed operations, with exponential backoff and jitter, at one layer only.
  • Circuit breakers for dependencies that can fail for minutes, with thresholds tuned for real traffic volumes.
  • Bulkheads keep one slow dependency from using all threads or connections.
  • Fallbacks are defined and tested, or the service fails fast with a clear error.
  • Partner quotas are respected with a rate limiter.

docs.title: Data and messaging
docs.text:
• (must) No dual writes: events are published through a transactional outbox or CDC (Distributed Data Patterns).
  • (must) Every message consumer is idempotent (Messaging Patterns).
  • Poison messages go to a dead letter channel after bounded retries, with an alert and a replay procedure.
  • Multi-step business transactions have a saga with compensations, and stuck sagas are detected.
  • Database migrations are backward compatible (expand, migrate, contract).
  • Connection pool sizes are set from database capacity (Build & Tooling Configuration).

docs.title: Caching
docs.text:
• Every cache is bounded by size and has a TTL or explicit invalidation (Caching Patterns).
  • Hot keys are protected from stampedes (single-flight or refresh-ahead).
  • Cache hit rate, evictions and load time are exported as metrics.
  • The service works, slower, when the shared cache is down.

docs.title: APIs
docs.text:
• (must) Write endpoints that can be retried accept an idempotency key (API Design Patterns).
  • Errors use a consistent format (Problem Details) without leaking internals.
  • Lists are paginated with a maximum page size.
  • A versioning and deprecation policy is published; contract tests protect consumers.
  • Mobile screens get aggregated endpoints instead of many chatty calls (UI and Mobile Patterns).

docs.title: Security
docs.text:
• (must) Inputs are validated at the boundary; queries are parameterised.
  • (must) Secrets come from a secret store, never from code or images.
  • Authorisation is checked in the service, not only in the gateway.
  • Deserialization of untrusted data uses allow-lists; no Java native serialization from outside.
  • Dependencies are scanned; an SBOM is published.

docs.title: Observability
docs.text:
• (must) Structured logs with a correlation or trace ID on every line.
  • (must) Metrics for request rate, errors and latency (RED) per endpoint and per dependency.
  • Distributed tracing across service and message boundaries.
  • Circuit breaker state, retry counts, pool usage and queue depths are visible on a dashboard.
  • Alerts are based on SLOs, and each has a runbook link.

docs.title: Testing
docs.text:
• (must) Unit tests for domain rules; integration tests for adapters (database, broker, partners) with real containers where possible (Testing Patterns).
  • Contract tests for APIs and events shared with other teams.
  • Failure tests: dependency timeouts, broker unavailable, duplicate messages.
  • A load test at expected peak plus headroom, with profiles checked (Performance Cost of Patterns).

docs.title: Operations
docs.text:
• Health and readiness endpoints reflect real dependencies without cascading failures.
  • Graceful shutdown: stop accepting work, finish in-flight requests, commit offsets.
  • Feature toggles for risky features, with owners and removal dates (Legacy Modernisation).
  • Rollback is tested; database changes don't block rollback.
  • JVM settings: heap sized for the container, heap dump on OOM (Build & Tooling Configuration).
  • On-call owners, runbooks and an escalation path are documented.

docs.title: Java Version History for Patterns
docs.text:
TL;DR

Java's evolution keeps changing how patterns are written. Generics made factories and iterators type-safe, lambdas turned Strategy and Command into one-liners, records made value objects and builders shorter, sealed types and pattern matching replaced most Visitors, and virtual threads changed concurrency patterns. This page lists, version by version, what changed and why it matters for pattern code.

How to read it. Each row is a feature that changed pattern code, with the pattern it affects. LTS versions are marked. The playbook targets Java 21 (LTS); notes on later versions say when something requires them.

docs.title: Timeline
docs.text: Version (year) Feature What it changed for patterns 1.0 (1996) java.util.Observable, Enumeration Observer and Iterator in the platform from day one 1.1 (1997) Inner classes, event listener model Anonymous-class Strategies and Commands; Observer in AWT 1.2 (1998) Collections framework Iterator, Comparator as Strategy, unmodifiable views as Proxy 1.3 (2000) java.lang.reflect.Proxy Dynamic proxies for AOP, remoting and mocks 5 (2004) Generics, enums, annotations, java.util.concurrent, JSR-133 memory model Type-safe factories; enum Singleton and enum Strategy; annotation-driven frameworks; correct double-checked locking with volatile 6 (2006) Public ServiceLoader SPI and plugin discovery 7 (2011) try-with-resources, invokedynamic, MethodHandles Resource handling without finally blocks; foundation for lambdas 8 LTS (2014) Lambdas, method references, streams, Optional, default methods, java.time, CompletableFuture Strategy, Command and Observer as lambdas; Template Method via higher-order functions; interfaces evolve with defaults; injectable Clock 9 (2017) JPMS modules, Flow (reactive streams), VarHandle, List.of factories, Observable deprecated Enforced encapsulation; standard publish/subscribe interfaces; static factories everywhere 10 (2018) var Less noise around builders and factories 11 LTS (2018) HttpClient Standard client for adapters to remote services 14 (2020) Switch expressions Strategy and State selection as expressions 15 (2020) Text blocks, hidden classes Readable templates; lambda and proxy classes as hidden classes 16 (2021) Records, pattern matching for instanceof Value objects, DTOs and immutable builders' results in one line 17 LTS (2021) Sealed classes, strong encapsulation of JDK internals Closed hierarchies for State and Composite; frameworks must stop deep reflection into the JDK 18 (2022) Core reflection reimplemented with method handles Faster reflective frameworks 19 / 20 (2022–23) Previews of virtual threads, record patterns, scoped values Preparing Java 21 idioms 21 LTS (2023) Virtual threads, record patterns, pattern matching for switch, sequenced collections Visitor becomes an exhaustive switch; thread-per-request is cheap again; fewer reactive pipelines for simple I/O 22 (2024) Unnamed variables and patterns (_), Foreign Function & Memory API Cleaner pattern-matching code; native adapters without JNI 24 (2025) Virtual threads no longer pin on synchronized (JEP 491), AOT class loading cache (JEP 483), Stream gatherers (JEP 485) synchronized is fine with virtual threads again; faster startup for framework-heavy apps; custom stream stages 25 LTS (2025) Scoped values (JEP 506), module import declarations (JEP 511), flexible constructor bodies (JEP 513) Context propagation without ThreadLocal; validation before super(...) in constructors

docs.title: The same Strategy across Java versions
docs.text:
// Java 1.1 to 7: anonymous class
DeliveryFee fee = new DeliveryFee() {
    public long feePaise(long basket) { return basket >= 50000 ? 0 : 2900; }
};

// Java 8+: lambda
DeliveryFee fee = basket -> basket >= 50000 ? 0 : 2900;

// Java 21: sealed types and pattern matching when the strategy needs data
sealed interface FeeRule permits FreeAbove, Flat {}
record FreeAbove(long thresholdPaise, long feePaise) implements FeeRule {}
record Flat(long feePaise) implements FeeRule {}

long fee(FeeRule rule, long basket) {
    return switch (rule) {
        case FreeAbove(long t, long f) -> basket >= t ? 0 : f;
        case Flat(long f) -> f;
    };
}
